stories.headline: The True Story of the Dewey Lake Monster: The Week Dewey Lake Went Wild
stories.short: The week Dewey Lake went wild
stories.dek: In June 1964, berry pickers near Dewey Lake said they saw something huge and hairy at the edge of the dark. Within days the back roads jammed, armed men walked the fields, and Chicago papers called Sister Lakes “Monster Town, U.S.A.” The monster never turned up. But the road to Dewey Lake had a warning on it long before, written on a tree in red chalk.
stories.sdek: A real panic, empty berry fields, no monster, and a red-chalk warning on the road from long before.
pic: /img/news/the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild
Two halves: a sepia photograph of a survey party posing with a Bigfoot, and a 1964 night scene of men with flashlights and rifles in a strawberry field, with a tall hairy figure at the tree line
The 1964 scare was real.
stories.tldr:
In June 1964, strawberry pickers near Dewey Lake, west of Dowagiac, said they had seen a hairy thing about nine feet tall with red eyes. For a week the Sister Lakes country went wild: front-page headlines in Detroit, traffic jams, armed hunters in the fields, a $1,000 reward and “monster burgers.” The searches found nothing, and the papers called it nonexistent.

But the county’s oldest books hold older frights: a blood-drinking “monster” cat, a serpent in neighboring Indian Lake, and a warning chalked in red on a tree at a fork in the road. Read against the old township map, that warning, “Turn to the left and go to the Devil,” pointed down the road to Dewey’s Lake. And the reports have never quite stopped.
body: Sister Lakes, Mich. It was the second week of June 1964, and the strawberries were ripe. Out by Dewey Lake, the pickers worked the rows until the light went. Then, on the night of 9 June, some of them came out of the fields saying they had seen something standing at the edge of the dark. Something big. Something covered in hair.
The sheriff’s men drove out with flashlights. They walked the rows and the tree line. They found nothing.

Within two days, that nothing was on the front page of The Detroit News. Cars crawled bumper to bumper down the back roads. Men with rifles walked the fields after dark. The pickers would not go back in. Chicago papers gave Sister Lakes a new name, “Monster Town, U.S.A.” And then, within a week, it was gone, as if it had never been there at all.

We went back to what the papers printed that week. Then we went back further, into the county’s own oldest books, and found that the road to Dewey Lake had a warning on it long before anyone saw a monster. It was written on a tree. In red.

How to read this page

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known); a New finding is something we found in the record that we could not find in any earlier telling. Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

What
A reported hairy, man-like “monster,” said to stand far taller than a man
Where
The farms and berry fields near Dewey Lake, in the Sister Lakes country west of Dowagiac, Silver Creek Township, Cass County, Michigan
When
First reported on 9 June 1964; the scare had faded within about a week
Coverage
The front page of The Detroit News on 11 and 12 June 1964; the South Bend Tribune; the Chicago papers
Described as
About nine feet tall and 500 pounds, with a black, leathery face and red eyes (the first witnesses, as reported)
Result
Searches found no creature; a $1,000 reward was offered and withdrawn
Before it
A red-chalk warning on the road to Dewey’s Lake about 1839; a “sea serpent” in neighboring Indian Lake in 1898
Our verdict
The scare was real and drew national notice. There is no evidence of any creature.
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • It was front-page news in Detroit. The Detroit News of 11 June 1964 ran “Frankenstein Snarl of Traffic Loosed by ‘Monster’ Hunt” on page one.
  • The berry pickers stayed out of the fields. The next day’s front page: “‘Monster’ Scare Idles Pickers.”
  • Searches found nothing. By 12 June the South Bend Tribune called the monster “nonexistent.”
  • The road had a warning on it long before. The county history of 1882 tells of a tree by the road to Dewey’s Lake, marked in red chalk: “Turn to the left and go to the Devil.”
  • It was not the first thing in the dark. The same old books tell of a blood-drinking “monster” cat in Volinia Township, and papers of 1898 told of a serpent in Indian Lake, next door to Dewey.

What it does not show, yet

  • What, if anything, people actually saw.
  • The first witnesses’ own words, on the page. We have their description as Robert Atkinson gathered it from the 1964 papers: nine feet, 500 pounds, a black face, red eyes.
  • Who led the search on the first nights. Atkinson names the sheriff, Robert Dool; one dealer’s note names another man.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are nine things people say about the Dewey Lake Monster and the country around it. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“The monster scare was front-page news in Detroit.”

True

The Detroit News put it on page one on 11 and 12 June 1964.

“Police caught, or photographed, the creature.”

False

The searches found nothing, and by 12 June the South Bend Tribune called the monster “nonexistent.”

“Berry pickers refused to go into the fields.”

True

“‘Monster’ Scare Idles Pickers,” said The Detroit News of 12 June 1964, with “Workers Afraid To Go Into Fields.” It was strawberry season.

“The first witnesses said it stood about nine feet tall.”

True, as reported

About nine feet and 500 pounds is what the first witnesses told the deputies, as Robert Atkinson gathers the 1964 reports. A woman who saw it on 11 June said seven feet. The ten feet of some later tellings came later still.

“It was said to cry like a baby.”

True, as told

The story told in the Sister Lakes country today, as Visit Southwest Michigan tells it: a large, hairy creature with glowing red eyes, and “it cried, like a baby.”

“There was a $1,000 reward for it.”

True

A local beer distributor offered $1,000 for the monster taken alive by 22 June, then withdrew it at the sheriff’s request when the calls poured in (as Atkinson reports).

“Someone once warned travelers off the road to Dewey Lake.”

True

The county history of 1882 (p. 356): on a peeled tree at the fork, in red chalk, “Turn to the left and go to the Devil.”

“The Dewey Lake Monster has been called a Sasquatch.”

True

The Wikipedia article on it gives the name “Sister Lakes Sasquatch.” And in 2001, near Dowagiac, two friends reported a large, hairy, ape-like figure.

“An old county book calls a creature here a “monster.””

True

The 1882 history, telling of a great cat in Volinia Township: “the monster had killed a colt … and sucked its blood” (p. 285).
## Before the headlines

DocumentedThe thing at Dewey Lake did not arrive in June 1964. According to Robert Atkinson’s survey of the 1964 papers, people had been reporting a large, hairy creature on two legs since 1962, among the cherry orchards, the berry patches and the swampland south of the lake. Most of them kept quiet. Nobody wants to be the one who saw the monster. In June the sheriff’s deputies told the press the sightings had come on and off for nearly two years.
ReadingTwo summers of silence, then. Two summers of people coming in from the fields and not saying what they had seen at the tree line.
## Tuesday night, 9 June

DocumentedThe call came from the farm of Mrs. Evelyn Utrup, south of Dewey Lake in Silver Creek Township. Seasonal workers had driven onto the farm after dark: Gordon Brown, who was twenty-five, his wife Mary, who was seventeen, his brother Randall, and a girl from a neighboring place. Between the barn and a shed, they said, they saw something large.

DocumentedThe Brown brothers went after it with a flashlight, about three hundred yards, as Robert Atkinson reconstructs it from the 1964 papers. Then they understood that the tree they had just passed was not a tree. It was the thing, standing still, letting them go by. They ran.

DocumentedWhat they told the deputies is the description the whole country would repeat: about nine feet tall, some five hundred pounds, a black, leathery face, and eyes that glowed red. It made a sound, they said, like a baby crying, or a goose honking.

DocumentedMrs. Utrup said she had never actually seen it. But she had heard it, often, outside, in the summers. Once, she said, it had chased her into the house, and its stamping had shaken the ground and the house with it.

DocumentedThe deputies found a track: three and three-quarter inches across the heel, six inches wide across the middle. They poured plaster into it. The soil was sand, and the cast came out soft and uncertain.
ReadingRead that line again: often, in the summers. Whatever was out there, by her account, had been coming around for a long time before anyone picked up a telephone.
## Wednesday, 10 June

DocumentedBy morning someone had nailed up a sign, MONSTER, with an arrow pointing down the road to the Utrup farm. The deputies took it down. It did not matter. A radio newscaster in Benton Harbor told his listeners, wrongly, that the Cass County authorities wanted help hunting the creature, and the St. Joseph Herald-Press ran the story under “Monster Chases Woman!”

DocumentedThat night they came. Men drove the back roads with shotguns, rifles, tire irons and knives, some from as far away as Ohio; the license plates were from Indiana and Illinois too. The deputies spent the night directing traffic and sending would-be posses home. Officers came over from Van Buren County to help. At one stop they took a loaded magnum revolver from three boys from the Detroit area; at another, baseball bats from seven more; at another, tire irons and clubs from a caravan of eight carloads of teenagers. The crowd did not thin until about three in the morning.
## Thursday morning, 11 June

DocumentedAt a quarter past nine in broad daylight, three girls were walking near Swisher Street and Town Hall Road: Joyce Smith, thirteen, and two sisters, Gail Clayton, thirteen, and Patsy Clayton, twelve. Something crossed the road in front of them. It walked on two legs.

DocumentedJoyce Smith fainted. The Clayton sisters brought her round, and the three of them ran to the nearest house to call the police. Dowagiac’s police chief, Richard Wild, passed the call to the sheriff. Two sheriff’s cars came, and a conservation officer, and a State Police plane was called for. They found nothing.

DocumentedPatsy Clayton had the best look. It was seven feet tall, she said, with a black face, and it was “definitely not human.” Joyce Smith said it looked like a bear, but it walked on its hind legs.

ReadingThe road names are older than the monster. On the Silver Creek Township plat of about 1928, “S. Swisher” holds 160 acres in Section 8, the section that runs down from the south shore of Dewey Lake. Swisher Street very likely carries that family’s name.
DocumentedThat day’s Detroit News put it across the top of page one: “Frankenstein Snarl of Traffic Loosed by ‘Monster’ Hunt.”
## Friday, 12 June

DocumentedRobert Walker of Dowagiac came forward with what he called “big ape tracks” in the woods near Dewey Lake. He said he had seen the creature himself the summer before, and had not wanted to say so. He knew its nightly rounds, he said, and the commotion had driven it off: “It hasn’t showed up for two nights: it shows he is scared.” The deputies who looked at his tracks thought they looked more like a dog’s.

DocumentedIn Chicago, Chicago’s American put the monster on its front page. Its reporter, Michael McGovern, had asked Mary Brown to draw what she saw, in his notebook, balanced on an oilcan. The paper ran her drawing under the words “Have YOU Seen THIS Monster?” and quoted her husband: “It was an extreee giant looking thing, a whale of a joker.”

DocumentedThe Detroit News had a different worry: “‘Monster’ Scare Idles Pickers,” with “Workers Afraid To Go Into Fields.” Among the migrant families who had come north for the berry harvest, a rumor had spread that the monster had eaten four people. Some families packed up and left. Some of those who stayed, Atkinson writes, slept locked in their cars.

ReadingIt is easy to laugh at the monster. It is harder to laugh at a family sleeping in a car with the doors locked, a long way from home, in a country where something was said to walk the fields at night.
## Monster Town, U.S.A.

DocumentedSister Lakes did what a resort town does with a crowd. The taverns poured “Monster Brew.” Reid’s Drive-In put a stuffed monster out front to sell its “Monster Burger.” Harvey’s East variety store sold a “Monster Hunting Kit” for $7.95: a baseball bat, a wooden mallet, an arrow, a net and a flashlight (other papers add a squirt gun and a stake). Gas stations sold “getaway gas.” The radio station at St. Joseph, WSJM, played monster songs between its live reports, and a Dowagiac theater booked The Horror of Party Beach and The Curse of the Living Corpse. A group calling itself the Monster Boosters promoted the whole thing; the Sister Lakes Chamber of Commerce said it had nothing to do with it.

DocumentedThen came the money. Jack Handly, a beer distributor, offered $1,000 for the monster taken alive by five o’clock on 22 June. The sheriff, Robert Dool, was already swamped with calls from around the world. He persuaded Handly to withdraw it.

DocumentedThere was gunfire only once. A hunter saw a black shape in the dark, fired twice and missed. It was a Shetland pony. Chicago’s American had the headline: “Itchy Gun Fingers Blast Away at Pony.”

DocumentedNot everyone was amused. “They call us ‘Beast Town’ now in Detroit,” a Dowagiac Daily News columnist wrote. “Gives us a rather uncouth image doesn’t it.” The Chicago papers, by then, were calling the place “Monster Town, U.S.A.”
DocumentedOn Saturday and Sunday, 13 and 14 June, there were no more sightings. The hunters went back to work. The summer people went back to the water.
## What the experts said

DocumentedTwo University of Michigan zoologists were asked what it could be. As Atkinson quotes the 1964 press, Dr. William H. Burt thought of a bear: “When they get up on their hind legs … they might be five or six feet.” Professor Frank Eggelton doubted it, “Bears don’t stand on their hind feet too often,” and suspected an escaped circus gorilla. No zoo or circus reported an animal missing.

DocumentedThe county officials liked the bear. Dick and Dorothy Grabemeyer, who farmed by the swampland near Dewey Lake, said they had seen bears there before. But the Brown brothers were hunters, and they insisted it was no bear; and every witness said it walked, a long way, on two legs.

New findingThe Grabemeyers’ name is on the old map too. The township plat of about 1928 shows “F. W. Grabemeyer” on 119 acres in Section 6, in the north-west corner of the township, a mile or so west of Dewey Lake.

ReadingAnd the red eyes? Many animals have a mirror at the back of the eye that throws a flashlight beam straight back: deer, raccoons, dogs, bears. Human eyes do not. Every night-time witness in 1964 saw red eyes. Whatever was out there, it was looking back at them.

DocumentedBy 12 June the South Bend Tribune’s headline read “Dewey Lake ‘Monster Is Nonexistent.’” By 14 June it was “‘Hairy Monster’ Scare Lessens”; nobody, the paper said, “seems frightened anymore.” On 18 June the Dowagiac Daily News ran “Policeman Says ‘No Monster.’”
DocumentedIn 1983 the Tribune’s “Action Line” column looked back and suggested the monster had been dreamed up by strawberry pickers who had been drinking.
ReadingNonexistent, said the paper. Nobody frightened anymore. It is the kind of thing people say in daylight.
## The copycats

DocumentedWithin a week the monster had imitators. Early on 17 June, a hundred and thirty miles north at Ionia, two brothers reported a ten-foot hairy creature crossing Interstate 96. A State Police trooper and his tracking dog, Jocko, chased a figure about six feet tall into the dark; it escaped, leaving a rubber glove and tufts of dry hair behind. It was a young man in a fur coat. Ionia officers also picked up eight teenagers in ponchos, sitting on one another’s shoulders to look taller.

DocumentedThe next summer, in August 1965, the Benton Harbor News-Palladium reported that the monster which “caused a flurry in this area last summer” had moved to Monroe, on Lake Erie, where two women said it attacked them. The police there called it a hoax.
ReadingEvery hoax made the next report easier to dismiss. That is the trouble with a hoax: it does not only fool people. It teaches them to stop listening.
## The road with a warning on it

DocumentedDewey Lake takes its name from a pioneer. The county history of 1882 says Henry Dewey moved to Silver Creek because “the land in the vicinity of the lake which bears his name possessed many attractions, among others its proximity to the lake, which at the time was alive with fish.”

DocumentedOn the same page is an older fright. Timothy Treat brought his family from Aurora, New York, in the autumn of 1837, lived two years at Ontwa, and then moved on to Silver Creek. They came in from the south. At Indian Lake they found a track running north-east, “winding around fallen trees and swamps.” And “at the southeast corner of Section 16 the road forked, one branch leading to Dewey’s Lake, the other to their future home.”

DocumentedSomeone had been there before them. “Some disconsolate emigrant had preceded them,” the book says, “and evidently was not favorably impressed with the country to which they were going.” He had stripped the bark from a tree, and on the bare wood he had written in red chalk:
“Turn to the left and go to the Devil.”

ReadingThe book never says which branch was the left one. But the map can. Dewey Lake lies across Sections 4, 5, 8 and 9 of Silver Creek Township, north-west of Section 16. Indian Lake lies in Sections 30 and 31, in the south-west corner. A traveler coming up the track from Indian Lake toward the north-east, and reaching the south-east corner of Section 16, would have to bear left, to the north-west, to reach Dewey’s Lake.
New findingRead that way, the warning was not a joke about the whole country. It pointed one way. Turn to the left, it said, and go to the Devil. The left-hand road went to Dewey’s Lake.
ReadingThe Treats came to the fork about 1839, so the warning was already old by then, and its writer long gone. The family took the other branch, and the book moves on.
New findingWe have found no modern telling of the Dewey Lake Monster that mentions the red-chalk sign on the road to “Dewey’s Lake,” or that names the lake’s pioneer from the 1882 history.
## Older things in the dark
The monster of 1964 was not the first thing the people of this country saw at the edge of the trees. The old county books keep a few others.

DocumentedThe cat on the leaning tree. In Volinia Township, north-east of Dowagiac, in the early days, families who let their fire go out sent a child to a neighbor’s to borrow coals. The 1882 history tells what one boy saw: “Reuben F. Gard was sent on such an errand one frosty morning to the house of George Newton, and when there remarked that he saw an immense cat, crouched on a tree that leaned over the path he passed along.”

DocumentedThe book goes on: “A panther at once suggested itself, and a search showed where the monster had killed a colt belonging to D. C. Squires, and sucked its blood. It was a narrow escape.” (History of Cass County, 1882, p. 285.)

DocumentedThe cries on the road home. In Porter Township, the same book says, Mr. and Mrs. Rinehart, coming home from church in Newberg, “were followed for several miles by a panther, who encircled them while emitting his blood-curdling cries,” until it left them near Birch Lake (p. 303).

ReadingThose were real animals: the cougar was native to Michigan until it was wiped out in the early 1900s. But notice the word the old historian reached for. In 1882, in plain print, it was already “the monster.”

DocumentedThe serpent next door. In October 1898, Michigan papers reported “a huge sea serpent” troubling people at “spring-fed Indian Lake, in Michigan’s southwest,” as a modern article quotes the Isabella County Enterprise of 14 October. Two weeks later the Evart Review had an answer: “an otter and a muskalonge.” In July 1899 it was back. The Gladwin County Record, as quoted, said it could “propel itself through the water like an arrow,” and that people feared it “might suddenly rise some time under a boat.”

ReadingWhich Indian Lake? Michigan has more than one. But the Evart Review, as quoted, gave the lake as 500 acres with no inlet or outlet, and Cass County’s spring-fed Indian Lake covers about 506 acres. And the 1899 report, as the same article gives it, speaks of “Cass county’s unknown beast.” Everything points here: to the lake where the Treats picked up the track toward the fork, a few miles from Dewey.
OpenWe have not yet read those three papers ourselves, only as a modern article quotes them.
## Something that learned to keep its distance

Drive the back roads of this valley at dusk and you will see how much of it is still dark. Between the towns lie river bottoms and tamarack swamps, wet woods along the creeks, woodlots no one has cut in a lifetime, and lakes whose far shores show no lights at all. A few miles from Dewey Lake, the Dowagiac Woods alone keeps 384 acres of forest, the Michigan Nature Association’s largest sanctuary in the Lower Peninsula.

ReadingCountry like that keeps its secrets. A deer can live a whole life a hundred yards from a road and never be seen. So can a fox, a bobcat, a mink. And the stories people tell about this country all share a shape: something seen at the edge of the light, at the edge of the trees, watching. Something that does not come closer. Something that, if it is there at all, has learned to stay away.
DocumentedPeople have another name for the Dewey Lake Monster now. The Wikipedia article on it calls it the “Sister Lakes Sasquatch.” Another word for Sasquatch is Bigfoot.

DocumentedAnd it has not been reported only once. In the database of the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization, a group that collects such reports, Michigan has 227 listings, three of them in Cass County. One comes from near Dowagiac, on 27 July 2001, at about half past two in the morning. Two friends, roused by a frightened goose and the sound of snapping branches, took their flashlights outside and found, they said, a large, hairy, ape-like figure crouched in a ditch about thirty feet away. For some ten minutes it froze whenever the lights were on it and stirred when they went off. When the batteries began to fade, one of them ran in for the car keys, to use the headlights. When he came back, it was gone.

DocumentedWiden the circle and the count climbs. The same database lists 227 reports in Michigan, 82 in Indiana, 305 in Illinois and 335 in Ohio: 949 in the four Great Lakes states closest to this valley. Around this valley alone it lists three in Cass County, three in Berrien, three in Kalamazoo, one in St. Joseph County, Indiana, one in Elkhart County and two in La Porte.

DocumentedAcross the country, the same group says it has received nearly 75,000 reports since the 1990s, and counts some 5,500 of them as credible. The state-by-state counts in its database add up to more than 5,700.

ReadingNone of that is proof of anything. A report is a story someone tells; it is not a body, or a bone, or a photograph that holds up. But it is worth knowing that the pickers of 1964 were not the last people in this valley to come in from the dark with that look on their faces. Thirty-seven years later, a few miles away, two more did. And somewhere out past the last porch light, in the swamps and the river bottoms and the long dark woods, the valley is keeping its counsel.
## Other footsteps in the valley

The Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization’s database is only one collection of stories, and nobody checks them all. But read the reports it holds for the counties around this valley one after another, as we did, and something begins to show: the same kind of night, the same kind of place, the same dog that will not go on.

DocumentedNear Union, Cass County, the late 1960s. A few years after Dewey Lake, a summer-camp riding instructor was out on a trail near the camp in the evening, in the hardwoods near U.S. 12, toward the St. Joseph River, when her horse spooked and bolted. Something large and pale kept pace with them through the trees, running alongside, about as tall as she was in the saddle. She let the horse run. The report, given years later by her nephew, says she was badly frightened and rarely spoke of it again.

DocumentedStevensville, Berrien County, a winter night about 1974. In a house near the wooded dunes and a cemetery, a twelve-year-old was babysitting four younger brothers when a sound came from right outside the living-room window: a “howling scream that sounded like something dying,” which turned, as it went on, into a gurgling, low, laugh-like chuckle. The child waited half an hour, then went out with a flashlight. There was fresh snow on the ground. There were no tracks. And the family dog was gone.

DocumentedNear Buchanan, February 1993. On a cloudy Saturday morning a hunter went looking for his German shepherd at a beaver pond among the orchards. What he took at first for a clump of dark bushes resolved into a shoulder, an arm and a head. He put it at seven to eight feet, “very muscular.” It turned, took two steps and was gone into the brush. His dog would not go near the place afterward.
DocumentedNear Dowagiac, July 2001. The goose, the snapping branches, the thing in the ditch that froze in the flashlight beam, told above.
DocumentedNear Plainwell, May 2002. North up the Kalamazoo, four people reported a sighting together, at night.

DocumentedOsceola, Indiana, May 2008. At half past three on a Sunday morning, by the swamps and marsh along Baugo Creek, a man heard a howl he had never heard before and could not name. His dog, which went after anything that moved outside, ran out the door, turned straight around and came back in without a sound. It “sent chills up my spine,” he wrote.

DocumentedThe Paw Paw Lake country, June 2012. At dusk, in the woods between Lake Michigan and Paw Paw Lake, a man walking his dog heard what sounded like a large stick break. The dog stared into the trees, “the fur on the back of his neck … standing straight up.” In the morning there was a print in the soil, he said, five inches longer than his own shoe, sunk deep where his own weight left no mark. The investigator noted that the photograph was poorly defined, and could have been made by a person.

ReadingNow look at them together. Almost every one is at the edge of water: a lake, a river, a creek, a beaver pond, a swamp. Almost every one is at the edge of the dark: dusk, night, the early hours. Again and again the first witness is not a person but a dog, or a horse, or a goose. And again and again, the thing does not come closer. It watches, or it paces, or it turns and takes two steps and is gone.

ReadingThere are plain explanations for every one of them, and they deserve to be said. A red fox’s scream can sound like a woman, or a child. A bear standing up is taller than a man, and a man in camouflage in a swamp can look like a bush. A goose and a dog will panic at a raccoon. People who have heard a story tend to see it. And a report is not a body, or a bone, or a photograph that holds up; none of these has been proved.
OpenBut none of them has been explained, either. Each one is a story somebody told, from somewhere in this valley, about a night they never forgot.
## The legend that would not die
DocumentedThe monster outlived the week that made it. The sellers of 1964 had their monster burgers and their monster getaway gas; a Sister Lakes brewery has since brewed a “Dewey Lake Monster” beer.

ReadingThat is how a legend works. The papers said it was nonexistent, and the sheriff called off the reward, and the pickers went back into the fields. But the name stayed. Sixty years on, people who never heard of the 1964 headlines still know there is something called the Dewey Lake Monster, and still, now and then, slow the car on the back roads at dusk and look into the trees.
## If you go out there

After dark at the Sister Lakes

Stay on the public roads, and leave the farms, the fields and the private shores alone. Turn the engine off. Wait. Listen for the frogs to stop, the way they do when something moves. And if, out past the last porch light, you hear what sounds like a baby crying in the trees, you will know, at least, that you are not the first.
## A timeline of frights

• Early days Volinia Township: a boy sees “an immense cat” on a leaning tree; a colt is found killed, its blood drained.
  • Pioneer days Porter Township: a panther follows a couple home from church for miles, “emitting his blood-curdling cries.”
  • About 1839 The fork at Section 16: “Turn to the left and go to the Devil,” in red chalk on a peeled tree.
  • Oct 1898 Michigan papers report “a huge sea serpent” in a spring-fed Indian Lake; two weeks later, an otter and a muskie.
  • July 1899 The Indian Lake beast is back, said to move “through the water like an arrow.”
  • 1962–64 Reports of a large, hairy thing on two legs south of Dewey Lake; most witnesses keep quiet.
  • 9 June 1964 The Utrup farm: the Browns see it between the barn and a shed, and chase a “tree” that is not a tree.
  • 10 June 1964 A MONSTER sign, a radio appeal, and a night of armed hunters on the back roads.
  • 11 June 1964 9:15 a.m.: three girls see it cross the road on two legs. One faints.
  • 11–12 June 1964 Front page of The Detroit News: the traffic, the hunt, the empty berry fields.
  • 12–14 June 1964 South Bend Tribune: the monster is “nonexistent”; nobody “seems frightened anymore.”
  • 12 June 1964 “Big ape tracks”; Mary Brown’s drawing on the front page in Chicago; berry pickers sleep in their cars.
  • 17 June 1964 Ionia: a young man in a fur coat on I-96. The first copycat.
  • 18 June 1964 Dowagiac Daily News: “Policeman Says ‘No Monster.’”
  • 1983 The Tribune looks back and blames strawberry pickers who had been drinking.
  • Aug 1965 The Benton Harbor paper reports the monster has “moved” to Monroe. A hoax, say the police there.
  • Late 1960s Near Union: something pale runs alongside a bolting horse through the trees.
  • About 1974 Stevensville: a scream like something dying, then a low chuckle. Fresh snow, no tracks.
  • Feb 1993 Near Buchanan: a dark, muscular figure at a beaver pond, seven or eight feet tall.
  • 27 July 2001 Near Dowagiac, 2:30 in the morning: two friends with flashlights report a large, hairy figure crouched in a ditch. Then it is gone.
  • May 2002 Near Plainwell: four witnesses, one night sighting.
  • May 2008 Osceola, Indiana: a howl by Baugo Creek, and a dog that will not go out.
  • June 2012 The Paw Paw Lake country: a snapping stick, a dog’s raised hackles, a print in the morning.
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, or if your family was there in June 1964, please write to us.

1. Who led the search? Robert Atkinson names the sheriff, Robert Dool; a dealer’s note names Paul Parrish. The Dowagiac Daily News of 11 June 1964, “Daily News Goes On ‘Monster’ Hunt With Cass County Sheriff’s Men,” should settle who was in the fields.
  2. The first descriptions, on the page. Nine feet, 500 pounds, a black face and red eyes come to us through Atkinson’s survey; the papers of 10 to 12 June should show them in print.
  3. The reward, on the page. The $1,000 offer and its withdrawal should be in the Dowagiac Daily News of mid-June 1964.
  4. Where did the Treats settle? The left-hand road went to Dewey’s Lake. Their own land, on the right-hand road, should be in the Silver Creek land entries.
  5. The serpent’s first print. The 1898 and 1899 papers point to Cass County’s Indian Lake; the first local paper to print it, in the Dowagiac and Cassopolis weeklies of October 1898, should confirm it.

stories.headline: The Kentucky Raid of 1847
stories.dek: In the summer of 1847 a party of Kentuckians came to the Quaker farms of Cass County to carry nine people back into slavery. Their neighbors stopped them at O’Dell’s mill, a hearing at Cassopolis set the nine free, and the lawsuits ran on for five years. We went back to the papers of 1847, the court files and the county histories.
stories.sdek: Nine people seized, several hundred neighbors, one hearing at Cassopolis, and fifty-two on the road to Canada.
pic: /img/news/the-kentucky-raid-of-1847
The opening of the chapter headed THE KENTUCKY RAID in Rogers’s History of Cass County, 1875
The chapter heading in Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875), p. 131. Internet Archive.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. In the summer of 1847 a party of Kentuckians rode into Cass County to take back people who had escaped from slavery and were living and working on the Quaker farms around Young’s Prairie. In one night they seized nine. By the next morning the neighbors had caught up with them near O’Dell’s mill, at what is now Vandalia, and a crowd of several hundred walked raiders and captives together to Cassopolis. There a county commissioner heard the case and set the nine free, and that same day a party of fifty-two started north for Canada.

The story is told every year in Cass County, and some of what is told has grown in the telling. We went back to what was written at the time: the Covington, Kentucky, newspaper that spoke for the raiders, the federal court papers, a freedom seeker’s own account, and the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known); a New finding is something we found in the record that we could not find in any earlier publication. Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

When
Most likely Friday, 13 August 1847, for the raid and the stand near O’Dell’s mill, and Monday, 16 August, for the hearing at Cassopolis (our reading of a letter written at Niles on 21 August)
Where
The Quaker farms of Penn and Calvin townships, Cass County, Michigan; O’Dell’s mill, now Vandalia; the courthouse town of Cassopolis
Who came
A dozen or more men from Kenton and Boone counties, Kentucky: “some 12 or 15,” said their home paper; “12 or 13,” said a Centreville paper; “sixteen,” said a Niles eyewitness
Who was taken
Nine people, seized at the farms of Josiah Osborn, Stephen Bogue, Zachariah Shugart and others
What happened
A commissioner, Ebenezer McIlvain, freed all nine: the Kentuckians had no certified copy of the laws that made them slaves
Afterward
Fifty-two freedom seekers left for Canada from Ishmael Lee’s farm; the slaveholders sued the Quakers in federal court at Detroit; the main suits ended in 1851–52
Why it matters
One of the grievances of the slave states in the years before the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The raiders came from northern Kentucky. Their own paper, the Covington Licking Valley Register, called the runaways people “from this county” (Kenton), and others came from Boone County.
  • Nine people were seized, and several hundred neighbors stopped the raiders near O’Dell’s mill and took everyone to Cassopolis.
  • A commissioner freed the nine because no certified copy of Kentucky’s slave laws was offered in evidence. A Niles man who was there wrote that the commissioner also held that only a United States officer could certify ownership.
  • It was over within days. A letter written at Niles on Saturday, 21 August 1847, already tells of the seizure “on Friday morning last” and of the nine set free.
  • Fifty-two freedom seekers left for Canada from Ishmael Lee’s farm, in the charge of Zachariah Shugart.
  • The slaveholders sued in federal court. The jury disagreed in January 1851; two defendants settled, and the suits against Josiah Osborn and Stephen Bogue were dismissed in 1852.

What it does not show, yet

  • The exact day, in so many words. No paper of 1847 that we have found prints it; the Niles letter of 21 August points to Friday, 13 August.
  • What the Niles Republican and the Detroit papers said. They survive on microfilm and in subscription archives, and we have not yet read them.
  • The sum Nicholson and Lee paid. The settlement paper names none.
  • Any record that Henry Clay or anyone in Congress spoke of the Cass County raid in 1850.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are eight things people say about the raid. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“The raiders came from Bourbon County, Kentucky.”

Not as the record shows

The county histories say Bourbon, but the raiders’ own Covington paper wrote of runaways “from this county,” Kenton, and the freedom seekers’ accounts name Boone County.

“A commissioner freed the nine because there was no copy of Kentucky’s slave laws.”

True

Rogers (1875, p. 141): McIlvain decided against the Kentuckians “on the ground that there was no certified copy of the statutes of Kentucky offered in evidence.” Their own paper complained of “a demand … to prove that slavery was tolerated by the Constitution of Kentucky!”

“Hundreds of local people turned out to stop the raiders.”

True

The Kentucky paper itself said “a furious mob of several hundred.” The 1882 history says “at least three hundred.”

“Henry Clay cited the Cass County raid in the Senate.”

No record

We have found no record of it. The Senate report behind the 1850 law speaks of the Marshall case, not Cass County.

“The raiders’ wagon was rolled into Birch Lake.”

No record before the 1930s

The Kentucky paper of 17 September 1847 says the wagon’s wheels were taken, but that it “was then delivered up.” The earliest telling of the lake story we know of is in newspapers of 1936–37.

“Fifty-two freedom seekers left for Canada together.”

True, as printed

Rogers (1875, p. 141): at Ishmael Lee’s farm “a party of fifty-two runaway slaves was made up, put in charge of Zachariah Shugert and started toward Canada.”

“The Quakers won the federal case outright.”

No

The jury disagreed in January 1851. Two defendants then settled with the slaveholders’ lawyer, and the suits against Josiah Osborn and Stephen Bogue were dismissed in 1852.

“A thousand freedom seekers passed through Cass County.”

No count

The “thousand” was Dr. Nathan Thomas’s estimate for his own station at Schoolcraft. The 1882 history guessed “probably not less than fifteen hundred” through Cass County, which is a guess, not a count.
## The Quaker line

DocumentedCass County lay on what the county history of 1875 called the “Quaker line,” a chain of Quaker settlements reaching up from the Ohio River through Indiana, at which freedom seekers “were harbored, fed and directed on their way.” Rogers names two stations in the county, “kept by Stephen Bogue and Zachariah Shugert.”

DocumentedIn the spring of 1847 two groups escaped from northern Kentucky. A Cincinnati paper of 28 April reported a “Grand Stampede” of twenty to twenty-five people from Kenton County, and a second party came from Boone County. One of them, Perry Sanford, told a Battle Creek paper in 1884: “Into that boat eleven of us crowded.” Many of them stopped on the Quaker farms of Young’s Prairie and stayed to work. Zachariah Shugart’s own account book lists arrivals that May.
ReadingThey had reason to think they were far enough away. They were not. The slaveholders of Kenton and Boone counties found out where they were.
## The raid

DocumentedAbout the first of August, Rogers says, “a party of thirteen men” arrived at Battle Creek, some of them posing as salesmen, and were turned away by Erastus Hussey and the townspeople there. In Cincinnati, the Quaker Levi Coffin got warning of the plan and sent a messenger to Young’s Prairie, but, he wrote, the raiders had “started several days earlier.”

DocumentedThey came in the night, working in separate parties, to the farms of Josiah Osborn, Stephen Bogue, Zachariah Shugart and the East settlement. Perry Sanford remembered it: “About 4 o’clock, there came a knock at the door.” He fought and got away through a cornfield. Nine people were taken.

DocumentedA man who saw the end of it wrote from Niles on Saturday, 21 August: “On Friday morning last, a gang of Kentuckians, to the number of sixteen, … commenced their diabolical work just before the break of day, after having divided themselves into companies of three and four each; being armed with carbines, pistols, dirks, &c.” His letter, signed J. I. Alexander, was printed in Ann Arbor’s antislavery paper, the Signal of Liberty, on 28 August, and was copied as far as New York.

DocumentedBy morning the alarm had spread. “In the neighborhood of O’Dell’s mill,” Rogers wrote, the raiders “were speedily surrounded by an excited mob of citizens armed with rifles, shot-guns, straw cutters, axes, clubs and whatever other weapons chance threw in their way, who resolutely opposed their southward progress.”

Documented“A parley was had,” Rogers wrote, “high words and threats exchanged, weapons drawn, and a bloody riot seemed imminent; but, fortunately, more moderate counsels prevailed.” The two sides agreed to go to Cassopolis and put the case to the law. The 1882 history describes the procession: “thirteen Kentuckians, their nine shackled captives and a crowd of at least three hundred citizens.”
## The hearing at Cassopolis

DocumentedAt Cassopolis the Kentuckians were arrested on complaints of kidnapping and trespass, and bailed. Their lawyers sought to hold the nine as fugitives; the freedom seekers’ lawyers, Ezekiel S. Smith and James Sullivan, with James Brown of Niles, asked for a writ of habeas corpus. The county’s own commissioner was away, and the case was heard, “on the third day after the arrests,” by Ebenezer McIlvain, circuit court commissioner of Berrien County.

DocumentedThe Niles letter tells the same days from the inside. The Kentuckians were charged with assault and battery and held to bail “in the sum of three thousand dollars, which they obtained by depositing $900 and their horses in the hands of some of the citizens.” Their trial was “deferred four days to enable them to send to Kalamazoo for counsel.” Meanwhile “two of the friends in Cassopolis came to Niles to obtain a writ of habeas corpus from E. McIlvaine Esq.,” and the writer rode back with them. The Kentuckians asked for time “to send to Indiana for witnesses,” and were refused.

DocumentedMcIlvain decided “adversely to the Kentuckians, on the ground that there was no certified copy of the statutes of Kentucky offered in evidence showing the legal existence of slavery in that State.” The nine were free. The Niles letter gives a second ground: that McIlvain, “being a State officer, had no jurisdiction in the case—that no one but a United States officer could give a certificate of ownership.” The two accounts do not contradict each other.

Documented“Immediately upon the decision,” Rogers goes on, the freed people “were taken in charge by their friends and hurried to the farm of Ishmael Lee, where a party of fifty-two runaway slaves was made up, put in charge of Zachariah Shugert and started toward Canada.” The 1882 history says that Dr. Nathan Thomas and his wife fed the party at Schoolcraft on the way north.
## What Kentucky read

DocumentedThe Covington Licking Valley Register told its readers about it on 3 September 1847, under the heading “INFAMOUS!” A party “of some 12 or 15 gentlemen,” it said, had gone to reclaim “some 20 or 30 Slaves, from this county,” and been met by “a furious mob of several hundred abolitionists.”

DocumentedTwo weeks later the paper printed a “fuller account.” It called McIlvain an “unprincipled scoundrel” who had “no jurisdiction of the case, he being only a county officer, and resided in another county,” and it raged at “a demand of our citizens to prove that slavery was tolerated by the Constitution of Kentucky!”

New findingThe same account gives two details the later histories do not. It says the raiders’ bail came to “something over four thousand dollars,” where the 1882 history, and every account since that we have found, says $2,600; the Niles letter, written within days, says three thousand. And it says the raiders’ baggage wagon, seized by “the demons in the neighborhood” and its wheels taken, “was then delivered up.” The earliest telling we know of the story that the wagon was rolled into Birch Lake, cited by the House Divided project, is in newspapers of 1936–37.
## Five years in court

DocumentedThe slaveholders could not take the nine back, so they went after the people who had helped them. Under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 they sued for the value of the freedom seekers in the federal court at Detroit: Thornton Timberlake against Josiah Osborn and others, and companion suits against Stephen Bogue, Zachariah Shugart, David T. Nicholson, Ishmael Lee, Ebenezer McIlvain and their neighbors. Abner Pratt of Marshall acted for the Kentuckians; Jacob M. Howard of Detroit defended the Quakers.

DocumentedThe county histories date the filing to February 1848; the court dockets, as historians have read them, to January 1849. A Cassopolis doctor who had watched the Kentuckians in the village gave a deposition in April 1850: “I don’t know that I saw any of them use violence at all.” The case was tried before Judge Ross Wilkins over the winter of 1850–51, and in January 1851, says the 1882 history, “it was concluded, the jury disagreeing.”

DocumentedOn 3 December 1851, at Cassopolis, David T. Nicholson and Ishmael Lee signed a paper with the slaveholders’ lawyers: the suit had been “this day settled,” it would be discontinued and “not again to be instituted” against them, and “no judgement fo[r] costs” would be entered for either side. The paper names no sum. The suits against Josiah Osborn and Stephen Bogue were dismissed in February 1852.

ReadingThe amount is told several ways, and three different things have run together. Rogers (1875) says Nicholson paid “$2,755.” The 1882 history says he paid “$1,000 to clear himself and Ishmael Lee,” and that “the total costs of the case, which amounted to about $3,000, were borne by the several defendants”: that $3,000 is the whole defense’s costs, not the settlement. The legal historian D. G. Chardavoyne (2004) gives $1,000 plus costs “estimated at $300 to $500,” and says his figure comes from a letter Nicholson wrote to the Covington Journal in February 1852; that is where the “about $1,300” of later accounts comes from. We have not yet read Nicholson’s letter.

DocumentedThe court files themselves, six suits from Graves, Timberlake and Scott, are digitized and free to read in the National Archives catalog: Timberlake v. Osborn alone runs to 67 pages. Among them is a case no history we know of mentions: United States v. Jonathan Crews, for perjury, against a witness in the Timberlake trial.
## Where the nine went

DocumentedThe suits name the people the Kentuckians claimed. Thornton Timberlake claimed Jonathan, Nancy, Mary, Robert and Gabriel; John L. Graves claimed Joseph, Cena and Benjamin; Charles Scott claimed Lewis. Perry Sanford, telling the story in 1884, named among those taken Joe Sandford, “his wife and daughter,” and the daughter of the man later known as William Casey.

DocumentedOne of them told his own story. In Canada West in the 1850s, Joseph Sanford gave his narrative to the Boston writer Benjamin Drew: “There were thirteen of us started away in company.” It breaks off in Cincinnati, and the next narrative in the book, by John Hatfield, who hid Sanford and his wife there, finishes it: “they were afterwards all captured in Michigan: but they got off before a judge, and were then sent over the line into Canada.”

ReadingLibrary and family research carries several of them further, and we have not yet checked it against the census ourselves. Gabriel took the name James Johnson in Canada and farmed at Colchester, Ontario, where he died in 1915; the Amherstburg Freedom Museum tells his family’s story. The Ughbanks family is traced to Colchester as well, and Joseph and Cena Sanford to Anderdon, near Amherstburg. The family of Lewis Gardner, who became William Casey, is placed by one source in Battle Creek and by another in Canada. Perry Sanford, who got away through the cornfield, lived on in Battle Creek and died there in 1905.
OpenThe old histories say nine were taken, but their own farm-by-farm counts, and the names in the suits, come to ten. Which nine stood before McIlvain is not yet settled.
## Did it change the law?

DocumentedIn March 1847, before the Cass County raid, Kentucky’s legislature had already asked Congress for stronger laws to reclaim fugitives, after a rescue at Marshall, Michigan. The Senate committee’s report of May 1848 rests on the Marshall case and does not mention Cass County.

ReadingThe 1882 county history is the first we have found to tie the Cass raid to the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, and even it is careful: the raid, “with the Van Zant case in Ohio, it had a strong bearing upon the passage of the fugitive slave law of 1850 …” It is fair to call the raid one of the grievances behind the 1850 law. The record we have read does not show that it caused it.
OpenWe have found no record that Henry Clay, or anyone in Congress, named the Cass County raid in the debates of 1850. If you know of one, please tell us.
## How the story is told today

DocumentedThe fullest modern retelling is Cindy Yawkey’s The Kentucky Slave Raid of 1847, Cass County Michigan, written and illustrated by the head docent of the Bonine House and published by the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County about 2019. It goes farm by farm, with her own drawings and a hand-drawn map of the prairie, and it is the version most visitors to Vandalia will meet. The society’s narrated presentation Out of Bondage: The Perry Sanford Story takes its title from Sanford’s own 1884 interview.

DocumentedMuch of it comes straight from the county histories, and checks out against them: the spy who called himself Carpenter and posed as an abolitionist from Worcester County; the Rev. Mr. Stevens taking a baby from a cabin and making it cry until its mother came out of hiding; Perry Sanford’s knock at the door at four in the morning; the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 as the law the Kentuckians stood on.

ReadingHer book dates the raid to “Tuesday, August 17, 1847.” The arithmetic of the old histories points elsewhere. Rogers puts the hearing “on the third day after the arrests,” and the 1882 history says the commissioner “heard the case on Monday.” And a letter dated at Niles on Saturday, 21 August 1847, already reports the nine set free, so the Monday hearing can only have been 16 August, and the raid, three days earlier, Friday the 13th: neither the Tuesday of her book nor the Friday the 20th of most accounts online.

OpenA few details we have not yet found in any record: that twelve-year-old Angeline Osborn hid a mother and daughter in her father’s house, and was later made to testify against him; that forty freedom seekers, not Rogers’s fifty-two, went north from Ishmael Lee’s farm; and that the slaveholders’ suit was first brought in 1850, where the histories and the dockets give 1848 or 1849. Her sources may hold them, and we would like to see them.

DocumentedHer picture book They Have My Shoes, I Have My Freedom, which won a Michigan State History Award in 2016, carries a fictional freedom seeker named Lucinda from Georgia to the Bonine carriage house. We write about it in our story The Bonine House at Vandalia.
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. What day was the raid? Modern accounts give 16, 17 or 20 August 1847. J. I. Alexander’s letter, dated Niles, 21 August 1847, and printed in the Signal of Liberty of 28 August, says the Kentuckians struck “on Friday morning last” and that McIlvain had already freed the nine. With Rogers’s “third day after the arrests” and the 1882 history’s “Monday,” that points to Friday, 13 August for the raid and Monday, 16 August for the hearing. The Cassopolis Advocate’s own account, reprinted in the Covington Licking Valley Register of 15 October 1847, may settle it; we have not yet seen it.
  2. What did the Niles and Detroit papers say? The Niles Republican of 21 and 28 August 1847 survives on microfilm at the Cass District Library’s Local History Branch in Cassopolis and at the Library of Michigan; the Detroit Free Press of 1847 is in subscription archives. Both should be read page by page.
  3. How much did Nicholson and Lee pay? The settlement paper of 3 December 1851 names no sum. The figure most often given, $1,000 plus $300 to $500 in costs, rests on Nicholson’s own letter to the Covington Journal of February 1852, which we have not yet read.
  4. Which nine, and where did they go? The suits name ten people claimed; the histories say nine were taken. Joseph Sanford’s own account and the narrative beside it in Drew’s The Refugee (1856) put him and his wife in Canada after the hearing. The later lives traced by library and family research are still to be checked in the census.
