stories.headline: The Bonine House at Vandalia
stories.dek: A Quaker family from Indiana, a farm of 1,600 acres, an elk park that answered to its owner’s call and sent elk to the King of Italy, and a house now kept by the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County. What the record says about the James E. Bonine House, and what it has yet to show.
stories.sdek: A Quaker farm, an elk park, a King of Italy, and a house that keeps the story of the Underground Railroad.
pic: /img/news/the-bonine-house
The 1882 county history on James E. Bonine: 1,600 acres, the elegant brick house with fine fountain, and the elk and deer park
James E. Bonine’s farm as the county history described it in 1882: History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago, 1882), p. 251. Internet Archive.
body: Vandalia, Mich. At the corner of M-60 and Penn Road, just west of Vandalia, stands a brick house with a tall mansard tower, and across the highway a small Gothic carriage house. They were built, by the society’s account, by James E. Bonine, a Quaker farmer whose family came to Young’s Prairie from Indiana in the 1840s, and since 2010 they have belonged to the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County, which opens them to visitors and tells the story of the freedom seekers who passed through this country before the Civil War.

The house is now the best-known Underground Railroad site in the county. We went back to the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906, and to the first national list of Underground Railroad workers, to see what the record says about the Bonines, the house and the farm around it.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known); a New finding is something we found in the record that we could not find in any earlier publication. Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

The place
The James E. Bonine House and carriage house, M-60 at Penn Road, Penn Township, Cass County, Michigan
The family
Isaac Bonine, a Quaker who “could not tolerate slavery,” came from Wayne County, Indiana, about 1842; his son James E. came a year later
The marriage
James E. Bonine married Sarah Ann Bogue, daughter of the abolitionist Stephen Bogue
The farm in 1882
1,600 acres, “five houses and eight barns,” an “elegant brick house, with fine fountain,” and an elk and deer park
The builder
James E. Bonine, born in Wayne County, Indiana, 5 September 1816; died at his home in Niles, 18 February 1897
The elk park
Begun about 1862 with a pair of elk from Iowa; 40 acres behind a ten-foot fence by 1885; “more than a score” of elk in 1941; still kept, 12 to 15 head, in 1953, the year the farm left the family
The house
Begun as a Greek Revival farmhouse in the 1840s and remade in the Second Empire style after the Civil War, by the society’s account
Today
Owned by the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County since December 2010; open for tours in season
Why it matters
It keeps the memory of the Quaker farms of Young’s Prairie, where freedom seekers found shelter and work
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The Bonines were Quakers of the anti-slavery kind. Isaac Bonine “could not tolerate slavery,” says the 1882 history, and the Anti-Slavery Friends met in a log building in a grove that was, by 1906, “the farm of the late James E. Bonine.”
  • James E. Bonine married into the Bogue family. His wife, Sarah Ann, was the daughter of Stephen Bogue, whose farm the Kentucky raiders struck in 1847.
  • The farm was famous for its elk. The 1882 history says seven of its elk were sold to “King Emmanuel, of Italy, who sent a war vessel for them.” A visitor who stood at the park fence in 1885 was told a smaller story: two elk, “to grace the Royal Park,” and no warship.
  • The elk outlived the family who started them. James E. Bonine’s son, grandson and great-grandson kept the herd; it was still there, 12 to 15 head on 40 acres, in 1953, the year the farm passed out of the family.
  • James E. Bonine died on 18 February 1897, at his home in Niles, after an illness of four months. His obituary ran in the Quaker weekly The American Friend.
  • Wilbur Siebert’s national directory of 1898 names a Bonine: Isaac, the father.

What it does not show, yet

  • Any record of the 1840s or 1850s naming James E. Bonine, or his house, in the work of the Underground Railroad.
  • A document for the story that freedom seekers sheltered in the carriage house. It is told by the society and by local tradition; we have not found it in a written source.
  • When the house and the carriage house were built. No 19th-century source we have read dates them.
  • An Italian record of the Bonine elk. A report from the king’s own park, printed in 1871, tells of his agent buying elk “in America,” but it names no state and no seller.
  • Where James E. Bonine is buried.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are ten things people say about the Bonine House. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“James E. Bonine’s wife was the daughter of Stephen Bogue.”

True

The 1882 history’s sketch of Stephen Bogue names “Mrs. J. E. Bonine” among the children of his first marriage.

“The 1898 national list of Underground Railroad workers names James E. Bonine.”

No

Wilbur Siebert’s list gives, for Cass County, “Bogue, Steven. Bonine, Isaac. Shugart, Zachariah.” The Bonine it names is Isaac, James E.’s father.

“The tower was a lookout for slave catchers.”

No

The mansard tower came with the remodeling after the Civil War, by the society’s own account. It did not exist in the years of the Underground Railroad.

“Elk from the Bonine farm were sold to the King of Italy.”

True, as printed, but how many?

The 1882 history says seven, carried off by a war vessel. In 1885 a visitor heard “two went to Victor Emanual, the King of Italy, … to grace the Royal Park,” with no warship. No Italian record we have found names the Bonines.

“The Bonine elk came when they were called.”

True

In 1885 James E. Bonine took a pail of salt to the park and called “Come Bill! come Bill!” Nine of the ten elk came and licked the salt thrown through the fence. The old bull, with “five feet of branching horns,” did not.

“The elk park was gone by 1900.”

No

It lasted more than half a century longer. A 1953 newspaper photograph shows a herd of 12 to 15 elk on the 40-acre park, still owned by James E. Bonine’s great-grandson.

“A tunnel ran from the house to the carriage house.”

No record

No tunnel has been found, and the society itself says the story “has yet to be verified.”

“The 1882 county history tells of freedom seekers hiding in the carriage house.”

No

It describes the building opposite the house only as “the finely-built storehouse,” and says nothing of fugitives there.

“The Anti-Slavery Friends worshipped on the Bonine farm.”

True

Glover’s history of 1906: their meeting “was held in a log building in the grove on the farm of the late James E. Bonine in Penn township, and known as the Elk Park.”

“The Bonine House is on the National Register of Historic Places.”

No record

We have found no listing. In 1957 the state registered an “Underground Railroad” historic site at “Bonine Elk Park,” which is a marker site, not a listing of the house.
## Quakers from Indiana

DocumentedIsaac Bonine, the 1882 history says, was “born of Quaker parents, he accepted their religious faith, and could not tolerate slavery.” He came to Young’s Prairie from Wayne County, Indiana, in 1842 (other sources say 1843), and his son James E. Bonine “came in one year subsequent to his father, and purchased eighty acres of land.”

New findingOne more record disagrees on the order. The roll of the county’s Pioneer Society, printed by Glover in 1906, gives the year each member came to the county: “James E. Bonine … Indiana … 1841,” and, further down the same page, “Isaac Bonine … Indiana … 1842.” By that roll the son came first. Every modern account we have read says 1843.

New findingThe family genealogies give the dates the modern accounts leave out. James E. Bonine was born in Wayne County, Indiana, on 5 September 1816, and Sarah Ann Bogue in Preble County, Ohio, on 30 April 1825. They were married at Cassopolis on 8 August 1844. Sarah Ann died at Vandalia on 17 September 1909.

DocumentedYoung’s Prairie, in Penn and Calvin townships, was already a Quaker settlement. James E. Bonine married Sarah Ann Bogue, a daughter of Stephen Bogue, the Quaker whose farm on the prairie the county history calls one of the two Underground Railroad stations in Cass County.
## An elk park

DocumentedBy 1882, the county history says, James E. Bonine was “the possessor of 1,600 acres, containing five houses and eight barns. Everything around him betokens the man of thrift and cultivated taste, from the elegant brick house, with fine fountain and attractive surroundings to the farthermost field.”

Documented“On his farm is a beautiful grove, twelve acres of which are included in an elk and deer park, established some twenty years since by procuring one pair of elk from Iowa, and one pair of deer, also from the West. Since that time he has sold $1,000 worth of elk, seven of which were sold to King Emmanuel, of Italy, who sent a war vessel for them.” There were buffalo, too, “which adds a certain picturesqueness to the scene.”

New findingThe same page describes, “exactly opposite his residence, which is on a corner,” “the finely-built storehouse,” with “two rows of arbor vitæ” running from it. Standing where it does, opposite the house on the corner, this is almost certainly the building now called the carriage house. It is the earliest description of it we have found, and it calls it a storehouse.
## “Come Bill!” A visit in 1885

New findingIn August 1885 a writer for the Michigan Farmer, signing himself A. C. G., toured the farms of Young’s Prairie and stopped at “the famous farm of James E. Bonine, covering 1,600 acres.” His account is the earliest eyewitness description of the elk park we have found.

New findingBetween the house and the village, he wrote, lay “a park of 40 acres enclosed by a picket fence ten feet high on two sides,” with rails and stakes of the same height on the other two. “In this enclosure are ten elk and thirteen deer. This is the only private park in Michigan.”

New findingThen the owner put on a show. “Mr. Bonine procured a pail of salt and went with us to the park,” and called, “Come Bill! come Bill!” “Nine of the elk came at the call, and timidly licked at the salt which was thrown through the fence.” The elk, the visitor thought, were “natural trotters,” circling “like a shy horse.” Only “the old patriarch, with his five feet of branching horns,” would not come. A hound and a bird dog had tried “an excursion through the park” the year before: “they were bound to have a hunt.”

New findingThe house matched the park. “Mr. Bonine’s residence is in harmony with his possessions. A large fountain ornaments the front yard, and the walks are large square flagging stones, set in a fine lawn.” By then the 1,600 acres were “divided into four farms and occupied by his children.” The fountain, which the 1882 history mentions in passing, and the flagstone walks appear in no modern account of the house we have read.
## Two elk or seven? The King of Italy

DocumentedThe 1882 history’s story is grand: seven elk, sold to “King Emmanuel, of Italy, who sent a war vessel for them.” The visitor of 1885, who walked to the park with the owner, tells it more modestly: “He has sold several elks to go to other States for city parks, and two went to Victor Emanual, the King of Italy, to grace the Royal Park.” Two elk, a royal park, and no warship.

ReadingThe name helps date the sale. Victor Emmanuel II, the first king of united Italy, died in January 1878. If he was the buyer, the elk left Vandalia before then, and probably after the park was founded in the 1860s.

New findingThe Italian side has its own record, and it explains why a king would buy elk from a Michigan farm. In 1871 Benvenuto Comba, the naturalist of the royal park of La Mandria, near Turin, reported to the Acclimatisation Society of Paris on the king’s wapiti. Two bought at Antwerp and four in London in 1863 died within days. Then, he wrote, “M. le comte de Castiglione fut envoyé par Sa Majesté en Amérique pour y acheter des Cerfs wapiti”: the king sent the Count di Castiglione to America to buy elk. “The first shipment was of 60 animals, of which 47 arrived alive in Italy,” and those died too. In 1865 the count sent more.

DocumentedThe losses went on. A French hunting writer, Henri de la Blanchère, summing up Comba’s figures in 1876, counted eleven wapiti dead at La Mandria in 1871 and six more in the first months of 1873. Comba blamed the animals’ diet; the royal vets blamed disease.

ReadingA king whose elk kept dying was a king who kept buying them, all through the years when the Bonine park was selling. Comba names no state and no seller, so his report does not prove the Bonine sale. It makes it believable, and it shows where the proof would be: in the royal household’s accounts for the elk Castiglione and others bought in America.

DocumentedBy 1908 a syndicated newspaper story was back to seven elk and a “man-of-war.” It added that the Bonine elk sold for $100 a head at any age over six months, that others had gone to parks in Detroit and Grand Rapids, “where some were placed in the parks at the Soldiers’ home,” and that the family had given up its buffalo, which “did not do well here except in summer.”

ReadingTwo in 1885, written by a visitor who spent the afternoon with the owner; seven in print before and after. The smaller number, set down at the farm, is the one we would trust, until an Italian record says otherwise.
## Friends against slavery

DocumentedSome Quakers of the time went further than their meetings would go. Glover’s county history of 1906 tells of the “Anti-Slavery” Friends: “They would not use cotton cloths, sugar or anything they knew to be made by slaves.”

New finding“The meeting in Cass county was held in a log building in the grove on the farm of the late James E. Bonine in Penn township, and known as the Elk Park. The pastor was the Rev. Charles Osborn, a renowned minister among Friends.” A school for their children met in the same building. Modern accounts say the Bonines were members of the Anti-Slavery Friends; we have not found one that says the meeting met on their farm.

DocumentedCharles Osborn, their pastor, was one of the best-known anti-slavery Quakers in the country. In 1879 James E. Bonine and others built the brick Friends’ church at Vandalia, and he and Sarah A. Bonine were among its first elders.
## Station or story?

New findingThe national directory of Underground Railroad workers in Wilbur H. Siebert’s The Underground Railroad from Slavery to Freedom (1898), names three for Cass County: “Bogue, Steven. Bonine, Isaac. Shugart, Zachariah.” The Bonine it names is Isaac, the father, not James E.

DocumentedWe have found no letter, newspaper or court paper of the 1840s or 1850s that places freedom seekers at James E. Bonine’s house or carriage house. The society that owns the house says so itself: “To date there is little evidence of the house itself being a UGRR station.” The carriage house, it says, has a stronger tradition.

ReadingThat is not the same as saying nothing happened there. The Bonines were anti-slavery Quakers, married into the Bogue family, on a prairie where freedom seekers lived and worked in the open by 1847, and where the Kentucky raiders came looking for them. What is missing is a written record that names this house.

DocumentedSome of what is told can be checked. The tower that is said to have been a lookout was added after the Civil War, and no tunnel has been found; the society’s own volunteers say both stories are unproven.
## The house in the society’s telling

DocumentedThe Underground Railroad Society’s story of the house is best told in the books of Cindy Yawkey, the Bonine House’s head docent, who writes and illustrates them herself. The society publishes them and says they inform its story.

DocumentedHer picture book They Have My Shoes, I Have My Freedom: A Story About the Underground Railroad, which won a Michigan State History Award in 2016, follows Lucinda, a woman escaping from Georgia barefoot after her master took her shoes. She crosses the Ohio, is carried by wagon from Levi Coffin’s Richmond to Bristol, and comes at last to Calvin Township, to “a light in the window of the Bonine house.” There James and Sarah Bonine meet her: “We have food, clothing, shoes, and a place to rest on the third floor of the carriage house,” Sarah says.

ReadingIt is a story, and it says so: Lucinda is a character, not a name from a record. What it preserves is the society’s tradition that the carriage house loft sheltered freedom seekers. That tradition is worth keeping, and worth testing: we have not yet found it in a written source of the 1840s or 1850s.

DocumentedHer second book, The Kentucky Slave Raid of 1847, Cass County Michigan (the society, about 2019), retells the raid farm by farm, with a hand-drawn map of the prairie on which “James E. Bonine” sits among the farms of the raid’s story. We compare it with the record in our story The Kentucky Raid of 1847.
## The house today

DocumentedBy the society’s account, the house was begun as a Greek Revival farmhouse in the 1840s and, “soon after the Civil War,” enlarged and remade “in one of the most flamboyant American-Victorian styles, Second Empire,” with its central mansard tower. The Gothic Revival carriage house across the road is dated to about 1850.

DocumentedIn 1957 the state of Michigan registered an “Underground Railroad” historic site at “Bonine Elk Park, M-60.” The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County bought the house and carriage house in December 2010, and has been restoring them since.
## A man of affairs

DocumentedJames E. Bonine was more than a farmer. In the 1850s he took premiums at the state fair for Durham heifers, a French and Spanish buck and the best boar; the federal agriculture reports of the 1860s list his Merino sheep; and in 1883 the Michigan Farmer wrote of “a flock of one thousand head belonging to J. E. Bonine of Cass County.”

New findingIn 1870 he was one of the first directors of the First National Bank of Cassopolis. He was superintendent of the Air Line railroad through Penn Township, to which, the 1882 history says, he gave “three years time, $6,000 right of way, and $6,000 cash.” That was the Michigan Air Line, built from Jackson to Niles and opened through Vandalia in 1871, which gave the village its station. No modern account of the house we have read mentions his part in it.

DocumentedIn 1879 he and his brother Lot built the brick Friends’ church at Vandalia. By the society’s account it later became the Masonic lodge, and it has since been torn down. In 1887 the Sharpless family genealogy still called him “a banker and farmer, Vandalia”; by 1906 Glover writes of “the late James E. Bonine.” After his death his widow, by the 1908 account, was the largest stockholder of the Cassopolis bank.

New findingJames E. Bonine died on 18 February 1897. The Quaker weekly The American Friend reported it that April: “Died at his home in Niles, Michigan, Second month 18th, 1897, James E. Bonine, in the eighty-first year of his age.” He had been “for many years an elder,” it said, and had given so freely to the church that he built “principally one house for worship,” very likely the Vandalia church of 1879, and helped to build three others. His last illness lasted four months.

DocumentedA Berrien County history of 1906 gives a fuller sketch, and a different year. It calls him “the leading banker of Cass county for many years,” says he cleared 800 of his 1,600 acres, and says he moved to Niles in 1866, went back to the farm, and spent his last days in Niles, “where he died in 1898 at the age of eighty-two years.” The obituary, printed weeks after his death, is the one to trust.
OpenWe have not found where he is buried. His parents lie in Prairie Grove Cemetery in Penn Township, and his grandson in Silverbrook at Niles; either is possible.
## The Elk Park’s later life

DocumentedThe elk did not end with James E. Bonine. On 14 October 1907 his son Isaac A. Bonine wrote to the federal Biological Survey that he had been breeding elk and deer “for about thirty-five years.” The government printed his letter in a 1910 bulletin on raising game animals.

Isaac A. Bonine to the Biological Survey · 14 October 1907

“We find that deer are not so hardy as elk and require more care. Elk winter well on hay and corn fodder with a little grain, and they live and thrive during summer months on blue grass. … The growing of both elk and deer for park purposes may be made profitable.”
OpenHis “thirty-five years” would start the herd about 1872. The 1882 history’s “some twenty years since” and a 1953 caption both point to about 1862. We cannot yet say which is right.

New findingIsaac’s son, Dr. J. Gordon Bonine, kept the herd in his turn. When he died in 1934 his obituary called the farm of 1,500 acres “the famous Elk park farm,” where “he kept [a] herd of elk that drew many tourists at all times of the year,” and “a show place in Cass county.” In October 1953 a newspaper photograph showed “a herd of 12 to 15 elk at Bonine Elk Park” on M-60, “an outstanding tourist attraction,” on a forested 40-acre park owned by G. Elwood Bonine, the founder’s great-grandson.
DocumentedBy 1941 the park was a sight on the highway, and the WPA’s guide to Michigan sent motorists to it.

Michigan: A Guide to the Wolverine State · 1941

“On the western border of Vandalia … is Bonine Elk Park (R), a woodland tract of 60 acres. Here more than a score of American elk browse in the open, except during the most severe weather. They are sold to zoos, parks, and private gardens, and sometimes to Elk lodges for ceremonial purposes.”

New findingThe end came with the farm. When G. Elwood Bonine died in 1976 his obituary said he had “farmed the Elk Park Farms which had been in his family from 1837 to 1953.” He moved to Lansing in 1953, the year of the last photograph of the herd we have found.

ReadingThat is ninety years of elk on one farm. The state’s 1957 marker went up at “Bonine Elk Park,” but by then the farm had left the family, and by 1963 a writer spoke of the park in the past tense. The last elk most likely went with the farm, about 1953.
## Who’s who

<aside class="nw-glance" aria-label="Who’s who"><dl><dt>Isaac Bonine</dt><dd>The father. A Quaker from Wayne County, Indiana, who “could not tolerate slavery.” Named by Siebert in 1898 as an Underground Railroad worker.</dd><dt>James E. Bonine (1816–1897)</dt><dd>The son. Farmer, stock breeder, banker, railroad superintendent and founder of the Elk Park; the builder of the house, by the society’s account.</dd><dt>Sarah Ann Bogue Bonine (1825–1909)</dt><dd>His wife, daughter of Stephen Bogue. An elder of the Vandalia Friends’ church in 1879.</dd><dt>Stephen Bogue</dt><dd>Her father, whose farm the county history calls one of the two Underground Railroad stations in Cass County, and which the Kentucky raiders struck in 1847.</dd><dt>Charles Osborn</dt><dd>Pastor of the Anti-Slavery Friends, who met in the log building in the Bonine grove.</dd><dt>The children</dt><dd>Evan E. (1845–1865); Mary E. (born 1847, Mrs. W. T. Dougan); Isaac A. (born 1849), who kept the elk after his father; Elsie E. (born 1851, Mrs. N. B. Hannum).</dd><dt>The keepers of the elk</dt><dd>Isaac A. Bonine; his son Dr. J. Gordon Bonine (1874–1934); and G. Elwood Bonine (1896–1976), state senator for Cass County from 1942 to 1952, who farmed the Elk Park until 1953.</dd></dl></aside>
## The farm through the years

• 1816 James E. Bonine born in Wayne County, Indiana, 5 September (Sharpless 1887)
  • 1841–43 Isaac Bonine and his son come to Young’s Prairie; the sources disagree on the year and on who came first
  • 1844 James E. Bonine marries Sarah Ann Bogue at Cassopolis, 8 August
  • 1847 The Kentucky raiders come to Young’s Prairie
  • 1850s State-fair premiums for his cattle, sheep and hogs
  • c. 1862 The elk park begun with a pair of elk from Iowa (1882 history; a 1953 caption). Isaac A. Bonine’s letter points to about 1872
  • 1863–65 The King of Italy sends the Count di Castiglione to America to buy elk; most of the first herds die
  • 1866 The Bonines move to Niles for some years, then go back to the farm
  • 1863–78 Elk go to Victor Emmanuel II, King of Italy: two by the 1885 account, seven by the 1882 history
  • 1870 A first director of the First National Bank of Cassopolis
  • 1871 The Michigan Air Line opens through Vandalia, with Bonine its superintendent in Penn Township
  • 1879 The brick Friends’ church at Vandalia is dedicated
  • 1882 1,600 acres, five houses, eight barns, an elk and deer park and buffalo (county history)
  • 1885 A visitor finds ten elk and thirteen deer in a 40-acre park, and a fountain on the lawn
  • 1897 James E. Bonine dies at his home in Niles, 18 February
  • 1906 Glover writes of “the late James E. Bonine”
  • 1907 Isaac A. Bonine writes to the Biological Survey on raising elk
  • 1908 Elk selling at $100 a head; the buffalo given up
  • 1909 Sarah Ann Bonine dies at Vandalia, 17 September
  • 1934 The Elk Park farm called “a show place in Cass county”
  • 1941 The WPA guide: “more than a score of American elk browse in the open”
  • 1953 12 to 15 elk still on the park; the farm leaves the family
  • 1957 State historic site registered at “Bonine Elk Park, M-60”
  • 2010 The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County buys the house and carriage house
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Is there a written record of freedom seekers at the Bonine farm? Isaac Bonine’s account book of 1838–1850, at Earlham College, may hold clues.
  2. When were the house and the carriage house built? A deed, a tax roll or a dated letter would settle it.
  3. Two elk or seven, and when? The royal household’s accounts for the elk bought in America, or an American newspaper of the 1860s or 1870s, would settle it.
  4. Where is James E. Bonine buried? Prairie Grove in Penn Township or Silverbrook at Niles.
  5. When did the Elk Park begin, and when did the last elk leave? About 1862 or about 1872; and probably about 1953, when the farm was sold.

stories.headline: Stone Lake, the lake that keeps secrets
stories.short: Stone Lake, the lake that keeps secrets
stories.dek: No stream runs into Stone Lake, and none runs out. The village of Cassopolis was laid out on its shore in 1831, the county history of 1882 called it the most peculiar lake in the county, and people once believed it rose and fell with Lake Superior. Here is what the record says, and the seven mysteries it still keeps.
stories.sdek: A lake with no inlet, soft water, a shore of boulders, and a river from Lake Superior that never was.
pic: /img/news/stone-lake-the-lake-that-keeps-secrets
Detail of the 1872 plan of Cassopolis: Broadway, York, Disbrow and State streets, the public square, and Stone Lake filling the lower right
Stone Lake and the village on the Plan of Cassopolis in the Atlas of Cass County, Michigan (Philadelphia, 1872), detail. Internet Archive.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Stone Lake lies at the foot of Broadway in Cassopolis, close enough to the courthouse that the village was laid out around its shore. It is not large, and it is not famous. But it has puzzled people for a long time. No stream runs into it, and none runs out. Its water was soft when its neighbor’s was hard. And in the 1880s, by the county history’s account, many people in Cass County believed it was fed by an underground river from Lake Superior.
We went back to the county histories of 1882 and 1906 and the county atlas of 1872 to see what the record says about the lake, and what it still keeps to itself.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known); a New finding is something we found in the record that we could not find in any earlier publication. Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

The place
Stone Lake, on the south side of the village of Cassopolis, the seat of Cass County, Michigan
The name
From the boulders: its shores “were originally very thickly strewn with stone, in the form of bowlders” (1882)
Size
188 acres, in the county history’s table of 1882
The water
“No visible inlet or outlet; its water is very fine and very soft,” while Diamond Lake’s, half a mile away, “is hard” (1882)
The village
Platted in 1831 beside the lake; the plat was “broken on the southwest corner by the lake” (1906)
Drinking water
From 1891 the village water works pumped from “the depths of Stone lake” (1906)
Why it matters
The lake shaped where the village grew, and it still keeps seven open questions
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The lake is named for its stones: boulders the glaciers left on its shores.
  • It has no visible inlet or outlet, and its water was “very fine and very soft” in 1882, when Diamond Lake’s was hard.
  • People believed in a river from Lake Superior. The 1882 history reports the belief that the lake was fed by “the great subterranean stream” from Superior, and rose and fell with it.
  • The village was laid out on its shore, and for years drew its drinking water from it.

What it does not show, yet

  • Whether the lake still rises and falls when its neighbors don’t. Only people on the shore can tell us.
  • Whether its water is still soft. A few dollars of test strips would answer it.
  • Where the icehouse stood that, around 1899, supplied ice to the Diamond Lake cottages.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are eight things people say about Stone Lake. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“The 1882 county history called Stone Lake the county’s most peculiar lake.”

True

“The largest is Diamond Lake … and the most peculiar is Stone Lake.” History of Cass County (1882), p. 11.

“In 1882 Stone Lake’s water was hard, like Diamond Lake’s.”

No

Its water was “very fine and very soft”; Diamond Lake’s, “only half a mile distant, is hard.” 1882, p. 11.

“Stone Lake is named for the boulders on its shores.”

True

Its shores “were originally very thickly strewn with stone, in the form of bowlders.” 1882, p. 11.

“An underground river from Lake Superior feeds Stone Lake.”

No record

The 1882 history says only that it was “supposed by many people.” No study has ever shown it.

“Cassopolis once drank Stone Lake water.”

True

From 1891 the water works pumped “from the depths of Stone lake, where the water is crystal pure and ice cold, and free from lime, or ‘soft.’” Glover (1906), p. 152.

“The lake took a corner out of the village plat.”

True

The 1831 plat was a rectangle “broken on the southwest corner by the lake.” Glover (1906), p. 149.

“The first manufacturing business in Cassopolis stood on Stone Lake.”

True, as printed

In 1833, Glover says, the Silvers brothers “put up a distillery on the banks of Stone lake, the first manufacturing institution of Cassopolis.”

“Stone Lake is the largest lake in Cass County.”

No

In the 1882 table it is 188 acres; Diamond Lake, half a mile away, is 1,083.
## A shore of stones

DocumentedThe 1882 county history explains the name plainly. Of all the county’s lakes, “the most peculiar is Stone Lake — so named from the fact that its shores were originally very thickly strewn with stone, in the form of bowlders.”
ReadingThe boulders came with the glaciers, dragged down from the north and dropped when the ice melted, as they were all across this county. Most of them are gone from the shore today.
OpenWhere did they go? If you know of a building in Cassopolis made of Stone Lake stone, we would like to hear about it.
## No stream in, no stream out

Documented“This lake has no visible inlet or outlet; its water is very fine and very soft. That of Diamond Lake, only half a mile distant, is hard.” The same history adds: “There is known to be a chain of soft-water lakes extending for a considerable distance across the country from north to south.”

DocumentedThe village put that soft water to use. In 1891 Cassopolis built water works, and, Glover wrote in 1906, “the water is pumped into the mains from the depths of Stone lake, where the water is crystal pure and ice cold, and free from lime, or ‘soft.’”

OpenIs it still soft? Water-hardness test strips cost a few dollars at a hardware or pool store. Dip one at a public spot on Stone Lake and one on Diamond Lake, and send us the numbers. You could settle a question that goes back to 1882.
## The river from Lake Superior

Documented“It is supposed by many people,” the 1882 history says, “that Stone Lake is one of the surface spots of the great subterranean stream by which Lake Superior is believed to discharge its waters into the Gulf of Mexico; and, it is averred in support of this theory, that the rise and fall in Stone Lake corresponds closely with that of the ‘shining’ big sea water.”
ReadingThe “shining big sea water” is Longfellow’s, from The Song of Hiawatha (1855): “By the shining Big-Sea-Water.” The history does not name him, but its readers would have known the line.
OpenNeighbors on the shore may be the only people who can answer this one: does Stone Lake rise and fall when the other lakes around it don’t?
## The village on the shore

DocumentedWhen the county seat was fixed at Cassopolis in 1831, the proprietors laid out their village beside the lake. Glover, in 1906, describes the original plat: a rectangle of 119½ by 191 rods, “broken on the southwest corner by the lake.” “The lake,” he adds, “occupied the principal natural position in influencing the location of residence and business enterprises at the early period.”

DocumentedThe first manufacturing in the village was on its banks: in 1833, Glover says, Jacob, Abiel and Benjamin F. Silvers “put up a distillery on the banks of Stone lake.” By 1882 there was a bowl factory on the shore, and the road to Niles in early days, the 1882 history says, “led through the woods on the high ground west of Stone Lake.”
DocumentedThe county atlas of 1872, whose plan of Cassopolis heads this page, shows the lake at the foot of the village, with Broadway, Disbrow and the public square laid out beside it.
## Ice in winter

DocumentedBefore refrigerators, the lake had a winter crop. The Diamond Lake Association’s history, drawn from Lois Webster Welch’s A Diamond Sparkles (1970), records under 1899: “Ice deliveries were made from the Stone Lake Icehouse.” We have not yet found the newspaper of the time.
ReadingSo for a while the iceboxes at the Diamond Lake cottages most likely ran on Stone Lake water, and the two lakes that never shared their water did, a block at a time.
OpenWhere did the icehouse stand, and who ran it? Do you have a photograph of an ice harvest, or of a summer day on Stone Lake? Tell us, and tell us where it came from.
## Seven secrets still kept

Stone Lake has its own treasure hunt, on Facebook, with seven mysteries open. Answers count when they come with the page they came from: a book, a map, a deed, a newspaper. We will not give the answers here, but here are the questions.

1. Who was the settler who gave away forty acres of lakefront for the village?
  2. Where is the 1831 parchment deed today?
  3. Where does Stone Lake’s water really come from?
  4. Where did the boulders on the shore go?
  5. What powered the flour mill on a lake with no stream, and where did it stand?
  6. Who was the doctor who dug into a mound in this county in 1878? (Not on this lake.)
  7. What became of the thigh bone, and of everything else from that grave?
Cracked so far: none. When someone solves one, we will name them here.
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Does the lake still rise and fall on its own? Readings from the shore over a year would show it.
  2. Is the water still soft? Test strips, or the village’s own water reports, would tell.
  3. Where did the icehouse stand? A plat book, a tax roll or a photograph might show it.
  4. Where is the 1831 plat, the one Glover said had copies “still extant”?

To cite this page: Michael Urbanski, “Stone Lake, the lake that keeps secrets,” Project Scroll, projectscroll.com/news/stone-lake-the-lake-that-keeps-secrets/, first published 22 October 2026. Corrections are welcome, and any we make are noted on this page.

stories.kicker: How the towns got their names
stories.headline: How Kalamazoo got its name
stories.dek: Everyone in Kalamazoo knows two stories: a footrace against a boiling pot, and a founder run out of town over a stolen cherry tree. We went back to the record, from a Jesuit’s route notes of about 1760 to the act of 1836, to see where each story really starts, where the letter L came from, and what the Potawatomi names for the place and the river say today.
stories.sdek: A footrace, a cherry tree, a missing letter L, and the oldest spelling on paper.
pic: /img/news/how-kalamazoo-got-its-name
An oil painting of cabins under green trees beside a bayou of the Kalamazoo River, with red roofs and a boy in a white shirt
William Greason, Bayou on the Kalamazoo River, Douglas, oil on canvas, 1934. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
body: Kalamazoo, Mich. Ask anyone in Kalamazoo why the city is called Kalamazoo and you will hear about a footrace: a young man running to the river and back before a pot of water boiled away. Ask why it is not still called Bronson and you will hear about a stolen cherry tree. You will find both on the city’s own website. Neither one, it turns out, rests where people think it does.

We went back to the paper: a Jesuit’s route notes of about 1760, a French map of 1744, the treaty of 1821, an atlas map of 1822, the act of the legislature that changed the name in 1836, the county’s first histories, and the linguists who have argued over the word for 170 years. Then we set beside them the names that the Potawatomi people use for the place and the river today. The record does not hand over a single tidy answer. It does show which stories are old, which are new, where the letter L came from, and which explanation has the oldest written support.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known). Each exhibit links to the page it comes from, and every source is listed at the foot of the page. The page photographs are from the libraries that hold the books; press any picture to see the whole page.

At a glance

The place
Kalamazoo, Michigan: city, township, county and the river they are named for
First name
The Village of Bronson, platted by Titus Bronson and Stephen Richardson, 12 March 1831
Renamed
By act of the Michigan Legislature, approved 2 March 1836, effective 31 March 1836
Oldest spelling
“kikanamaso,” a “little” and a “great” river of that name, in the route notes of Father Pierre Potier, dated by his editor to the autumn of 1760
With an L
“Kekalamazoo” and “Ke-kal-i-ma-zoo,” both in the Treaty of Chicago, 1821; “Kikalemazo R.” on the Carey & Lea map of Michigan Territory, 1822
The meanings
Boiling pot (in print by 1867); otters under the water (Schoolcraft, 1855); “it smokes” (Verwyst, 1892; Gerard, 1911); mirage or reflecting river (undated, rejected by scholars)
The names today
Gzigmezé, describing a boiling (a Potawatomi language specialist on WMUK, 2018). Gun Lake Tribe: Gzigmezék for the village and city, Giknamezo zibé for the river
Why it matters
The race story is old, but its hero, “Fleet Foot,” first appears in 1922. The cherry tree has no source we can find before modern times. And the river’s Potawatomi name today is close to the oldest spelling on paper
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The name came from the river, and the river’s name is old. A form of it, “kikanamaso,” is in a Jesuit’s route notes dated to about 1760, nearly seventy years before the first settler’s cabin.
  • The L arrived late. The oldest spellings have an N; the L first appears in the treaty of 1821. The Potawatomi language has no L sound.
  • The race story was in print by 1867, told as an anonymous “Indian” runner and a pot boiling on the fire at Toland’s Prairie. The hero’s name, “Fleet Foot,” his bride and the year 1810 first appear in a newspaper of 1922.
  • The village became Kalamazoo by an act of the state legislature, approved 2 March 1836. The county’s 1880 history credits three men, and probably a fourth, with getting it done, and gives no reason beyond “some good reason, we presume.”
  • The Potawatomi names in use today are Gzigmezé or Gzigmezék for the place and Giknamezo zibé for the river.

What it does not show, yet

  • Any record of the cherry tree: no court record, no newspaper, nothing in the first county histories.
  • What the word meant to the people who first said it. Every published meaning is someone’s explanation, not a speaker’s testimony on record.
  • Which river was the “little” kikanamaso in the 1760s.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Kalamazoo tells itself some good stories. Here are eight things people say about the name. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“Kalamazoo was first called Bronson.”

True

Titus Bronson and Stephen Richardson recorded the plat of the Village of Bronson on 12 March 1831. It was the county seat under that name until 1836 (Exhibit E).

“The state legislature changed the name.”

True

“An act to alter the names of the township of Arcadia and the village of Bronson” was approved on 2 March 1836. From 31 March both were to be “known and called Kalamazoo.”

“Bronson lost his town over a stolen cherry tree.”

No record yet

Today’s histories say so, but we could not find the cherry tree anywhere in the nineteenth-century record: not in Durant (1880), not in the 1906 Compendium, not in the county’s 1877 report. Durant, who wrote at length about the renaming, gives no reason at all.

“The footrace story was made up in the twentieth century.”

No, it is older

The race to the river and the boiling pot were in print by 1867, in George Torrey’s history of the village, quoting A. J. Sheldon. What the twentieth century added was the romance.

“The runner was called Fleet Foot, and he ran for his bride.”

Not before 1922

In the 1867 telling the runner has no name and there is no bride. “Fleet Foot,” the bride and the year 1810 first appear in the Kalamazoo Gazette of 20 August 1922.

“The oldest spelling of the name has an L in it.”

No

The oldest form we can find, “kikanamaso,” in Father Potier’s route notes of about 1760, has an N. The L first appears in the Treaty of Chicago of 1821.

“A famous explorer said the name was about otters.”

True

Henry Rowe Schoolcraft, in 1855: stones in the riverbed that looked like an otter swimming beneath the surface. In 1911 William Gerard called his explanations “etymological absurdities.”

“Kalamazoo means ‘reflecting river.’”

No early source

The “mirage” or “reflecting river” meaning has no early source that we can find, and Vogel’s Indian Names in Michigan rejects it.
## Who’s who

Match-e-be-nash-she-wish Potawatomi leader · village at the head of the river, 1821
The 1821 Treaty of Chicago reserved a tract “at the village of Match-e-be-nash-she-wish, at the head of the Kekalamazoo river,” on ground that is now the city. The reserve was ceded in 1827. The Gun Lake Tribe, the Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians, carries his name today.
Father Pierre Potier 1708–1781 · Jesuit missionary at Detroit
Missionary to the Wyandot at the Assumption mission across the river from Detroit. His papers include route notes for travellers; the one that names the “kikanamaso” is dated by his modern editor, Robert Toupin, to the autumn of 1760.
Titus Bronson 1788–1853 · founder of the village
Connecticut-born pioneer, known in his day as “Potato Bronson.” He settled on the site in 1829, platted the Village of Bronson in 1831, and left after the name was changed. He died at Middlebury, Connecticut.
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft 1793–1864 · explorer and Indian agent
Travelled through Michigan in 1820 and 1821. In 1855 he published the explanation that the name describes stones in the riverbed that look like swimming otters.
A. J. Sheldon and George Torrey early Kalamazoo residents and writers
Torrey’s history of the village, printed in the directory of 1867, quotes Sheldon’s version of the race to the river: the oldest printing of that story we have found.
Samuel W. Durant compiler, History of Kalamazoo County (1880)
Reprinted Torrey’s account and the act of 1836, and wrote that the name came from a Potawatomi word meaning “the boiling-pot.”
Father Chrysostom Verwyst 1841–1925 · Franciscan missionary and Ojibwe scholar
In 1892 explained Kalamazoo as a corruption of the Ojibwe kikanamoso, “it smokes, or he is troubled with smoke.”
William R. Gerard 1841–1914 · student of Algonquian languages
In 1911 took Schoolcraft’s otters apart and argued for a smoke word, kikalâmozo.
Virgil J. Vogel 1918–1994 · historian
Author of Indian Names in Michigan (1986), the standard reference, which weighs every theory and accepts none outright.
## The river and its places
Every place in this story lies along one river. Durant, in 1880, puts the race on “Galesburg, or Toland’s Prairie,” east of the town.
## Exhibit A: the oldest spelling, about 1760

DocumentedThe oldest form of the name we can find on paper is in the writings of Father Pierre Potier, the Jesuit at Detroit. Among his papers are itineraries: lists, stage by stage, of the rivers and portages along routes through the Great Lakes country. In them the word appears as two rivers, a “little” one and a “great” one: le petit and le grand kikanamaso. His editor, Robert Toupin, prints them in Les Écrits de Pierre Potier (1996), pages 144 to 151, and dates the itinerary to the autumn of 1760.

ReadingSpelled with an N, not an L. That one letter matters a great deal, as we will see. The date is the editor’s dating of the notes, not a date written on them, and route notes of this kind could be copied from other travellers; so “about 1760” is the safest way to put it. Either way, the river had this name well before any American surveyor saw it.
OpenWhy autumn 1760? Toupin ties the date to a journey of Potier’s, on page 144; we have seen that page only through a search of the borrowed book, and have not yet read his reasoning in full.

OpenWhich river was the “little” kikanamaso? Two streams of the same name suggest a main river and a branch, or two neighbouring rivers. We have not yet seen Toupin’s notes on the passage. The book is on loan through the Internet Archive and in university libraries.
## Exhibit B: the French maps

DocumentedThe French named the river differently. Jacques-Nicolas Bellin’s Carte des Lacs du Canada of 1744 marks the rivers on Lake Michigan’s eastern shore. Going north from the St. Joseph, the map shows the “Riv. Noire,” then “R. Marameg,” then “R. a la Barbue” and the “R. au Raisin,” and then the Grand River.

ReadingRead from the St. Joseph northward, the order matches the real coast: the Black River, then the Kalamazoo, then the Grand. That puts “Marameg” where the Kalamazoo should be. The Kalamazoo Public Library also reports the river called by forms of “Marame” on maps of the early 1800s, and the historian Larry Massie gives “Meramec” or “Merame” for the French name. Marameg was also the name of a band of the Miami people; Vogel says the river’s name in the French period was Meramec, which he translates “catfish.” And the next river north on Bellin’s map, “à la Barbue,” is French for “of the catfish.”

DocumentedThe same Handbook entry, though, writes the river as “Maramec (Kalamazoo) r.,” citing a French document of 1695 that places the “Miamis of Maramek” on it. What it rejects is the idea that the northern Marameg people lived there, not that the river was once called Maramec.

OpenWhether “Marameg” on the 1744 map really is the Kalamazoo is not settled. The Handbook of American Indians (1907) thought the Marameg people lived far to the north, near Sault Ste. Marie, and called the Kalamazoo identification of their name “certainly erroneous.” Only a full survey of the French maps and journals will decide it.
## Exhibit C: the treaty of 1821

DocumentedThe earliest American document we have found that names the river is the Treaty of Chicago, signed on 29 August 1821 by Lewis Cass and Solomon Sibley for the United States and by the Odawa, Ojibwe and Potawatomi. Its second article reserved, among other tracts, “One tract at the village of Match-e-be-nash-she-wish, at the head of the Kekalamazoo river.” A note after the signatures, fixing the size of that tract at three miles square, spells the river a second way: “Ke-kal-i-ma-zoo.”

ReadingTwo spellings in one document, both with an L, both with the extra syllable in front: “Ke-.” The village of Match-e-be-nash-she-wish stood on the ground of the present city. The 1827 Treaty of St. Joseph took the reserve back, and the first settlers arrived two years later.
## Exhibit D: the map of 1822

DocumentedThe Kalamazoo Public Library and others report that the river is spelled “Kikalemazo” on an atlas of 1823 (“five years before any white settlement,” in the library’s words; Titus Bronson came in 1829), without saying which atlas. Henry Carey and Isaac Lea’s American Atlas, published at Philadelphia in 1822 and reissued in 1823, includes a Geographical, Statistical, and Historical Map of Michigan Territory. Its river, rising in the interior and running west to Lake Michigan between the Grand and the St. Joseph, is lettered “Kikalemazo R.”
ReadingWe think this is the atlas the library means. The Carey & Lea map is dated 1822, the atlas was reissued in 1823, and its spelling matches the library’s exactly.

ReadingSo by the early 1820s the name had two forms on paper: a government spelling with “Ke-” and an L, and a map spelling that still kept the old “Kik-” at the front, close to Potier’s “kikanamaso.”

ReadingThe library calls that atlas the first appearance of a word like today’s spelling. The treaty of 1821, with its “Kekalamazoo,” is a year older than the map and two years older than the 1823 issue.
## Exhibit E: the county, the village and the act of 1836

DocumentedKalamazoo County was laid out by a territorial act of 29 October 1829 and organized on 30 July 1830, when its northern half became the township of Arcadia. Titus Bronson and Stephen H. Richardson recorded the first plat of the village on 12 March 1831 (Durant, page 214), and named it Bronson. The county seat was Bronson. The Pioneer Society of Michigan’s county list of 1877 puts it in one line: “County-seat, Kalamazoo,—first Bronson, then changed to Kalamazoo.”

DocumentedThe change itself was made by the first legislature of the new State of Michigan, in “An act to alter the names of the township of Arcadia and the village of Bronson.” From 31 March 1836 the township and the village were both to be “known and called Kalamazoo.” It was approved on 2 March 1836, nearly eleven months before Congress admitted Michigan to the Union on 26 January 1837.

DocumentedDurant’s History of Kalamazoo County (1880) tells it on page 220, under the heading “Changing Names.” In the winter of 1835–36, he writes, a movement was set on foot “for some good reason, we presume,” and “the change was brought about” mainly through “Messrs. Burdick, Sheldon, and Lyon,” probably with Anthony Cooley, a proprietor of the village. Bronson “felt that he had been deeply wronged,” stayed only a short time, and later “is said to have died in straitened circumstances.” Durant adds a footnote: some had said the act was passed by the territorial legislature, but the session laws show otherwise.

ReadingDurant gives only surnames. Lyon is almost certainly Lucius Lyon, the surveyor who became one of Michigan’s first two senators, and Burdick almost certainly one of the Burdick brothers; Cyren Burdick ran the Kalamazoo House, the village’s first hotel. The town had more than one Sheldon. Durant himself, writing forty-four years later, did not know why they wanted the change, or would not say. He thought the new name “more musical and pleasing than Bronson,” but admitted it was hard to deny that the change had done the founder an injustice.
## The cherry tree

DocumentedToday’s histories say that Bronson was fined for stealing a cherry tree. The city’s own page adds that his rivals then had the town renamed; the Kalamazoo Public Library’s biography says the fine fed the discontent against him.

DocumentedWe could not find the cherry tree anywhere in the nineteenth-century record. It is not in Durant’s History of Kalamazoo County (1880), whose full text we searched; it is not in Fisher and Little’s Compendium of History and Biography of Kalamazoo County (1906); and it is not in the county’s report to the Pioneer Society (1877). Durant, who writes at length about Bronson and the renaming, gives no reason for it at all.

ReadingThat does not make the story false. Justice-of-the-peace dockets of the 1830s seldom reached print, and a neighbour’s complaint over a cherry tree is exactly the sort of thing a small town remembers and a county history leaves out. But as things stand, the most famous fact about the renaming is the least documented one.

OpenWhere did the cherry tree story come from? The likeliest places are the township justice dockets, the Kalamazoo Public Library’s subject file on Bronson, and Nick Kekic’s history of early Kalamazoo, A Fine Place for a City (1984). If you know the original record, please write to us.
## Exhibit F: the race to the river

DocumentedThe oldest printing of the race story we have found is in George Torrey’s history of the village, in the Kalamazoo directory for 1867, as reprinted by Durant. Torrey quotes a letter from A. J. Sheldon, who said he “took great pains among the Indians” to learn what the word meant. On Toland’s Prairie, east of the town, a wager was made that a runner could not reach a point on the river and come back before a little pot of water on the fire boiled away. The race was run, and the river was named “where the water boils in the pot.” The name, Sheldon added, at first belonged only to that stretch of the river.

DocumentedDurant himself gives the meaning as “the boiling-pot, or where the water boils like a pot” (page 56), and so does the county report in the first volume of the Pioneer Collections of Michigan (1877): the river’s name was “Ke-Kenamazoo (the boiling pot).”

DocumentedIn the 1867 telling the runner has no name, there is no bride and there is no date. The Kalamazoo Public Library’s files show the story growing. In a Kalamazoo Gazette article of 20 August 1922 the runner is “Fleet Foot,” he runs to win his bride, and the year is 1810. About 1951 the painter Zoltan Sepeshy put the race in a mural for the Fidelity Federal Savings and Loan on South Burdick Street.

ReadingSo the boiling pot is genuinely old in local tradition: older than any surviving explanation except Schoolcraft’s. The romance came later. Sheldon also credited Schoolcraft with the “boiling pot” meaning, but Schoolcraft’s own published explanation, as the next exhibit shows, is about otters.
OpenWhere did Torrey’s 1867 directory and the Gazette of 10 March 1901, “Origin of the name Kalamazoo,” get the story? Neither is online. The library’s subject file holds both.
## Exhibit G: the scholars

DocumentedSchoolcraft, 1855: otters. In the Summary Narrative of his 1820 expedition, published thirty-five years later, Henry Schoolcraft explained in a footnote that “Kalamazoo” contracted a phrase describing “the stones seen through the water in its bed” which, through the moving current, looked like an otter swimming beneath the surface. His original word was “Negikanamazoo,” from negik, an otter. He added a note that the letter L came in as Indian words passed into French.

DocumentedVerwyst, 1892: smoke. Father Chrysostom Verwyst, who spent his life among Ojibwe speakers, called the name a “corruption of kikanamoso (it smokes, or he is troubled with smoke—e.g., in his wigwam),” pronounced kee-kah-nah-mo-zo.

DocumentedGannett, 1902 and 1905: all of the above. The federal Origin of Certain Place Names in the United States gave “otter tail” on “one authority,” and listed “beautiful water,” “boiling water” and “stones like otters” besides, without choosing.

DocumentedGerard, 1911: not otters. William R. Gerard, writing in the American Anthropologist, called Schoolcraft’s explanations “etymological absurdities” and showed why the otter word could not be built that way. He argued that the name was an old Ojibwe word, kikalâmozo, “he is inconvenienced by smoke in his lodge,” and guessed, admitting it was only a guess, that it had once been a person’s nickname.

DocumentedVogel, 1986: none proven. Virgil Vogel’s Indian Names in Michigan treats “the boiling pot” as an alleged meaning, rejects the otters and the “mirage or reflecting river,” and suggests that the smoke explanations deserve Gerard’s label too. He thought it more credible that the name meant something like “it runs fast,” or that it was a mangled form of another river’s name, and he noted that forms with an L may come from the Miami language.

ReadingThe “mirage” or “reflecting river” meaning, still repeated on many websites, has no early source that we can find. The earliest we know of is a modern place-names dictionary, and Vogel rejected it.

DocumentedThe Kalamazoo Public Library also records a forest-fire legend, in which the name is translated “smothered.” It sits close to the smoke words of Verwyst and Gerard, though no early source for it has turned up.
## Exhibit H: the missing L

DocumentedPotawatomi has no L sound. A Potawatomi language specialist made the point on WMUK in 2018: if “Kalamazoo” comes from a Potawatomi word, it is not a close copy. The linguistic descriptions of the language agree. In Ojibwe, too, the old Algonquian sound that became L in some languages became N.
ReadingNow set the spellings side by side, in the order they were written:

• c. 1760 kikanamaso (Potier)
  • 1821 Kekalamazoo; Ke-kal-i-ma-zoo (Treaty of Chicago)
  • 1822 Kikalemazo (Carey & Lea)
  • 1829–30 Kalamazoo (the county)
  • 1855 Negikanamazoo (Schoolcraft, explaining)
  • 1867 Kih-Kalamazoo (Torrey and Sheldon)
  • 1877 Ke-Kenamazoo (Pioneer Society)
  • 1892 kikanamoso (Verwyst)
  • 2026 Giknamezo zibé, the river (Gun Lake Tribe)

ReadingThe oldest form and the tribal form of today both have an N in the middle. The L belongs to the years when American officials and mapmakers wrote the word down, and it may come from interpreters who spoke a language that had one, as Vogel and Gerard both suggested in different ways. The “Ke-” or “Kik-” at the front, lost in the English name, is in the oldest and in the newest forms alike.
## Exhibit I: the names today

DocumentedPotawatomi has its own names for the place and the river. On WMUK in 2018, a Potawatomi language specialist gave Gzigmezé as the Potawatomi name for Kalamazoo and said it describes a boiling, adding that he was not sure of the word’s origins.

DocumentedIn July 2026 the Gun Lake Tribe (the Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians) presented a talk in Kalamazoo under the title “Gzigmezék mine Giknamezo Zibé.” The event notice glosses Gzigmezék as the past Potawatomi village and present-day Kalamazoo, and Giknamezo zibé as the Kalamazoo River.

ReadingTwo names, then: one for the place, which describes a boiling, and one for the river, which is very close to the oldest spelling on paper. Giknamezo and Potier’s kikanamaso share their consonants in the same order. Verwyst’s kikanamoso of 1892, the “it smokes” word, is close too. If that is right, the old river name and the old village name may both lie behind the English “Kalamazoo,” and the town’s favourite story, the boiling pot, may preserve the place name while the spelling preserves the river’s.

OpenWhat Giknamezo means, and how Gzigmezé and Giknamezo are related, are questions for the people whose language it is. We have not asked them to confirm anything on this page, and nothing here should be taken as their view.
## What became of Titus Bronson

DocumentedBronson left Kalamazoo soon after the change. The library’s biography follows him to Davenport, Iowa, where he lost what he had in a land swindle in 1842, the year his wife Sally died, and then to Illinois. He went home to Connecticut and died at Middlebury in January 1853. His gravestone there calls him “A Western Pioneer, Returned to Sleep with his Fathers.”
ReadingDurant thought Kalamazoo had forgotten him; in 1880 not even a street bore his name, only the park. Today a hospital, the park and a boulevard do.
## The other Kalamazoos

DocumentedKalamazoo has been the name of other places too. Larry Massie told WMUK that two other communities once called themselves Kalamazoo: one in Sheridan Township near Albion, and the village at the river’s mouth that became Saugatuck. Allegan County’s 1907 history also records a paper town, Kalamazoo Harbor, laid out near the mouth of the river.
DocumentedThe painting at the top of this page, William Greason’s Bayou on the Kalamazoo River, Douglas (1934), was made near that mouth, at Douglas, across the river from Saugatuck.
OpenWe have not yet found the Sheridan Township Kalamazoo in any county history, or Saugatuck’s early name in Allegan County’s.

DocumentedThe name itself became famous for sounding like nowhere in particular: “from Timbuktu to Kalamazoo.” Carl Sandburg put it in a poem title, “The Sins of Kalamazoo” (1920), and Glenn Miller’s orchestra took “(I’ve Got a Gal in) Kalamazoo” to the top of the charts in 1942.
## A glossary

Plat
A surveyed map of a new village, dividing it into streets and lots, recorded with the county.
Reserve
Land held back from a treaty cession for a band or a person. The reserve at Match-e-be-nash-she-wish’s village lasted from 1821 to 1827.
Zibé
Potawatomi for “river,” as in Giknamezo zibé, the Kalamazoo River.
Folk etymology
An explanation of a word made up afterwards to fit how it sounds, rather than traced from what it once meant.
Itinerary
In Potier’s papers, a list of the stages of a journey, river by river and portage by portage.
## A timeline

• 1744 Bellin’s map shows a “R. Marameg” on Lake Michigan’s east shore, where the Kalamazoo should be.
  • c. 1760 Potier’s itinerary names the “little” and “great” kikanamaso.
  • 29 Aug 1821 Treaty of Chicago: a reserve “at the head of the Kekalamazoo river.”
  • 1822 Carey & Lea map of Michigan Territory: “Kikalemazo R.” (reissued 1823).
  • 1827 Treaty of St. Joseph: the reserve is ceded.
  • 1829 Titus Bronson settles on the site; the county is laid out on 29 October.
  • 30 Jul 1830 Kalamazoo County organized; Arcadia township created.
  • 12 Mar 1831 The Village of Bronson platted.
  • 2 Mar 1836 Act approved changing Bronson and Arcadia to Kalamazoo, effective 31 March.
  • Jan 1853 Titus Bronson dies at Middlebury, Connecticut.
  • 1855 Schoolcraft’s otters.
  • 1867 Torrey’s village history prints Sheldon’s race to the river.
  • 1877 Pioneer Collections: “Ke-Kenamazoo (the boiling pot).”
  • 1880 Durant’s History of Kalamazoo County.
  • 1892 Verwyst: “it smokes.”
  • 1911 Gerard rejects the otters.
  • 20 Aug 1922 Kalamazoo Gazette: “Fleet Foot,” his bride, and the year 1810.
  • c. 1951 Sepeshy’s mural of the race.
  • 1986 Vogel’s Indian Names in Michigan.
  • 2018 Gzigmezé, “describes a boiling,” on WMUK.
  • Jul 2026 The Gun Lake Tribe’s Gzigmezék and Giknamezo zibé.
## The poster

The whole story on one page, for a classroom, a library wall or a refrigerator door: “How Kalamazoo Got Its Name,” from about 1760 to today, every date from the record, with the spellings in order along the foot. Letter size, landscape; it prints well larger.
## What we are not saying

• Not that we know what Kalamazoo means. Nobody has a speaker’s explanation on record from the time the name was first written down. Every meaning on this page is somebody’s explanation.
  • Not that the race never happened, or that the cherry tree is false. We say only where each story first appears in print, so far as we can find.
  • Not that “Marameg” on Bellin’s map is certainly the Kalamazoo. The position fits; the identification is disputed.
  • Not that Potier walked the river in 1760. The date is his editor’s, and the notes may have been compiled from other travellers.
  • Not that we speak for any Potawatomi nation. We report the names as they have been published, and nothing more.
If anyone can show the cherry tree in a record of the 1830s, or the race story in print before 1867, we will say so on this page, with thanks.
## The picture album

Every picture on this page in one place. The maps, the painting, the portrait and the book pages are all in the public domain; each caption names the library that holds the original. Press any picture to see it full size.

Pictures we know of but cannot yet show. The photograph of Zoltan Sepeshy’s mural of the race, about 1951, is in the Kalamazoo Public Library’s collection; whether the mural itself survives we have not learned. The original plat of the Village of Bronson, 1831, is at the Kalamazoo County Register of Deeds. Titus Bronson’s gravestone stands in Middlebury, Connecticut.
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. Each one says where the answer is most likely to be. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Where is the cherry tree? A fine for stealing a tree would be in a justice of the peace’s docket for Kalamazoo or Arcadia township, about 1832–36. The Kalamazoo Public Library’s subject files and the Western Michigan University archives are the places to ask.
  2. What else did Torrey’s 1867 directory say, beyond the passage Durant reprinted, and what did the Gazette print in 1901? Both are in the library’s file on the name.
  3. Which river was the little kikanamaso? Toupin’s edition of Potier, pages 144 to 151, and his notes.
  4. Was “Marameg” the Kalamazoo? The French maps after Bellin, and the journals of travellers on the lake shore, would settle it.
  5. What does Giknamezo mean? A question for the Potawatomi language programs, and theirs to answer.
  6. Who were “Burdick, Sheldon, and Lyon,” exactly, and why did they want the change? The legislative journals for February and March 1836 may show who brought the bill.
## The pages
Read them yourself. Every book on this page is free online, and the passages are short. The page photographs are below; the full books are linked under Sources.

stories.headline: How Cassopolis got its name
stories.dek: Everyone knows half of it: Cassopolis is the city of Cass. The other half is stranger. The county seat was first somewhere else, the man who won it for Stone Lake is said to have walked through a night of cold rain, and the village was spelled with an A for nearly forty years.
stories.sdek: A governor’s name, a Greek word, a race through the rain, and the A that became an O.

Detail of the 1860 county map’s plan of Cassapolis: Broadway, Rowland and O’Keefe streets running down to Stone Lake
The plan of “Cassapolis” on Geil, Harley & Siverd’s Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien (Philadelphia, 1860), detail. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Ask how Cassopolis got its name and the answer comes quickly: it is the city of Cass, named for Lewis Cass, governor of Michigan Territory, with the Greek word for a city on the end. That much is true. But the county seat was first at another village, the man who won it for Stone Lake is said to have walked through a night of cold rain to do it, and for nearly forty years the post office spelled the name with an A.

We went back to the county’s three histories, of 1875, 1882 and 1906, to Michigan’s first gazetteer of 1838, and to the hand-coloured county map of 1860, to see what the record shows and what is only a good story.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known). Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

The place
Cassopolis, Michigan: the seat of Cass County, on the east shore of Stone Lake
The county
Named Cass by the act of the Legislative Council approved 29 October 1829
First county seat
Not Cassopolis: Geneva, on Diamond Lake, chosen in 1830
The plat
1831: “a village to be called Cassapolis,” laid out by its proprietors on Stone Lake
County seat
By Acting Governor Mason’s proclamation, 19 December 1831
The spelling
“Cassapolis” on the plat and at the post office until 1870; “Cassopolis” in print by 1838
Why it matters
The name everyone can explain has a vowel nobody can; and the town got its name by winning the county seat
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The county was named Cass in 1829. The act says only “the name thereof shall be Cass.” That it honours Lewis Cass is understood, not written.
  • The county seat came first to Geneva, on Diamond Lake, in 1830. A new commission moved it in 1831.
  • The village was platted in 1831 as “Cassapolis,” with an A, and proclaimed the county seat on 19 December 1831.
  • Three streets on the plat carry the commissioners’ names: Disbrow, Rowland and O’Keefe.
  • The O came slowly. “Cassopolis” is in print by 1838, but the post office kept “Cassapolis” until 1870, and the county map of 1860 still letters the village “Cassapolis.”

What it does not show, yet

  • The plat and the governor’s proclamation themselves. We have read them only as the county histories report them.
  • Who chose the name, and why “-polis.”
  • Why the A became an O. The 1906 history thought it was for the sound.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are eight things people say about the name. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“Cassopolis was Cass County’s first county seat.”

No

Rogers’s history of 1875 records that the seat was first located at Geneva, on Diamond Lake, in 1830. It moved to the new plat on Stone Lake by the governor’s proclamation of 19 December 1831.

“The village was first spelled Cassapolis.”

True

Rogers says the plat was “to be called Cassapolis,” and Glover’s history of 1906 says the original spelling, “as found on old letters and the first plat, was ‘Cassapolis.’”

“The law that created the county says it was named in honour of Lewis Cass.”

No

The act of 1829, as the 1882 history prints it, says only “the name thereof shall be Cass.” The honour is understood, not stated.

“Lewis Cass himself chose the name of the village.”

No record

The histories credit the local proprietors with the plat and its name. Nothing we have read connects Cass himself to the choice.

“Three of the town’s streets were named after the men who picked the county seat.”

True

The commissioners were Thomas Rowland, Henry Disbrow and George A. O’Keefe, and Disbrow, Rowland and O’Keefe streets are on the original plat, and on the county map of 1860.

“The change from Cassapolis to Cassopolis was made official by the post office.”

True

Glover says the change was “finally affirmed by the postoffice department.” Postal listings give Cassapolis from 1832 and Cassopolis from 1870.

“As late as 1860, the county map still spelled it Cassapolis.”

True

The plan of the village on Geil, Harley & Siverd’s map of 1860 is headed “CASSAPOLIS. County Seat of Cass Co.”

“The county seat was won in a race through the night.”

A good story

Rogers tells it in 1875, forty-four years after the event: E. B. Sherman heard of rivals’ plans and set out on foot “through the cold rain and dismal darkness in this race for a County seat.” No record of 1831 tells it.
## The county named Cass

DocumentedCass County was set off by an act of the Legislative Council of Michigan Territory approved on 29 October 1829. The act draws the county’s lines and ends that the land “be, and the same is hereby set off into a separate county and the name thereof shall be Cass.”

ReadingThe act names no one. That the county honours Lewis Cass, governor of the territory from 1813 to 1831, is the reading everyone has always given, and it is surely right; but it is understood, not written. Henry Gannett’s federal Origin of Certain Place Names (1905) lists the county and the village among the names given “for Gen. Lewis Cass, governor of Michigan in 1820.”
## The county seat that came first

DocumentedCassopolis was not the first county seat. Howard S. Rogers, in the county’s first history (1875), writes that “sometime in 1830 the County seat of Cass County was located at Geneva, on the bank of Diamond Lake,” by commissioners appointed by the governor. Geneva had been named, Rogers says, after the village of that name in New York.

DocumentedRogers also passes on a story about how Geneva lost: “it is said that some of the Commissioners ... withheld information of their decision one day, and in the mean-time sent an agent to the Land Office.”
Reading“It is said” is Rogers’s own warning. The story may be true, but it is a rumour he heard, not a record he read.

DocumentedOn 4 March 1831, Rogers reports, the Legislative Council passed an act for a new commission to relocate the seats of justice of Cass, St. Joseph and Branch counties. The commissioners for Cass, Glover’s history of 1906 says, were Thomas Rowland, Henry Disbrow and George A. O’Keefe, and they were to meet in the county “on the third Monday in May, 1831.”
## A race through the rain

DocumentedRogers tells how the new site was won. E. B. Sherman, one of the men who would own it, learned of other men’s plans for the land on Stone Lake, “kept his own counsel,” took his leave, and “started on foot for Edwardsburg”; and on he went, “through the cold rain and dismal darkness in this race for a County seat,” to enter the land first.

ReadingIt is a fine story, and it may be true in its outline: whoever owned the land the commissioners chose stood to gain a town. But Rogers wrote it down forty-four years later, from what old settlers told him, and we have found no record of 1831 that tells it.
## A village to be called Cassapolis

DocumentedRogers again: the proprietors “prepared a plat of a village to be called Cassapolis, containing one hundred and sixty acres of land, and each of the four proprietors signed an agreement to donate to the County one-half of his portion of the same, providing the County seat should be located thereon.” Glover, in 1906, counts not four but five proprietors whose names are signed to the plat: E. B. Sherman, A. H. Redfield, Abram Tietsort, Oliver Johnson and Ephraim McCleary.
DocumentedThe commissioners chose the site, and Acting Governor Stevens T. Mason’s proclamation fixing the seat of justice there was, the 1882 history says, “issued December 19, 1831.”

DocumentedThe proprietors had made sure of the commissioners’ goodwill. Glover writes that they “announced with effective ostentation the naming of three principal streets after the commissioners,” and he lists Disbrow, Rowland and O’Keefe streets on the plat. Copies of the original plat, he adds, “are still extant.”

ReadingCass for the governor and the county; polis, Greek for a city, for the town. It was a fashionable ending in the 1820s and 1830s; Indianapolis had been named in 1821. Nobody recorded who chose it.
## The A and the O

DocumentedThe first post office, the 1882 history says, had Alexander H. Redfield, one of the proprietors, as its postmaster. Postal-history listings give the office as “Cassapolis” from 1832 to 1870 and “Cassopolis” from 1870.

DocumentedThe O was in print long before the post office took it. John T. Blois’s Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838) has “Cassopolis, village, post office, and seat of justice” for Cass County.
DocumentedEven the town’s own historian used both. Rogers’s book of 1875 was printed at “Cassopolis, Mich.,” as its title page says, but his chapter on the village calls it “Cassapolis” throughout.

DocumentedGlover, in 1906, gives the only explanation we have: “the change from a to o, which was clearly dictated by euphony, took place gradually in custom and was finally affirmed by the postoffice department.”
Reading“Euphony” is Glover’s guess. An O also matches the other -opolis towns, from Annapolis to Indianapolis, and that may have pulled the spelling as much as the sound did.
## Stone Lake

DocumentedThe village grew on the east shore of Stone Lake. The 1882 history says the lake was “so named from the fact that its shores were originally very thickly strewn with stone.” A settler named Abram Tietsort had built a log cabin on the east bank in 1829 or 1830; the histories disagree by a year.
OpenWho named the lake, and when, we have not found.
## The name on paper
Play the spellings in order, from the county of 1829 to the town today.

• 1829 Cass (the county, by act of 29 October)
  • 1831 Cassapolis (the plat)
  • 1832 Cassapolis (the post office)
  • 1838 Cassopolis (Blois’s gazetteer)
  • 1860 Cassapolis (the county map)
  • 1870 Cassopolis (the post office)
  • 1875 Cassopolis (Rogers’s title page, with Cassapolis inside)
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. What exactly does the plat say? The original is recorded with Cass County; the histories quote it only in part.
  2. Who chose the name? Nothing yet found says which proprietor, or why -polis.
  3. Where is the earliest “Cassopolis”? We have it in 1838. Letters or newspapers of 1832–37 may have it sooner.
  4. Was the race in the rain real? A land-office entry for the plat’s quarter-section, with its date, would test Rogers’s story.
  5. Who named Stone Lake?
