stories.kicker: How the towns got their names
stories.headline: How Dowagiac got its name
stories.dek: Dowagiac was a river before it was a town. The railroad made the village in 1848 and the village took the creek’s name; the county history of 1875 says the word means “fishing-water,” and a newspaper of 2023 says “foraging ground.” We went back to the record.
stories.sdek: A creek’s name, a railroad town, a paper town called Venice, and two meanings.
pic: /img/news/how-dowagiac-got-its-name
A colour postcard of the mill and mill pond at Dowagiac, a tall frame mill beside the dammed creek, with a concrete bridge and autumn trees
Mill and Mill Pond, Dowagiac, Mich., colour postcard, Tichnor Brothers, about 1930–45: the dammed creek that gave the town its name. Boston Public Library, Tichnor Brothers Collection.
body: Dowagiac, Mich. Dowagiac is the rare valley town that did not grow slowly from a cabin and a mill. It was made almost at once, in 1848, when the Michigan Central Railroad came through and two men laid out a village beside the depot. The name was already waiting for it: the Dowagiac was the creek, and had been in print for at least ten years.
What the word means is another matter. We went back to Michigan’s first gazetteer of 1838, the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906, and what is said about the name today.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known). Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

The place
Dowagiac, Michigan: a city in Cass County, on Dowagiac Creek and the Michigan Central line
The creek first
“Dowagiake river” in Blois’s Gazetteer of 1838, ten years before the town
The plat
Recorded 16 February 1848, beside the planned depot grounds
Founders
Nicholas Cheeseborough, the railroad’s right-of-way agent, and Jacob Beeson of Niles
Before
Venice, a “paper town” laid out nearby in 1836 that was never built
The meaning
“Fishing-water,” says the county history of 1875; “foraging ground,” say writers today; no early source for either
Why it matters
The town is the railroad’s; the name is the creek’s
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The name belonged to the creek first. Blois’s state gazetteer of 1838 lists the “Dowagiake river” among the county’s water-courses.
  • The village was made by the railroad. Its plat was recorded on 16 February 1848, and “Front street runs parallel to the track.”
  • A paper town, Venice, had been laid out nearby in 1836 and never built.
  • The first post office was kept in a boarding house for railroad hands, the Cataract House.

What it does not show, yet

  • Who first called the new village Dowagiac.
  • What the word meant to the people who first said it. The county history’s “fishing-water” gives no source.
  • An earlier spelling than Dowagiake, on the maps of the 1820s and 1830s.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are eight things people say about the name. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“Dowagiac was a creek’s name before it was a town’s.”

True

Blois’s Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838) lists the “Dowagiake river” in Cass County, ten years before the town was platted.

“The Michigan Central Railroad chose the name Dowagiac.”

No record

Rogers calls the village “Born of the Michigan Central Railroad,” but no source says who picked the name. It was already the creek’s.

“The village plat was recorded in 1848.”

True

Glover, 1906: the original plat “was recorded in the register’s office February 16, 1848.”

“A town called Venice was laid out near the site twelve years earlier.”

True

Rogers calls Venice, laid out in August 1836, a “paper town … known only by name and record at the County Seat.”

“The 1875 county history says Dowagiac means ‘fishing-water.’”

True

Rogers: “The name Dowagiac is of Indian origin, and signifies fishing-water.” He gives no source for it.

“The nineteenth-century histories say the name means ‘foraging ground.’”

No

The 1875 and 1882 histories both say “fishing water.” “Foraging ground” appears in writing of our own century.

“Dowagiac had a long pioneer history before the railroad came.”

No

Rogers, 1875: “Dowagiac had little or no pioneer history.”

“The town’s first post office was kept in a railroad boarding house.”

True

Rogers: the Cataract House, built as a boarding house for railroad hands. “In it the Postoffice was first kept.”
## The creek

DocumentedThe oldest form of the name we have found is in John T. Blois’s Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838). Among the water-courses of Cass County it lists “Christiana river, Corbett’s river, Dowagiake river, Putnam’s creek,” and it says Putnam’s creek discharges “into the Dowagiake river.”
DocumentedThe low ground around the creek bore the name too. “In 1838,” Rogers writes, “the first road across the Dowagiac Swamp was partially built, and completed the next year.”
OpenThe hand-coloured maps of the territory from the 1820s and 1830s almost certainly letter the creek too. We have not yet read their lettering.
## Venice, the town that never was

DocumentedBefore Dowagiac there was Venice, on paper. Rogers: “The ancient town of Venice, situated in that part of the Township, where Dowagiac now stands, was a ‘paper town’ laid out by Orlando Crane, in August 1836, and known only by name and record at the County Seat.” Glover, in 1906, found “a plat of the village of Venice, filed for record August 6, 1836,” and places it diagonally across the township corner from the later town.
ReadingVenice was one of many paper towns of the land boom of 1836, platted for sale and never built. It shares nothing with Dowagiac but the ground, or the ground next door.
## A town born of the railroad

DocumentedRogers tells it plainly. In 1847 Nicholas Cheeseborough (Glover spells it Cheesebrough) “was employed by the Michigan Central Railroad Company to procure the right of way from Kalamazoo to Niles. As soon as the location of the depot sites was determined at headquarters, he associated with himself Jacob Beeson, of Niles, and together they purchased (in Mr. Beeson’s name) the northeastern eighty acres in Pokagon Township and soon after had it platted in village lots.” They gave the railroad its right of way and “spacious depot grounds, a portion of which was set aside as a public park.”

DocumentedGlover adds that the eighty acres, in the northeast corner of Pokagon township, were bought of Patrick Hamilton, and that the original plat of Dowagiac “was recorded in the register’s office February 16, 1848.” The railroad was not yet running; trains reached Niles that October. “In the words of the plat, ‘Front street runs parallel to the track of the Michigan Central railroad.’”

DocumentedThe first post office, Rogers says, was kept in the Cataract House, a boarding house built for the railroad hands. Postal listings date the Dowagiac office from 1848. The first sermon in the village was preached in July 1848. “Dowagiac,” Rogers sums up, “had little or no pioneer history.”
ReadingNobody records who decided to call the new village Dowagiac. The creek and the swamp already had the name, and the depot sat in the creek country; the name was the obvious one.
## Fishing-water, or foraging ground?

DocumentedRogers, 1875: “The name Dowagiac is of Indian origin, and signifies fishing-water.” The 1882 history agrees: “The name of this stream is of Indian origin, and its meaning is ‘fishing water.’” Neither says who told them.

DocumentedSome writers today give “foraging ground.” A Dowagiac newspaper series for the city’s 175th anniversary, in 2023, gives the source word as Ndowagayuk and the meaning as “foraging ground,” reflecting the area’s game, fruit, grain and herbs.

ReadingBoth meanings are explanations, not records. The nineteenth-century one came from settlers’ hearsay; the modern one is a reading from the language, and may well be the better. What the word meant to the people who first named the creek is not written down anywhere we have found.
## The name on paper
Play the names in order, from the paper town to the city.

• 1836 Venice (the paper town nearby)
  • 1838 Dowagiake river (Blois’s gazetteer)
  • 1848 Dowagiac (the plat, 16 February)
  • 1848 Dowagiac (the post office)
  • 1875 Dowagiac (Rogers)
  • 2023 Ndowagayuk (a modern reading)
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Who named the village Dowagiac? The recorded plat of 16 February 1848, at the Cass County register of deeds, may say who signed it and under what name.
  2. How do the early maps spell the creek? The territorial maps of the 1820s and 1830s are the next place to look.
  3. Where did “fishing-water” come from? Rogers names no informant.

stories.kicker: How the towns got their names
stories.headline: How Niles got its name
stories.dek: Before it was Niles it was Pog-wa-tigue, a trading settlement on the St. Joseph. The village took the name of a Baltimore newspaper editor in 1829, the county history explains why only in 1906, and of the four flags of its nickname, the record shows three, one of them flown for a day or less.
stories.sdek: Pog-wa-tigue, a Baltimore editor, a plat recorded in Lenawee County, and three flags, one of them for a day or less.
pic: /img/news/how-niles-got-its-name
Detail of the 1860 county map’s plan of the City of Niles, coloured by additions, with the St. Joseph River, Main Street and E. Lacey’s Addition

The City of Niles on Geil, Harley & Siverd’s Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien (Philadelphia, 1860), detail; the Laceys’ name is still on an addition by the river. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division.
body: Niles, Mich. Niles is named for a newspaper editor who never lived here: Hezekiah Niles of Baltimore, whose Weekly Register was read across the young republic. That much is in every guidebook. Less often told is that the settlement had another name first, written at the head of a trader’s account book; that the village plat was recorded in a county more than a hundred miles away; and that the county’s own history gave no reason for the name until 1906.
We went back to the Berrien County histories of 1880 and 1906, the state’s historical marker at the fort, and the county map of 1860, to see what the record shows.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known). Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

The place
Niles, Michigan: a city in Berrien County on the St. Joseph River
First name
“Pog-wa-tigue,” the trading settlement, 1828–29
The plat
Signed 1 August 1829 for the traders Walling & Lacey; recorded in Lenawee County on 29 August 1829 as “the plat of the village of Niles”
Named for
Hezekiah Niles, editor of the Niles’ Register of Baltimore, chosen by Obed P. Lacey, says the county history of 1906
Village and city
Incorporated as a village 12 February 1835; city charter 12 February 1859
Nearby
The French Fort St. Joseph, south of the city, from the 1690s
Why it matters
The name is a reader’s tribute, and the explanation of it came late
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The trading settlement was called “Pog-wa-tigue” in 1828–29; a trader’s account book of 1 January 1829 is headed with it.
  • The village plat was signed on 1 August 1829 and recorded in Lenawee County, then the county for this part of the territory, as “the plat of the village of Niles.”
  • The name honours Hezekiah Niles of Baltimore, chosen, says the 1906 history, by Obed P. Lacey, a reader of his paper.
  • France and Britain held Fort St. Joseph, and Spain held it for a day or less in February 1781: hours, says the state marker; a few days, says Coolidge.

What it does not show, yet

  • A record of 1829 that gives Lacey’s reason. The 1880 history does not explain the name at all.
  • What “Pog-wa-tigue” meant. The 1880 history says “running water,” and gives no source.
  • Any record of a United States flag or garrison at the fort.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are eight things people say about the name. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“Niles was named for Hezekiah Niles, the Baltimore editor.”

True, as printed

Coolidge’s county history of 1906 says Obed Lacey named it “after the name of the editor of the Niles Register.” The 1880 history gives no reason at all.

“Niles was named after the town’s own newspaper editor.”

No

In 1829 the settlement had no newspaper. The editor was Hezekiah Niles, in Baltimore.

“Before it was Niles, the settlement was called Pog-wa-tigue.”

True

The traders’ account books open “Pog-wa-tigue, Jan. 1, 1829,” and in 1828 “the settlement was then called Pog-wa-tigue,” says the 1880 history.

“Pog-wa-tigue means ‘running water.’”

No record

The 1880 history prints “(running water)” beside it, but gives no source, and we have found no linguist’s analysis.

“The village was platted on 1 August 1829.”

True

The plat was signed by William Justus and by Samuel B. Walling for Walling & Lacey on 1 August 1829.

“The first plat of Niles was recorded in Berrien County.”

No

It was “registered in liber A, folios 134 and 135, records of Lenawee County” on 29 August 1829. Berrien County had only just been set off, and was not yet organized.

“The Register was a Whig paper when Niles was named.”

No

The 1906 history calls it “a Whig newspaper,” but the Whig party did not exist until 1833–34, four years after the plat.

“Four flags, the Stars and Stripes among them, flew over Fort St. Joseph.”

Three, and one barely

France and Britain held the fort, and a Spanish force from St. Louis raised its flag there for a few hours in February 1781. We have found no record of a United States flag or garrison at the fort.
## Pog-wa-tigue

DocumentedThe traders came first. The account books of Walling & Lacey for 1829, the 1880 county history says, open under the heading “Pog-wa-tigue, Jan. 1, 1829.” In 1828, the same history says, “the settlement was then called Pog-wa-tigue (running water).”
ReadingThe gloss “running water” is printed without a source, and we have not found a linguist’s account of the word. It may be right; it is not yet proven.

DocumentedThere was a post office before there was a plat. In the fall of 1828, the 1880 history says, “Obed P. Lacey was appointed as acting postmaster; the office was kept in Mr. Walling’s house.” Isaac Gray received the first regular commission in 1830.
## The plat of the village of Niles

DocumentedOn 1 August 1829, the 1880 history says, a village plat was laid out on the southwest fractional quarter of section 26, “signed by William Justus and by Samuel B. Walling, on behalf of Walling & Lacey,” and acknowledged before Ezra Beardsley, a justice of the peace. It was “registered in liber A, folios 134 and 135, records of Lenawee County, Saturday, Aug. 29, 1829,” and recorded “as the plat of the village of Niles.”

ReadingLenawee? In August 1829 there was no Berrien County government yet. The county was set off that October and organized later, and this corner of the territory was attached for record-keeping to counties far to the east. The earliest dated “Niles” we have found is that plat of 1 August 1829.

DocumentedOn 29 October 1829 the township of Niles was erected, the same day Berrien County was set off. The village was incorporated by an act approved 12 February 1835, and Niles became a city by charter on 12 February 1859.
## Why Niles?

DocumentedThe 1880 history, for all its detail, never says why the village was called Niles. The explanation enters the county histories with Orville W. Coolidge in 1906: “The village was designated by Obed Lacey as Niles after the name of the editor of the Niles Register,” which Coolidge calls “a Whig newspaper published at Baltimore, which was a favorite journal of Mr. Lacey.”

ReadingCoolidge was writing seventy-seven years later, and his “Whig” is wrong for 1829: the Whig party formed in 1833–34. But the attribution is reasonable. Hezekiah Niles (1777–1839) had published his Weekly Register at Baltimore since 1811, and it was one of the most widely read news digests of its day.
DocumentedSome modern summaries say the town was named for “the town newspaper editor.” In 1829 Niles had no newspaper.
## Three flags and a few hours

DocumentedNiles calls itself the City of Four Flags. The French built Fort St. Joseph on the river south of the present city; the state’s historical marker of 1957 dates it to 1691. Britain took the fort in 1761. In February 1781 a Spanish force from St. Louis, Coolidge writes, “captured Fort St. Joseph, hauled down the British flag and raised the Spanish flag. The Spanish troops remained but a few days.” The state marker says the Spanish flag flew “for a few hours.”

ReadingThe United States gained the region by treaty in 1783 and took possession of the western posts in 1796, but we have found no record of an American flag or garrison at the fort itself. The phrase “four flags” is in print by 1907, in Daniel McCoy’s address Old Fort St. Joseph; or, Michigan under Four Flags.
OpenAn earlier printing of “four flags,” or a record of the Stars and Stripes at the fort, would change this section.
## The name on paper
Play the names in order, from the trader’s ledger to the city.

• 1829 Pog-wa-tigue (Walling & Lacey’s account book, 1 January)
  • 1829 Niles (the plat, 1 August)
  • 1829 township of Niles (29 October)
  • 1835 village of Niles (the act of incorporation)
  • 1859 City of Niles (the city charter)
  • 1860 City of Niles (the county map)
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Why Niles? A letter, a newspaper or a record of 1829 that gives Obed Lacey’s reason would settle it.
  2. What did Pog-wa-tigue mean? A published dictionary of the language, not the county history’s gloss, is needed.
  3. When did the post office take the name Niles? The Post Office Department’s register would say.
  4. Who first wrote “four flags”? We have it by 1907.

stories.kicker: How the towns got their names
stories.headline: How Edwardsburg got its name
stories.dek: It began as Beardsley’s Prairie, had a post office before it had a plat, and was named for an Edwards. The county histories say which one; an old family memoir says another. We went back to the record.
stories.sdek: Beardsley’s Prairie, a storekeeper, a major, and a disputed Edwards.
pic: /img/news/how-edwardsburg-got-its-name
Detail of the 1860 county map’s plan of Edwardsburgh, with Silver’s Addition in green and Silver and Sherwood’s in pink along the Chicago Road
The plan of “Edwardsburgh” on Geil, Harley & Siverd’s Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien (Philadelphia, 1860), detail. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division.
body: Edwardsburg, Mich. Edwardsburg is named for an Edwards; nobody disputes that. Which Edwards is another matter. The county histories name the storekeeper who opened the first store in the county here in 1828. A memoir printed by Michigan’s pioneer society in 1888 names his father, the major. And before there was any Edwardsburg at all, the place was Beardsley’s Prairie.
We went back to the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906, the pioneer society’s memoir, Michigan’s first gazetteer of 1838 and the county map of 1860, to see what the record shows.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known). Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

The place
Edwardsburg, Michigan: a village in Cass County on Pleasant Lake and the old Chicago Road
First name
Beardsley’s Prairie, after Ezra Beardsley, the first settler on it, about 1826
Post office
By 1830, a year before the plat
The plat
Laid out by Alexander H. Edwards, 12 August 1831
Named for
Thomas H. Edwards, the county’s first merchant, say the histories of 1875 and 1882; “Maj. Edwards,” says a memoir of 1888
Spellings
Edwardsburgh and Edwardsburg, side by side in 1838; Edwardsburgh still on the county map of 1860
Why it matters
The county’s government began here, in Ezra Beardsley’s house, in 1831
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The prairie came first. It was “named after Ezra Beardsley, the first settler on it.”
  • There was a post office by 1830, “near the house of Ezra Beardsley,” a year before the village was laid out.
  • Alexander H. Edwards laid out the village on 12 August 1831, thirty-one blocks.
  • The histories of 1875 and 1882 name Thomas H. Edwards, the first merchant, as the man the town was named for. A memoir of 1888 says “Maj. Edwards,” the family’s father.
  • Cass County’s government began here: the first circuit court in August 1831 and the first board of supervisors in October, at Beardsley’s house.

What it does not show, yet

  • Which Edwards the founders meant. No naming document has been found.
  • The plat itself and the first post-office record, seen in the original.
  • Where the township name Ontwa really came from.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are eight things people say about the name. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“Before it was Edwardsburg, the place was Beardsley’s Prairie.”

True

The prairie was “named after Ezra Beardsley, the first settler on it,” says the 1882 history, and an 1888 memoir says a family arriving in 1828 “reached Beardsley’s prairie, Cass county, now Edwardsburg.”

“Ezra Beardsley named the village.”

No record

His name stayed on the prairie. Every source gives the village name to the Edwards family.

“The town was named for its first storekeeper.”

True, say the histories

Rogers (1875) and the 1882 history both name Thomas H. Edwards, who opened the county’s first store here in 1828. An 1888 memoir credits “Maj. Edwards” instead, almost certainly his father.

“Edwardsburg was platted in 1828.”

No

1828 is when Edwards opened his store. Rogers dates the plat, by Alexander H. Edwards, to “August 12th, 1831.”

“Edwardsburg had a post office before it had a plat.”

True

A road act of 30 July 1830 runs the Chicago road “a few rods west of the post office, near the house of Ezra Beardsley.” Postal listings date the Edwardsburg office from 1830.

“Cass County’s government began in a house in Edwardsburg.”

True

The first circuit court opened at Ezra Beardsley’s house in August 1831, and the first board of supervisors met there on 4 October 1831.

“The name was once spelled Edwardsburgh.”

True

Blois’s gazetteer of 1838 prints both “Edwardsburgh” and “Edwardsburg,” and the county map of 1860 still letters the village “Edwardsburgh.”

“Ontwa Township was named for a Native girl who worked for Edwards.”

A story

Rogers tells it in 1875, but no earlier document confirms it. “Ontwa” was also the title of a long poem published in New York in 1822, seven years before the county existed. Nothing yet links the township to either.
## Beardsley’s Prairie

DocumentedThe first name on this ground belongs to the prairie. Rogers’s history of 1875 describes “a settlement made by Ezra Beardsley, on the prairie that still bears his name,” and the 1882 history says the prairie was “named after Ezra Beardsley, the first settler on it.” Glover’s history of 1906 places it beside “the beautiful sheet of water rightly named Pleasant lake.” Beardsley, Rogers says, kept the first hotel, on the bank of the lake.
DocumentedThe two names lived side by side for a while. A list of Bishop Chase’s preaching stations, printed in the 1882 history, has “Beardsley’s Prairie or Edwardsburg.”
ReadingStrictly, Beardsley’s Prairie was the name of the open ground, not of a village. We have found no plat or post office under that name.
## A post office before a plat

DocumentedA territorial road act of 30 July 1830, quoted in the 1882 history, runs the Chicago road “a few rods west of the post office, near the house of Ezra Beardsley.” Postal-history listings date the office, as “Edwardsburg” or “Edwardsburgh,” from 1830.

DocumentedThe county’s first circuit court opened at Beardsley’s house on 9 August 1831, and the first board of supervisors met there on 4 October 1831, “at the house of Ezra Beardsley (now Edwardsburg),” as Rogers puts it.
## Which Edwards?

DocumentedRogers, 1875: “Edwardsburg was laid out by Alexander H. Edwards, August 12th, 1831, comprising thirty-one blocks.” On the same page he names the man the village was named for: Thomas H. Edwards, who in 1828 “commenced to sell goods and was the first merchant in the County.” The 1882 history agrees, “Thomas H. Edwards, from whom Edwardsburg was named,” and adds that he kept his goods in a pole shanty on Lake Street, and in the fall of 1831 sold his stock and his village lots to Jacob and Abiel Silver and moved on.

DocumentedThe Pioneer Society of Michigan printed a different account in 1888, in a memoir of the Edwards family. A family arriving from Detroit in 1828 with ten children, it says, “reached Beardsley’s prairie, Cass county, now Edwardsburg, named after Maj. Edwards.” The memoir calls him “the late Major Abram Edwards” and names Oliver and Alexander among his sons.

ReadingThe two accounts are easily reconciled. Alexander, who laid out the village, and Thomas, who kept the store, were very probably the major’s sons; the town took the family’s name. Which of them the founders had in mind, the record does not say.
## Burg and burgh

DocumentedBlois’s Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838) prints the name both ways: “Edwardsburgh,” where it describes the proposed southern railway, and “Edwardsburg village and post office,” ten miles southwest of Cassopolis on the Chicago turnpike. The plan of the village on the county map of 1860 is headed “EDWARDSBURGH.”
ReadingThe -burgh ending, as in Pittsburgh, was common for American towns of the time, and it wore away in everyday use. No source we have read comments on the change.
## Ontwa

DocumentedEdwardsburg lies in Ontwa Township, organized in 1833. Rogers says the township “was called after an Indian girl of that name, who, for a number of years, was in the employ of Thomas H. Edwards.”

ReadingRogers gives no source, and there is another candidate. A long poem titled Ontwa, the Son of the Forest was published in New York in 1822, seven years before the county existed. Neither explanation is proven.
OpenWhere the name Ontwa came from is still open.
## The name on paper
Play the names in order, from the prairie to the village today.

• c. 1826 Beardsley’s Prairie (the first settler)
  • 1830 Edwardsburgh (the post office, per postal listings)
  • 1831 Edwardsburg (the plat, as Rogers reports it)
  • c. 1832 Beardsley’s Prairie or Edwardsburg (Bishop Chase’s stations)
  • 1838 Edwardsburgh (Blois, with Edwardsburg too)
  • 1860 Edwardsburgh (the county map)
  • 1875 Edwardsburg (Rogers)
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Which Edwards? A letter, a deed or a newspaper of 1830–31 that names the village after one of them would settle it.
  2. What does the plat say? The original of 12 August 1831 is recorded with Cass County.
  3. Was there an earlier post office here? A “Saint Josephs” office is listed in Cass County for 1829–30; whether it stood at Beardsley’s is not yet known.
  4. Where did the name Ontwa come from?

stories.headline: How Paw Paw got its name
stories.short: How Paw Paw got its name
stories.dek: Paw Paw is named for its river, and the river for the pawpaw tree. But “pawpaw” is not a Native word, the village was laid out as Paw Paw, not Lafayette, and the first Paw Paw in local government was in the next county. We went back to the record.
stories.sdek: A river, a tree, an English word, and a township called Lafayette.
pic: /img/news/how-paw-paw-got-its-name
Detail of the 1860 county map’s plan of Paw Paw, county seat of Van Buren County, with the Paw Paw River winding past the village and Gremps Street

The plan of Paw Paw, “County Seat of Van Buren Co.,” on Geil, Harley & Siverd’s Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien (Philadelphia, 1860), detail. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division.
body: Paw Paw, Mich. Paw Paw takes its name from the Paw Paw River, and the river from the pawpaw, the small native tree with the big tropical-tasting fruit that grew, the county history says, thickly along its banks. So far, so simple. But the county history says the river was “named by the Indians,” and pawpaw is an English word; many people believe the village was first called Lafayette, though it was laid out as Paw Paw; and the first place in local government to be called Paw Paw was in Berrien County.
We went back to the county history of 1880, the federal place-names list of 1905, the state’s historical marker at the courthouse and the county map of 1860 to see what the record shows.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known). Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

The place
Paw Paw, Michigan: the seat of Van Buren County, at the forks of the Paw Paw River
Laid out
By the mill-owners Peter Gremps and Lyman J. Daniels, who bought the site in 1833: “a village which they called Paw Paw”
Post office
1835, with Peter Gremps as postmaster
County seat
1837, chosen by the supervisors over a governor’s commission’s choice of Lawrence
The township
Lafayette from 1835; renamed Paw Paw on 15 March 1867
First “Paw Paw”
A Berrien County township of 7 March 1831, now Watervliet and Hagar townships
Why it matters
The village kept its river’s name all along; it was the township that was called Lafayette
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The village was named for the river: the founders laid out “a village which they called Paw Paw.”
  • Lafayette was the township, from 1835, not the village. The township took the village’s name on 15 March 1867.
  • The post office opened in 1835 under Peter Gremps; the county seat came in 1837.
  • The first civil “Paw Paw” was in Berrien County, a township erected in 1831 on the same river.

What it does not show, yet

  • Any Native-language name of the river, in a published source.
  • When the village plat was recorded, and when the village was incorporated: 1837 and 1867 are both given.
  • Why the township was called Lafayette.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are eight things people say about the name. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“Paw Paw takes its name from the Paw Paw River.”

True

The 1880 county history says the township was named from the village in 1867, and the village “was itself called after the river.”

“The village of Paw Paw was first called Lafayette.”

No

Lafayette was the township, from 1835 to 1867. The founders “laid out … a village which they called Paw Paw,” and the county-seat papers of 1837 say “village of Paw Paw.”

“The township changed its name from Lafayette to Paw Paw in 1867.”

True

“The name of the township of Lafayette was changed to Paw Paw on the 15th of March, 1867,” says the 1880 history.

“‘Pawpaw’ is a Potawatomi word.”

No

It is an English word, most likely from the Spanish papaya, and was used for the North American tree by about 1760.

“The Indians named the river for the pawpaw fruit.”

No record

The 1880 history says so, but it prints no Native-language name for the river, and we have not found one in any published source.

“Peter Gremps was Paw Paw’s first postmaster.”

True

“Peter Gremps was the first postmaster of Paw Paw, his appointment dating from 1835.” A street on the 1860 map carries his name.

“The state first picked Lawrence, not Paw Paw, as county seat.”

True

The state’s historical marker at the courthouse says that in 1837 “a gubernatorial commission chose Lawrence as the seat, but the board of supervisors chose Paw Paw.”

“The first Paw Paw in local government was in Van Buren County.”

No

Berrien County had a “township of Paw Paw … erected March 7, 1831,” now Watervliet and Hagar townships, four years before Van Buren’s Paw Paw post office.
## The river and the tree

DocumentedThe 1880 county history says the township “was named from” the village in 1867, and the village “was itself called after the river, named by the Indians from the paw paw fruit, growing thickly upon its banks.” Henry Gannett’s federal Origin of Certain Place Names (1905) agrees, writing it as one word: Pawpaw, named for the “presence of pawpaw trees.”

ReadingThe tree is real enough. The pawpaw, Asimina triloba, grows wild in southwest Michigan, near the northern edge of its range. But “pawpaw” is an English word, most likely from the Spanish papaya, first used for the tropical fruit and applied to this tree by about 1760. So the river’s English name may translate a Native one; it cannot be one.
OpenThe history prints no Native-language name for the river, and we have found none in a published source. If the river had one, it is still to be found.
## A village which they called Paw Paw

DocumentedPeter Gremps and Lyman J. Daniels bought the mill property at the forks of the river in 1833, the 1880 history says, and “laid out upon it a village which they called Paw Paw.” A settler named Rodney Hinckley had taken up a farm on the north side of the future village in 1832.

Documented“Peter Gremps was the first postmaster of Paw Paw, his appointment dating from 1835.” The county’s supervisors met “at the village of Paw Paw on the 27th day of March, A.D. 1837,” and the seat of justice was located “in the village of Paw Paw.”

DocumentedThe state’s historical marker at the courthouse adds that in 1837 “a gubernatorial commission chose Lawrence as the seat, but the board of supervisors chose Paw Paw,” and that the county’s voters kept the seat in Paw Paw on 1 April 1901.
## The township called Lafayette

DocumentedIn 1835 the Legislative Council formed the whole of Van Buren County into one township, called Lafayette. When the county was divided in 1837, “the present Paw Paw retained the old name of Lafayette.” Then: “The name of the township of Lafayette was changed to Paw Paw on the 15th of March, 1867.”

ReadingSo for thirty years the village of Paw Paw stood in the township of Lafayette, and the two names were easily confused, even at the time: an early court paper is returnable “at the court-house in Lafayette.” That is almost certainly where the belief that the village was first called Lafayette comes from.
OpenWhy Lafayette? The Marquis de Lafayette’s tour of America in 1824–25 made his name popular for new towns, but the history does not say, and we have found no record of the choice.
## The other Paw Paw

DocumentedThe first Paw Paw in local government was not here. The 1880 history records that “the township of Paw Paw was erected March 7, 1831,” in Berrien County, on the lower river, on the ground of today’s Watervliet and Hagar townships. That was four years before the Van Buren County post office.
## The name on paper
Play the names in order, from the river township of 1831 to the town today.

• 1831 Paw Paw township (Berrien County, now Watervliet and Hagar)
  • 1833 Forks of the Paw Paw (a road act, as the 1880 history reports it)
  • 1835 Paw Paw (the post office)
  • 1835 Lafayette (the township, Van Buren County)
  • 1837 village of Paw Paw (the county-seat papers)
  • 1867 Lafayette becomes Paw Paw (the township renamed)
  • 1905 Pawpaw (Gannett, as one word)
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Did the river have a Native name? A published vocabulary or an early traveller’s account may hold it.
  2. When was the village plat recorded? The Van Buren County register of deeds would say.
  3. When was the village incorporated? The 1880 history says the spring of 1867; other summaries say 1837. The session laws will settle it.
  4. Why Lafayette?

stories.kicker: How the towns got their names
stories.headline: How Vandalia got its name
stories.dek: No source we have read explains why Vandalia is called Vandalia. The record shows a post office in 1850, a grist mill, a plat in 1851, and a creek named in 1822 by a missionary for his wife. Here is what is known, and the guesses that are not.
stories.sdek: A post office, a Quaker mill, a missionary’s wife, and a name nobody explained.
pic: /img/news/how-vandalia-got-its-name
The old mill at Vandalia, a weathered two-storey frame mill above its mill race and pond, about 1908–1918
The Old Mill, Vandalia, Mich., real-photo postcard, about 1908–1918. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan.
body: Vandalia, Mich. Some town names explain themselves, and some are explained in every county history. Vandalia is neither. It grew up around a grist mill on a creek in Penn Township, it had a post office called Vandalia by 1850, and its plat was filed early in 1851. Who chose the name, and why, no source we have read explains.

So this is a story about what the record does show, and about the guesses that fill the gap. We went back to the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906, Michigan’s first gazetteer of 1838 and the post-office lists.

How to read this page · Scrollmarks

Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known). Every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

The place
Vandalia, Michigan: a village in Penn Township, Cass County, on Christiann Creek
Post office
1850, the first record of the name
The mill
A grist mill of 1849 on the creek, “the nucleus for the village of Vandalia”
The plat
Laid out by Stephen Bogue and Charles P. Ball, 3 January 1851 (Rogers, 1875); filed 21 February 1851 (Glover, 1906)
Incorporated
1875
The creek
Named in 1822 by the missionary Isaac McCoy for his wife, Christiana
Why it matters
The village name has no recorded reason; the creek beside it does
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • The name is first on record for a post office, in 1850.
  • The village grew around a grist mill built on the creek in 1849 by two Quaker settlers, Stephen Bogue and Charles P. Ball, who laid out the village in 1851.
  • The plat followed in 1851: laid out on 3 January, Rogers says; filed on 21 February, Glover says.
  • The creek had its name first, from the missionary Isaac McCoy, who named it in 1822 for his wife.

What it does not show, yet

  • Who chose “Vandalia,” and why. Neither the 1875 nor the 1906 county history says.
  • Whether the name came from Vandalia, Illinois, as many assume.
{{toc}}
## Story or record? Play along
Here are eight things people say about the name. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows.

“Vandalia, Michigan, was named after Vandalia, Illinois.”

No record

It is the usual guess, and it may be right: the Illinois town had been the state capital and was well known by 1850. But neither the 1875 nor the 1906 county history explains the name.

“Vandalia comes from a Native-language word.”

No record

No source gives it a Native origin. It is a Latin-style European name, “land of the Vandals,” used for towns across the country.

“There was a Vandalia post office before there was a village plat.”

True

Postal listings date the Vandalia office from 1850; the village was laid out in January 1851.

“The village grew up around a grist mill.”

True

Glover, in 1906: the grist mill on Christiann Creek “served as the nucleus for the village of Vandalia.”

“The creek through Vandalia was named for a missionary’s wife.”

True

Rogers, 1875: “It was so named by the missionary in honor of his wife, as they crossed it the 18th of December.” The 1882 history names him: the Rev. Isaac McCoy, in 1822.

“Cass County’s first grist mill stood near the later village.”

True

Rogers puts Carpenter’s mill of 1828 on the creek, “just below where Vandalia now stands.”

“The two county histories agree on when the village was laid out.”

No

Rogers (1875) says 3 January 1851; Glover (1906) says the plat was filed on 21 February 1851. Both may be right: one is the survey, the other the filing.

“Vandalia became an incorporated village in 1875.”

True

Glover calls it “one of the three incorporated villages in Cass county,” and gives the year as 1875.
## A post office first

DocumentedThe earliest record of the name we have found is the post office. Postal listings compiled from the Post Office Department’s records give “Vandalia” from 1850, and Rogers’s county history of 1875 names T. J. Wilcox as its first postmaster.

DocumentedThe village had grown up around a mill. Glover’s history of 1906 describes “a grist mill built on the banks of Christiann creek along the state road,” built in 1849 by two Quakers and pioneers of Penn Township, Stephen Bogue and Charles P. Ball, which “served as the nucleus for the village of Vandalia.”

DocumentedRogers says Bogue and Ball laid out the village on 3 January 1851. Glover says the plat of the village of Vandalia was filed on 21 February 1851, on the east side of the creek. It was incorporated in 1875; the railroad, Glover says, arrived in 1871.
## Why Vandalia?

OpenNobody we have found says. Rogers mentions Vandalia eight times and never explains it; Glover, writing at length about the village in 1906, does not either. Walter Romig’s Michigan Place Names, the standard reference, may; we have not yet been able to read it.

ReadingThe guesses are borrowed from elsewhere. Vandalia, Illinois, founded in 1819, was the state capital until 1839 and the western end of the National Road, and its name was well known. The Illinois town’s own history of its name is uncertain: the ancient Vandals, a failed colony of the 1770s called Vandalia, and a surveyor’s coinage have all been proposed. Any of these could lie behind the Michigan name, or none.
ReadingWhat the word means is plain enough: Vandalia is a Latin-style “land of the Vandals,” the name of a Germanic people of the late Roman empire. It has no Native-language origin.
## A station on the creek

DocumentedVandalia’s founders were Quakers, and their neighbourhood was one of the best-known stations of the Underground Railroad in Michigan. Stephen Bogue had come to the county in 1830; the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County calls him the county’s most famous stationmaster, and says his house, which still stands on M-60, sheltered many freedom seekers on their way to Canada.

DocumentedIn August 1847, slave catchers from Kentucky raided the Quaker farms of Calvin, Penn and Porter townships and seized freedom seekers living there. A crowd of white and Black neighbours, by some counts some hundreds strong, confronted the raiders at O’Dell’s Mill on Christiana Creek near Vandalia, and the Kentuckians agreed to stand trial at Cassopolis. The court commissioner found their papers wanting and released the captives, and dozens of people went on to Canada. The slaveholders’ lawsuit against the neighbours dragged on in federal court in Detroit for more than two years.

DocumentedThe house of James E. Bonine, Bogue’s son-in-law, stands at Penn Road and M-60. It was begun about 1844 and enlarged and restyled after the Civil War; the society, which bought it in 2010, says there is little evidence that the house itself was a station, but there is evidence that freedom seekers were sheltered in the Gothic Revival carriage house of the early 1850s across the road.

ReadingThe village that grew around Bogue and Ball’s mill was born a few years after the raid, in the middle of this Quaker country. The name they gave it is still unexplained; what they did there is not.
## Christiann Creek

DocumentedThe creek the village stands on has a recorded name and a recorded reason. Rogers, 1875: the stream that runs into the St. Joseph “near the present site of Elkhart … is known as the Christiana creek. It was so named by the missionary in honor of his wife, as they crossed it the 18th of December.” The missionary was the Baptist Isaac McCoy, founder of the Carey Mission; in October 1803, Rogers says, he had married Miss Christiana Polk. The 1882 history dates the naming to 1822.

DocumentedThe spelling has drifted ever since. Blois’s Gazetteer of the State of Michigan (1838) has “Christiana river”; Rogers has both “Christiana creek” and “Christianna Creek”; the 1882 history “Christianna Creek”; and Glover in 1906 “Christiann creek,” the form used in Vandalia today. Federal maps still call it Christiana Creek.
DocumentedThe creek turned mills long before the village. Rogers puts Carpenter’s mill of 1828, the county’s first grist mill, on the creek “just below where Vandalia now stands.”
## The name on paper
Vandalia has kept one spelling from the start. Its creek has not. Play the creek’s names in order.

• 1822 Christiana (Isaac McCoy names it for his wife)
  • 1838 Christiana river (Blois’s gazetteer)
  • 1875 Christiana creek (Rogers)
  • 1882 Christianna Creek (the county history)
  • 1906 Christiann creek (Glover, and the creek today)
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Why Vandalia? A letter or petition for the post office of 1850, in the National Archives, may name the person who proposed it.
  2. What does Romig say? His Michigan Place Names is the next place to look.
  3. Which date is the plat’s? The original at the Cass County register of deeds would settle 3 January against 21 February 1851.
