stories.headline: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
stories.dek: Two county histories record a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” at Cassopolis, Michigan, in the spring of 1846: four charter members named, a ball of two hundred badges, and the earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members named. Newspapers of the same year show the order already at work across the state line in Indiana. Here is the whole record, what it does and does not prove, and the questions still open.
pic: /img/news/e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846
Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875, page 253: the first secret society of which there is any record
Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), p. 253.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Picture a winter night in the county seat of a frontier county not yet twenty years old. The frame tavern on the square is lit up. Inside, more than two hundred people are wearing the badges of a secret society with a name few of them could have spelled the same way twice: the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus.” It is the winter of 1846–47, and the Cassopolis lodge is less than a year old.

In 1875 the first history of Cass County, Michigan, printed a short account of “the first Secret Society, of which there is any record” in the county: a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus,” instituted at Cassopolis in the spring of 1846. Seven years later a second county history printed it again. Neither book was written for the order now known as E Clampus Vitus, and so far as we can find, no historian of that order has ever cited either one.

A word to the Brethren

If you wear the red shirt, you know the story: Ephraim Bee and his commission, Joe Zumwalt carrying the ritual to Hangtown, the lodge at Mokelumne Hill by 1851, and Carl Wheat bringing the order back to life in San Francisco in 1931. You also know the line in the order’s own 1966 history, that by 1849 “the East and Middle West were dotted with Clamper Lodges,” not one of them named.

This page names one. It comes with a hall, a ball and four charter members, in the spring of 1846. And the newspapers of that year, just over the state line in Indiana, show the order alive and growing: a lodge at Connersville, a Tent No. 43 at Indianapolis meeting “in full regalia,” and a bill before the legislature to charter a lodge at Centreville. Credo quia absurdum, the motto runs: I believe because it is absurd. Here you will not need to. Every statement below is marked Documented (the record says so), Reading (our interpretation of it) or Open (not yet known), and every source is listed at the foot of the page.

At a glance

What
A lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus”
Where
Cassopolis, the county seat of Cass County, Michigan
When
Instituted in the spring of 1846; collapsed in 1847; revived in 1860 as “The Brothers of Charity”
Charter members
Dr. E. J. Bonine, Laban Harter, J. P. Osborn and Dr. L. Osborn; three of them married sisters of the Beall family
The ball
Winter of 1846–47, at the Union Hotel: “over two hundred badges”
First printed
Rogers, History of Cass County (1875), pp. 253–254, from an account by James M. Shepard
Printed again
Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174
Why it matters
The earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members named, and the first known in Michigan. Indiana newspapers of 1846 confirm the order, and its spelling, in the same year

New: E Clampus Vitus: the complete record. Every lodge of the order on record before 1905, sixty-one places from Texas to Hawaii, each with its earliest source, plus the words of the old order, the myths beside the record and the founding documents in full.
## The case in brief

What the record shows

  • A lodge at Cassopolis, spring 1846, with four charter members named, a ball of “over two hundred badges” at the Union Hotel, a collapse in 1847 and a revival in 1860 (Rogers, 1875; Mathews, 1882).
  • A family affair. Three of the four founders married sisters of one family, the Bealls.
  • The order alive in Indiana in 1846: a lodge at Connersville by February, Tent No. 43 at Indianapolis by July, and a “Jackson Lodge” at Centreville that asked the legislature for a charter.
  • The legislature’s answer was a joke at the order’s expense, printed in the official House Journal of January 1847.

What it does not show, yet

  • Any Michigan newspaper notice of the lodge or the ball.
  • The names of a single Indiana member.
  • How the order reached Cassopolis. But the founders’ family came from Centreville, the very town whose lodge asked for a charter.
{{toc}}
## Who’s who

Dr. Evan J. Bonine 1821–1892 · charter member
Quaker-born physician from Richmond, Indiana, who learned medicine at Centreville and married there in 1844; practising at Cassopolis at twenty-four. Went overland to California in 1849 and came back in 1851. Later surgeon of the 2nd Michigan Infantry, state legislator, and mayor and postmaster of Niles.
Laban Harter 1826–1888 · charter member
Born at Eaton, Ohio. He married Emily Beall at Cassopolis in 1847, went to California with Bonine, and became a merchant at Niles.
Jordan P. Osborn born 1823 · charter member
Of Cassopolis; later a village trustee and, in 1876, President of the Village.
Dr. Leander Osborn born 1825 · charter member
Jordan’s nephew. He began to read medicine under Bonine in 1847 and became the doctor at Vandalia.
The Beall sisters Evaline, Emily P. and Helen M.
Daughters of Nathaniel Beall, a farmer near Centreville, Indiana, and Sarah Talbot, who married at Centreville in 1826. They married Bonine, Harter and Leander Osborn.
James M. Shepard 1840 or 1842–1927 · the storyteller
Cassopolis dentist from 1868, later owner of the Cassopolis Vigilant and state senator. He set the account down in about 1875, from what someone told him, and helped with the county history of 1882.
Eber Root the innkeeper
Licensed to keep a tavern at Cassopolis on 24 January 1832. His frame tavern became the Union Hotel, where the ball was held.
Howard S. Rogers and Alfred Mathews the historians
Authors of the county histories of 1875 and 1882 that printed Shepard’s account.
Ephraim Bee 1802–1888 · the founder, by legend
Innkeeper and blacksmith of West Union, in what is now West Virginia, from whom the order traces its descent.
Joe Zumwalt the man who carried it west
Said by the order to have brought the ritual to Hangtown in 1849 and to have founded the lodge at Mokelumne Hill by 1851.
Carl I. Wheat the reviver
Revived the order in San Francisco in 1931 and, by the order’s historian, chose the spelling “Clampus.”
## Exhibit A: the page that started it

This is the passage as Alfred Mathews printed it in 1882, page 174, under the heading “The Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus.” A footnote credits it to “James M. Shepard, in Roger’s ‘History of Cass County.’” It is reproduced in full; the page photographs are below.

“The first secret society of which there is any record was a lodge of the Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus, which was instituted in the spring of 1846 with Dr. E. J. Bonine, Laban Harter, J. P. Osborn and Dr. L. Osborn as charter members.

“The order was in broadest burlesque of legitimate secret organizations, and was afterward merged in the ‘Sons of Malta,’ which died from exposure (by Frank Leslie) in the next decade.

“The candidates for admission were bound fast, blindfolded and dragged into the hall by halters. They were placed in the most ludicrous positions and required to pledge themselves to performances and courses of conduct which by a cunningly devised double entendre in the wording of the pledges were either impossible or eminently ridiculous.

“A peculiarity of human nature which renders the victim of a ‘sell’ restless and unhappy until he has inveigled others into the same meshes, insured the rapid growth and financial prosperity of this monstrous hoax. Numerous Neophites were found to assuage the grief and soothe the wounded pride of the earlier victims.

“A grand ball was given by the lodge in the winter of 1846–47, at the Union Hotel, at which over two hundred badges of the ‘Ancient and Honorable Order’ were displayed, and that, too, by men who stood the highest in popular esteem and respectability.

“The (dis)order collapsed in 1847, partly from lack of raw material and partly from a growing satiety amounting to disgust on the part of the better portion of the members, but it was successfully resurrected in 1860 under the alias of the ‘Brothers of Charity.’

“The second edition, although enlarged and improved, was of ‘few days and full of trouble’ to all except the charter members.”

The original, in Howard S. Rogers’s History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875), pages 253 and 254, differs in small ways that matter. Rogers prints the order’s name as “the ‘Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus,’” the respectable men as those who “stood among the highest,” and the last line as “to all except the charter (?) members.” The question mark is in the 1875 text; Mathews dropped it. The phrase “of few days, and full of trouble” is from the Book of Job (14:1), an old funeral text.
## The storyteller: who wrote it

Mathews names the author: James M. Shepard. He did not see the lodge. Shepard was a small child in 1846 (born at North Brookfield, Massachusetts, on 24 November; the year is 1840 in the histories of 1882 and 1906, and 1842 in Michigan Biographies of 1924 and in his obituary of 1927, which gives his age as 84) and came to Cassopolis only on 3 September 1868, as the village dentist; he joined the Cassopolis Vigilant in 1876 and became its sole proprietor in 1878, and was elected to the Michigan Senate in 1878 (Glover, 1906, pp. 556–558). When he wrote, in about 1875, all three of the founders we can trace were still living in or near the county. The account is a written record of local memory, set down about thirty years after the events, and it should be read as that, not as a minute book.
## Exhibit B: the newspapers of 1846

DocumentedShepard wrote his account about thirty years after the fact. The newspapers of 1846 did not wait. Just over the state line, in Indiana, the order was in print that very year, and under the same spelling the Cassopolis account uses.

Indiana American, Brookville · 27 February 1846

From a letter written at Connersville: the town’s citizens, it says, think two scoffing editors “naturally qualified members of the ‘Eclampsus Vitus’ society, an order of which, we have in our town.”

Indiana State Sentinel, Indianapolis · 16 July 1846

“The members of Tent No. 43 of the order of Eclampsus Vitus are notified to meet in their Hall on Thursday Evening, July 16, at early candle lighting, attired in full regalia. A general attendance is requested. By order.”

Indiana House of Representatives · winter of 1846–47

Mr. Julian of Wayne County brought in a bill “to incorporate the ancient order of E-clam-peis Vitus” (Indiana State Sentinel, 7 January 1847); the Richmond Palladium of 5 January says it was for a lodge “at Centreville.” On 14 January the committee on corporations recommended its “indefinite postponement,” and the bill was laid on the table.

Quotations are from the newspapers’ scanned pages at Hoosier State Chronicles. The scans are worn and their machine-read text is garbled in places (the Sentinel’s type reads “Eclumpees” and “E-clam-peis”), so we quote them as closely as the pages allow.

ReadingSo when the Cassopolis lodge was “instituted” in the spring of 1846, the order was already a going concern in Indiana: a lodge at Connersville by February, Tents at Indianapolis numbered to at least 43 by July, and a lodge at Centreville that wanted a charter from the state. That last detail is worth a smile: Shepard put a question mark after the Cassopolis “charter,” and the Centreville brethren actually asked the legislature for one. Exhibit C tells how that went.
{{fig:centreville-mansion-house}}

DocumentedThe Centreville connection. The road from Centreville to Cassopolis runs straight through the founders’ family. The Beall sisters were born at Centreville, where their father, Nathaniel Beall, farmed 160 acres until he died there in January 1845. Dr. Bonine read medicine at Centreville for three and a half years under Dr. John Pricket (Michigan Legislative Biography), and Dr. Pricket had married the girls’ aunt, Emily Talbot. Bonine married the eldest sister, Evaline, at Centreville on 8 August 1844, and brought her to Cassopolis. Her sister Emily married Laban Harter at Cassopolis in September 1847; the youngest, Helen, married Leander Osborn in 1854 (Cope, Genealogy of the Sharpless Family, 1887). OpenDid the Bealls’ circle bring the order north from Centreville, a few months before Centreville’s own Jackson Lodge asked the legislature for a charter? Nothing yet proves it. It is the likeliest route we know.
## Exhibit C: the Jackson Lodge and the Indiana House

DocumentedThe official Journal of the House of Representatives of Indiana for 1846–47 gives the Centreville lodge its name. On leave granted, Mr. Julian, one of the four members for Wayne County (the Journal lists them as William S. Addleman, Jacob B. Julian, Solomon Meredith and Robert Gordon), brought in House bill No. 242, “An act to incorporate Jackson Lodge of the ancient order of Eclampses Vitus, of Centreville, Indiana.” It was read twice and sent to the committee on corporations.
{{wide:journal-1846-bill}}
DocumentedThe committee’s report, printed in full in the Journal, is one of the funniest pages a state legislature ever published:

“The committee on corporations, to which was referred bill of the House No. 242, entitled ‘An act to incorporate the Jackson Lodge of the ancient order of Eclampses Vitus, of Centreville, Indiana,’ have had the same under consideration, and are not able to ascertain from the bill itself what objects are to be attained by the proposed corporation; but if they are correctly informed from other sources, the bill is for the benefit of a species of animals with which the country is now abundantly supplied, and of which it is not desirable either to increase the number or improve the breed. They therefore recommend that it be indefinitely postponed.”
{{wide:journal-1847-report}}

ReadingThe House concurred, and the bill was laid on the table. The committee never names the animal, and it did not need to: the same session had before it a bill “for the improvement of the breed of horses, jack-asses, and mules.” The joke is that the brethren were asses, and the Clampers of any age will recognise the kind of compliment it is. A page away in the same Journal, the same committee recommended passage of a bill to incorporate the Sons of Temperance.
DocumentedWe have searched the Indiana House and Senate journals and the session laws from 1842 to 1853 for the order under any of its spellings. This is the only bill.
## Exhibit D: the four founders

DocumentedDr. Evan J. Bonine. Born at Richmond, Wayne County, Indiana, on 10 September 1821, of Quaker family; read medicine at Centreville, Indiana, and graduated from the Ohio Medical College at Cincinnati in 1843; married Evaline (Eveline) Beall at Centreville on 8 August 1844 and practised at Cassopolis. His own mother was a Talbot of the same Quaker family as his wife’s mother. He was twenty-four in the spring of 1846. In 1849 he went overland to California with his brother-in-law Laban Harter, and returned in 1851 to settle at Vandalia. He was surgeon of the 2nd Michigan Infantry in the Civil War, sat in the Michigan House for Cass County (1853) and Berrien County (1865–68, 1873) and in the Senate (1869–70), and was mayor and postmaster of Niles, where he died in December 1892. (Michigan Legislative Biography; Portrait and Biographical Record of Berrien and Cass Counties, 1893, quoting the Niles Daily Star.)

DocumentedLaban Harter. Of the four he was the least known, and he is now the best placed. He was born at Eaton, Preble County, Ohio, on 28 April 1826, a son of Joseph Harter and Mary Howell (Cope, 1887), so he was nineteen or twenty in the spring of 1846; he died on 10 July 1888 and is buried at Silverbrook Cemetery, Niles, beside his wife Emily P. Harter (1832–1910) (Friends of Silverbrook Cemetery, grave records, lot City 21). Their only daughter, Martha, was “born on a farm near Niles Nov. 10, 1848” (Niles Daily Sun, 26 October 1914), so the young couple were settled near Niles before he went west with Bonine in 1849. Two later records place him in the town: an “L. Harter, Treasurer,” of the Niles Horse-Thief Association, organized in May 1853 (Ellis and Johnson, 1880), and “the old Loban Harter residence” at Niles, where Bonine’s son Dr. Fred N. Bonine was born on 21 October 1863 (Niles Daily Star, 23 August 1941). He married Emily P. Beall at Cassopolis on 5 September 1847, when she was fifteen, and became a merchant at Niles. OpenWhether he found the order in California is not known.
{{fig:miner-portrait}}

DocumentedJ. P. Osborn: Jordan P. Osborn. Born 6 August 1823, a son of the Quaker minister Charles Osborn; named by Mathews as “Jordan P., who is a resident of Cassopolis,” and later a village trustee and, in 1876, President of the Village of Cassopolis. He was twenty-two in the spring of 1846. His elder brother Parker B. Osborn, born 1821, kept a harness shop at Cassopolis but removed to Wilmington, Ohio; the charter’s initials, J. P., point to Jordan.

DocumentedDr. L. Osborn: Dr. Leander Osborn, of Vandalia. Born 27 December 1825, a son of Josiah Osborn and grandson of Charles Osborn (Mathews, 1882). He began reading medicine with Dr. Bonine in 1847 and was afterward his partner for two years. He married Helen M. Beall of Centreville on 12 November 1854 (Mathews, 1882), and was “a successful physician at Vandalia” (Portrait and Biographical Record, 1893, biography of his brother Jefferson Osborn). He was twenty in the spring of 1846 and not yet a doctor: the title in the 1875 account is the one he held when it was written.

DocumentedThree sisters. When Nathaniel Beall of Niles died in September 1898, his obituary listed among his survivors “Mesdames E.J. Bonine and Laban Harter,” of Niles, “and Mrs. Osborne, of Vandalia” (Niles Daily Star, 12 September 1898, reprinted in the Niles Weekly Mirror, 14 September 1898). Bonine married Evaline Beall at Centreville in 1844, Harter married Emily at Cassopolis in 1847, and Leander Osborn married Helen in 1854. Three of the lodge’s four charter members married sisters of one family. ReadingSo the lodge was very nearly a family affair: a young doctor, two men who were or would become his brothers-in-law, and Jordan Osborn, the uncle of one of them. In 1846 only Bonine was married; Harter and Osborn married into the family afterward, so the lodge may have helped make the family, as much as the family made the lodge. Two of the four, Bonine and Harter, would be in California within three years.

Bonine and Harter went overland to California in 1849 and came home in 1851, the very years the order took root in the diggings. These are the diggings as the daguerreotypists saw them then. We have no picture of either man.
{{row:miners-longtom,miners-group}}
## Exhibit E: the room

DocumentedThe Union Hotel was the frame tavern built by Eber Root, one of the first two men licensed to keep a tavern in Cassopolis, on 24 January 1832 (Rogers, 1875). It stood on the west side of Broadway at the public square (Glover, 1906). The 1860 wall map of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien counties prints one word on that block: HOTEL. Six years after the ball, on 12 June 1852, the county’s Masons held their first meeting “in the Union Hotel” (Mathews, 1882, p. 174): the kind of order the burlesque was made to mock, organizing under the same roof. The corner is still there; the hotel is not, and there is no marker. What became of the building is the subject of Case 2.
## Exhibit F: what became of the lodge

DocumentedBy the account’s own words, the lodge collapsed in 1847 and was “resurrected in 1860 under the alias of the ‘Brothers of Charity,’” and the order “was afterward merged in the ‘Sons of Malta,’ which died from exposure (by Frank Leslie) in the next decade.”

ReadingThat merger needs care. No lodge of the Sons of Malta is dated before 1854 (a New Orleans lodge, November 1854), so the lodge of 1846, gone by 1847, cannot have merged into it. The revival of 1860 could have, but only just. The Sons of Malta had reached Michigan by 1859, when a lodge was organized at Grand Rapids “largely for the cultivation of whatever was comic, droll or ridiculous” (Baxter, 1891). Then, in the first weeks of 1860, the order was exposed in print: the “Council of Ten” in Frank Leslie’s Illustrated Newspaper of 11 February 1860, a “Grand Exposure” in Vanity Fair of 25 February, and Thomas Williams’s pamphlet The Sons of Malta Exposed (New York, 1860). Shepard’s “died from exposure” is a pun on exactly that. A Cassopolis revival of 1860 could have joined the Sons of Malta only in that narrow window. No lodge of the Sons of Malta at Cassopolis or Niles has yet been found, and no other record of a burlesque “Brothers of Charity” has turned up.
{{wide:malta-lodge}}

Leslie’s artist spared nothing: hooded brethren, knights in armour, a skeleton, a gallows and, at the centre, the candidate. In later numbers came the initiation itself, and the signs and grips that were supposed to be secret.
{{row:malta-horsing,malta-sworn}}
{{row:malta-mystic,malta-grip,malta-drink}}
## The wider trail: where it fits in the order’s history

E Clampus Vitus is known today as the historical society of the old West, the “Clampers” whose plaques mark forgotten places across California and beyond. Its own history runs like this, and every date below is the order’s or its historians’, not ours.
{{fig:west-union-courthouse}}

DocumentedThe founding legend. The order traces itself to Ephraim Bee (1802–1888), innkeeper and blacksmith of West Union, in what is now West Virginia. The marker at West Union, put up in 2003, says that by legend Bee received his commission “around 1845.” No document from those years has been produced to date it. Jennifer Wilt of the Doddridge County Heritage Guild, working from the county’s court books and the period press, writes that “shortly after 1850” Bee proclaimed himself Grand Hototote, and that she has found newspaper references to the order “as early as 1853.” An 1896 account in the Parkersburg State Journal has its writer meeting Bee in the fall of 1847, and finding, when they met again “some years afterward,” that Bee “had concocted the celebrated secret order” in the meantime.

DocumentedThe eastern lodges. The order’s historian Dr. Albert Shumate, in a talk of 25 June 1991, wrote: “There is documentation of lodges in Bedford Pennsylvania, (1847); Metropolis, Illinois (1849); and Bowling Green, Missouri (1849).” He cited nothing, but all three can now be traced to print, and all three were first gathered in an ECV pamphlet, Credo quia absurdum (Placerville, 1949).

DocumentedMore early records. The Alexandria Gazette of 13 March 1852 reported “the new order introduced recently into Virginia, called the ‘E. Clampus Vitas,’” and claimed to expose it as “dog Latin” for “squeezing the life out of you.” The earliest California notice yet found is a call to “THE MEMBERS of the E. C. V.” in the San Joaquin Republican at Stockton, 14 April 1852. And by 1 February 1867 the Wheeling Intelligencer could call Ephraim Bee “the recognized American head” of the order, with the story of Caleb Cushing already attached. All sixty-one places are in the complete record.

DocumentedBedford, 1847. Judge William M. Hall’s Reminiscences and Sketches (Harrisburg, 1890) gives a whole chapter to “The Ancient and Venerable Order of Ecclampsis Vitis.” In 1847, he writes, “there came to Bedford, from the west, a traveling agent for a patented invention of a cutting-box,” who “instituted a new secret society.” It met in the grand jury room of the court house, by the light of a single tallow candle, under a “grand worthy patriarch” in a brown-paper hat. The candidate swore a blood-curdling oath, learned a sign “to keep the oats from falling out,” and was finally shown “a large picture of two mules,” “amid the uproarious shouts of laughter of the assembled throng.” There was a torch-light procession led by the Bedford band, and the regalia was “a strip of muslin” worn over the shoulder, “ornamented with a star cut out of the heavy purple colored paper that loaf sugar used to come in.” It lasted “some eight or ten weeks,” until a young doctor took offence and gave the secret away.

DocumentedMetropolis, 1849. The Huntington Library’s manuscript was first cited in 1941 by G. Ezra Dane, one of the men who revived the order, in Ghost Town: a “Division No. 110” record book “for 1849, loaned to us by Miss Nellie Smith of Stockton.” Credo quia absurdum (1949) adds that the book is from “Metropolis City, Illinois” and that “its roster indicates that several of the members had joined theretofore in Missouri, Alabama, Georgia and other Southern States.” We have not found it in the Huntington’s catalogue; it may be among the Dane family papers there.

DocumentedBowling Green, 1849. Not a lodge at all. The source, a Calaveras Prospect article of 30 May 1896 reprinted in Credo, says the first ritual brought to California “was printed in the office of the Bowling Green Journal in Pike County, Missouri,” where in 1849 Zumwalt “and one W. C. Wright went into the Journal office and each bought a ritual.”

ReadingSet side by side, the eastern record and Cassopolis tell one story. The order travelled with “drummers” and young professional men. Its officers in Bedford bore the titles of the Sons of Temperance, the great teetotal brotherhood founded in 1842, worthy patriarch and grand scribe; in Indiana it met in “Tents,” and Metropolis kept a “Division” book. It was, as Hall put it, “a burlesque on all secret societies,” and its punchline everywhere was the same animal: two mules in Bedford, the jack-asses of the Indiana committee report. Michigan’s first Grand Division of the Sons of Temperance was chartered on 29 January 1846, a few weeks before the Cassopolis lodge was instituted.

DocumentedCalifornia. The order’s own 1966 history, Then and Now, says it “is generally accepted” that Joe Zumwalt brought the ritual to Hangtown (Placerville) in 1849, where a lodge “didn’t last,” and that he “did establish the first lodge of ECV by 1851” at Mokelumne Hill. Shumate dates the Hangtown attempt to 1850. Its best-loved story, the initiation of Steamboat Jake, it dates to 1852; the earliest source, Harry Wells’s History of Siskiyou County (1881), sets it at Yreka in 1856.
{{row:placerville-1860s,mokhill-1866}}

DocumentedThe gap the order’s own history leaves. Then and Now says that travelling salesmen were taken into the order, “with or without authority from Bee,” and that by 1849 “the East and Middle West were dotted with Clamper Lodges.” It names none. Its closing postscript hopes that “some day someone will attempt to research and compile a complete list of the number and location of the lodges formed during this earlier period.”

ReadingRogers names one, and the Indiana papers of 1846 name more: Connersville, the Tents at Indianapolis, Centreville. Cassopolis, spring 1846, is the earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members’ names written down, and the first known in Michigan. With the Indiana lodges it makes the first lines of the list the order asked for in 1966, and proves that the order was alive in the Middle West three years before the gold rush carried it to California.
## The Clampers today

The order Carl Wheat revived in 1931 is best known now for its plaques: hundreds of them, in bronze and stone, on forgotten places across California and the West. Some of them are pictured here. If the Brethren ever want a plaque in Michigan, we know a good spot on the square at Cassopolis.
{{row:bodie-1972,ecv-hotaling-plaque,ecv-clampout}}
## A Clamper’s glossary
For readers who have never been a Poor Blind Candidate, and for Clampers who will enjoy checking our work.

Tent
What the order called a local lodge in Indiana in 1846: “Tent No. 43” at Indianapolis.
Clamper
A member of E Clampus Vitus.
Poor Blind Candidate
A man not yet initiated. The order’s 1966 history speaks of “a Poor Blind Candidate” led to his initiation.
Noble Grand Humbug
“The presiding officer” of a chapter (Then and Now, 1966).
Hall of Comparative Ovations
Wherever the Clampers meet, traditionally the back room of a saloon. At Cassopolis the ball, at least, was held at the Union Hotel.
Hewgag
“The great tin horn” of the order, which “sounded a horrendous blast” (Then and Now).
Credo quia absurdum
The order’s motto: “I believe because it is absurd.”
Wearing the tin
Today’s Clampers pin on tin badges with their red shirts. What the “over two hundred badges” of the Cassopolis ball were made of is not recorded; at Bedford in 1847 the regalia was a muslin sash with a star cut from loaf-sugar paper.
## The spelling

Both Michigan histories spell the name “Eclampsus,” with an S. The order’s historian writes that Carl Wheat chose the present spelling, “Clampus,” in 1931, when the order was revived in San Francisco. The 2003 marker in Ephraim Bee’s own town still reads “E Clampsus Vitus.” The Indiana papers of 1846 spell it the same way: “Eclampsus Vitus.” The Michigan books are not misspelling the name; they spell it as it was spelled before 1931.
## A timeline

• 24 Jan 1832 Eber Root licensed to keep a tavern at Cassopolis; he builds the frame house that becomes the Union Hotel.
  • c. 1845 The order’s legend: Ephraim Bee’s commission. (Undated in any surviving record.)
  • Feb 1846 A lodge of the “Eclampsus Vitus” at Connersville, Indiana (Indiana American, 27 Feb).
  • Spring 1846 The Cassopolis lodge is instituted: Bonine, Harter, J. P. Osborn and L. Osborn.
  • 16 Jul 1846 Tent No. 43 of the order meets at Indianapolis “in full regalia” (Indiana State Sentinel).
  • Winter 1846–47 The grand ball at the Union Hotel: “over two hundred badges.”
  • Jan 1847 House bill No. 242, to incorporate “Jackson Lodge” of the order at Centreville, Indiana, is reported on with a joke and tabled.
  • 1847 The lodge collapses. Bedford, Pennsylvania: the earliest dated eastern lodge. Leander Osborn begins reading medicine with Bonine.
  • 1847 (fall) The 1896 Parkersburg account’s first meeting with Bee.
  • 1849 Bonine and Harter go overland to California. Metropolis and Bowling Green lodges. Hangtown attempt (1966 history).
  • 1850 Hangtown attempt (Shumate). “Shortly after 1850”: Bee proclaims himself Grand Hototote (Wilt).
  • 1851 Mokelumne Hill: the first lasting lodge in California. Bonine returns to Michigan.
  • Mar 1852 The order “introduced recently into Virginia” (Alexandria Gazette, 13 Mar).
  • 14 Apr 1852 The earliest California notice yet found: the E. C. V. at Stockton (San Joaquin Republican).
  • 12 Jun 1852 The Masons’ first meeting at Cassopolis, in the Union Hotel.
  • 1853 Earliest newspaper references to Bee’s order in West Virginia (Wilt).
  • 1854 Earliest dated lodge of the Sons of Malta.
  • 1860 The Cassopolis lodge revived as “The Brothers of Charity.” Frank Leslie exposes the Sons of Malta.
  • Feb 1867 Bee initiating candidates at Wheeling, “the recognized American head” of the order.
  • 1868 James M. Shepard comes to Cassopolis.
  • 1875 Rogers prints Shepard’s account.
  • 1882 Mathews prints it again, naming Shepard.
  • 1931 The order revived in San Francisco; Carl Wheat fixes the spelling “Clampus.”
  • 1966 Then and Now asks for a list of the early lodges.
## What we are not saying

• Not that the order was founded at Cassopolis. The account says a lodge of the order was “instituted” there. Rogers uses the same word on the same page for the Odd Fellows lodge instituted at Cassopolis in February 1847 under a dispensation from a Grand Master: a local lodge of an order that already existed.
  • Not that the evidence is like for like. The Cassopolis account is local memory written down about thirty years later by a man who was not there. Wilt’s dates come from contemporary court books and newspapers. Ours is a claim about the surviving record, not about what may have happened unrecorded.
  • Not that Cassopolis was the first lodge. It was not, so far as the newspapers show: there was a lodge at Connersville, Indiana, by February 1846, and Tents at Indianapolis numbered to at least 43 by July. Our claim is narrower and, we think, still remarkable: Cassopolis is the earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members’ names on record, and the first known in Michigan.
  • Not that the question is closed. Seth Slopes’s history of the order (2000) has been read; Lois Rather’s Men Will Be Boys (1980) has not, the Metropolis book of 1849 has not been found, and the Indiana lodges of 1846 have not yet given up their members’ names. Any of them could change this page.
  • Not that Bonine or Harter carried the order west. The dates line up; no document connects them to any California lodge.
If anyone can show a lodge of the order dated earlier than the spring of 1846, with a place and names, we will say so on this page, with thanks and with their name.
## The picture album

Every picture on this page in one place. The Sons of Malta engravings, the gold-rush daguerreotypes and the Historic American Buildings Survey photographs are in the public domain; the modern photographs of Clamper plaques are shared by their makers under the Creative Commons licences named in each caption. Press any picture to see it full size.
{{album}}

Pictures we know of but cannot yet show. Ephraim Bee, drawn from life in 1846 by Joseph H. Diss Debar, is in his sketchbook at the West Virginia & Regional History Center, West Virginia University; the Center requires written permission to publish it, and no openly licensed copy exists. The order’s own photographs, from the revival of the 1930s on, are in its papers at the Holt-Atherton Special Collections, University of the Pacific, and at the Huntington Library, and none has yet been put online with open rights. The oldest Clamper photograph we can show is the Library of Congress stereograph of 1890 above. No picture of the Cassopolis lodge, its hall or its four founders has yet been found. If your family has one, we would love to see it.
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. Each one says where the answer is most likely to be. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Who were the Clampers of Indiana in 1846? The order was at Connersville by February 1846, at Indianapolis (Tent No. 43) by July, and at Centreville by that winter; it turns up again at Vincennes in 1854 and in the Springville and Mitchell lodges of Lawrence County in 1859. Every notice found is unsigned. A search of Indiana’s digitized newspapers for 1844–1862 under every spelling, and of the Wayne, Fayette, Marion and Lawrence County histories, names no member. The best chance is the original House bill No. 242, which may list the incorporators of Jackson Lodge: the Indiana State Library says bills before 1975 are at the Indiana State Archives (arc@iara.in.gov). Ask for House bill No. 242 of the 31st General Assembly, 1846–47, and the committee on corporations’ report on it of 6 January 1847. Lois Rather’s Men Will Be Boys (1980) has not yet been read; the Huntington Library holds a copy.
  2. Who told Shepard? He came to Cassopolis in 1868 and wrote in about 1875. Neither Rogers’s preface nor Mathews’s names his informant; Mathews thanks Shepard himself among his Cassopolis helpers, and lists Dr. Leander Osborn, a charter member, among his helpers in Penn township. Two charter members were alive and close by: Jordan P. Osborn, President of the Village in 1875, and Leander Osborn, who lived at Vandalia until 1901. The Michigan Pioneer and Historical Collections (volumes 1–40) say nothing of the lodge. Shepard’s obituary, in the Cassopolis Vigilant of August 1927 (microfilm reel A19, Cass District Library), has not yet been read. His question mark after “charter” suggests he was not sure the lodge ever had one.
  3. Did anyone write it down in 1846? Cassopolis had two papers that year, The Literary News and the Cass County Advocate, and few issues survive. Nothing has been found online: Digital Michigan Newspapers holds no Cass or Berrien County paper, and its Michigan papers of 1846–47, like those in Chronicling America, never mention the order. The best chance is the Niles Republican, which survives for every week of 1846–47 but one (31 January 1846). It is not online anywhere; it is on microfilm at the Cass District Library’s Local History Branch and at the Library of Michigan. The issues from November 1846 to March 1847, the season of the ball, are the place to start.
  4. What did the Bealls’ Centreville know? Cope’s genealogy of 1887 gives Harter’s parents as Joseph Harter and Mary Howell, and the Beall marriages to the day. What it cannot tell us is whether any Beall, Talbot or Pricket belonged to Centreville’s Jackson Lodge. The Wayne County histories of 1872 and 1884 say nothing of the order, and the Centreville and Richmond papers of 1845–47 that are online name no members. The bill at the Indiana State Archives is the likeliest place a name survives.
  5. Did Bonine or Harter meet the order in California? Bonine’s typescript “Journey to California” is listed in Will Bagley’s trail bibliography at the Fort St. Joseph Museum, Niles, with a copy in the Merrill J. Mattes Library of the Oregon-California Trails Association; neither has an online catalogue record, so the next step is to ask them. Neither man appears in the 1850 census index for Sacramento County. Has anyone seen their names in any early Clamper record?
  6. Does any badge survive? Two hundred were worn at one ball. Who made them, and of what, is not recorded. If they were like Bedford’s, they were muslin and paper, and very few would have been kept. No badge or regalia of the 1840s or 1850s has been found in any museum catalogue searched. The oldest object of the order yet traced is a printed ritual of about the late 1850s, inscribed “No. 6 Morristown Lodge,” sold privately at auction (Rumsey Auctions, sale 41, lot 31); where its Morristown was is not yet known.
  7. What was “The Brothers of Charity” of 1860, and was there ever a Sons of Malta lodge at Cassopolis? Nothing outside Rogers and Mathews names the Brothers of Charity. The Michigan State Gazetteer for 1860 lists Sons of Malta lodges at Detroit (Cadillac Lodge No. 77) and Grand Rapids (Brahmin Lodge, instituted March 1859), but none at Cassopolis or Niles; across the state line, Plymouth, Indiana, had a lodge and a hall in 1860. The Cass County Republican of Dowagiac, 1858–64, is free on Chronicling America, but its Sons of Malta items are all exchange news and its scans read poorly; the 1860 issues should be read page by page. The Niles Inquirer for 1858–60, on microfilm at the Cass District Library, is the other place to look.
  8. Where is the Metropolis book, and who is on its roster? G. Ezra Dane borrowed the “Division No. 110” record book of 1849 from Miss Nellie Smith of Stockton and wrote in 1941 that it was “now in” the Huntington Library. It is not in the online catalogue. The finding aid for the Dane family papers there (mssDane) has no Metropolis item, but Box 16 holds “E Clampus Vitus. Constitution, rules, roll of members etc., and clippings,” the papers of an 1880s lodge, and Dane’s own notes for a dissertation on the order. The Huntington’s Reader Services Department can say whether the roll in Box 16 is the Metropolis book or a copy of it. Its roster of members who joined “in Missouri, Alabama, Georgia and other Southern States” could map the order’s road before the gold rush.

body: The whole order, on paper. In 1966 the historians of E Clampus Vitus closed their history with a wish: that “some day someone will attempt to research and compile a complete list of the number and location of the lodges formed during this earlier period.” This page is that list, as far as the surviving record allows, and everything else we have been able to find about the order from its first appearance in print in 1846 to its fifty-one chapters today.

It began with one Michigan county history and a lodge at Cassopolis in 1846. That story has its own page. This one is the whole record: every place the order is known to have met before 1905, with the earliest surviving record for each and a link to it; the words and customs of the old order, dated by when they first appear; the claims that are often repeated, set beside what the records show; the founding documents in full; and the books and archives where the rest lies.

## The register of early lodges

A place remembered was written down years later, by someone who was there or heard about it. A record cited once existed and was described in print, but has not been found again. A legend has no record of its date at all. Sort the table by place, date or tier.

ReadingRead down the dates and the shape of the story is plain. The order was in print in Indiana in 1846, in Pennsylvania in 1847, in Missouri and Illinois in 1849, in Virginia, Texas and Georgia by 1852, and in California from the spring of 1852. In California it spread from Stockton and the southern mines in 1852 and 1853, boomed in 1855 and 1856, when Sacramento initiated “nearly five hundred persons … within three weeks,” and reached the northern camps by the end of the decade. It was still meeting in the 1880s and was initiating candidates at Sierraville in 1904.
## Maps: where it was, and where it is
## Before California, 1845–1853

DocumentedThe order’s first appearance in print is a joke in a newspaper letter from Connersville, Indiana, in February 1846. By July it had “Tents” at Indianapolis numbered at least to 43; by that winter a Centreville lodge was asking the Indiana legislature for a charter; and by the spring of 1846 a lodge was meeting at Cassopolis, Michigan, with four charter members whose names survive. The whole Indiana and Michigan record, with the House Journal pages, is in the Cassopolis case file.

DocumentedIn 1847 a travelling agent for a patent cutting-box came to Bedford, Pennsylvania, “from the west,” and founded a lodge that met in the grand jury room by the light of one tallow candle. Judge William M. Hall, a member, wrote it all down in 1890, down to the hailing sign, the oath and the names of the officers; his chapter is transcribed in full below. In 1849 a lodge at Metropolis, Illinois, kept a record book as “Division No. 110,” and the ritual was printed at the office of the Bowling Green Journal in Missouri.

DocumentedBy March 1852 the order had reached Alexandria, Virginia, where a correspondent of the Gazette “exposed” it as a hand in a vice. A travelling card of “San Antonio Sanhedrim No. 21,” Texas, is dated 30 May 1852, and a lodge room at Columbus, Georgia, was described in December 1852. Ephraim Bee’s town of West Union is first tied to the order in the Weston Herald of November 1853, known only from a quotation of 1931; by 1867 the Wheeling Intelligencer could call Bee “the recognized American head” of the order.
## Be initiated: Bedford, 1847
No ritual of the 1840s survives, but one member wrote down exactly what happened to a candidate. Step inside.

From Judge William M. Hall’s own account of the lodge at Bedford, Pennsylvania, in 1847 (Reminiscences and Sketches, 1890, pp. 121–127). Every quoted word is his.

  1. The door

    Your friend leads you to the courthouse. A sentinel armed with a musket stands in the entry. He raps three times; the door opens an inch, and a stern voice demands: Who is there and what is wanted? By virtue of what authority do you venture into the sacred precincts of the ancient and venerable order of the Ecclampsis Vitis?

  2. The room

    Two inside sentinels with bayoneted muskets take your arms and march you in. It is the grand jury room. The only light is a short piece of tallow candle standing on the table by a spot of its own grease; it serves only to make darkness visible and show the eyes of the circle of members.

  3. The patriarch

    Behind a long table the grand worthy patriarch rises and puts on a hat made of brown paper. The origin of the order, he tells you, was lost in the mist of antiquity. It will nurse you when sick and bury you when dead, and its benefits come without money and without price. How, you will learn in the royal arch degree.

  4. The oath

    You raise your hand and swear to keep the secrets, or else your heart may be cut from your living body and be burned, palpitating, before your eyes.

  5. The first sign

    Place your chin in your hand … Now wave your hand up gracefully in this way three times. And why? That, says the grand worthy, is to keep the oats from falling out.

  6. The grand hailing sign

    Hands at your temples, the fingers upward, like a mule’s ears. Move them backward and forward three times. Now repeat after him: When — shall — we — three — meet — again?

  7. Even now

    Even now, cries the grand worthy, and unrolls before you a large picture of two mules. The room, mute as mice until now, breaks into uproarious shouts of laughter. Some stand dazed; some get mad; in a few minutes everyone is ready to initiate somebody else.

  8. Satisfactory

    There is a torch-light procession behind the Bedford band, the regalia a muslin sash with a star cut out of the heavy purple colored paper that loaf sugar used to come in. It lasts some eight or ten weeks, until Dr. Keyser is initiated, gets furiously mad, and gives the game away. But we had fun — lots of it — while it lasted.
## California, 1852–1904

DocumentedThe first California notice yet found was printed in the San Joaquin Republican at Stockton on 14 April 1852, calling “THE MEMBERS of the E. C. V.” to their hall on the corner of El Dorado and Centre streets. By July the paper called the order “recently established in this city,” and its lodge, David Lodge No. 1, gave money to the Carson Valley road fund. In San Francisco the order met in the District Court room that summer and gave $100 to the firemen. At Murphys in February 1853 it gave $150 toward a school, and met in a room over Buffum’s saloon “built expressly for the purpose.”
{{row:mokhill-1866,placerville-1860s}}

DocumentedThe great years were 1855 and 1856. Lodges, “Sanhedrims” and “encampments” opened at Sacramento, Marysville, Weaverville, Nevada City, Shasta, Downieville, Yreka, San Andreas, Knight’s Ferry, Spanish Flat and Placerville. Members included lawyers and legislators: David S. Terry was Noble Grand Humbug at Stockton in 1855. The ritual was sold by mail at five dollars a set. Brigham Young, the Shasta Courier reported, “has thundered an anathema” against the order.

DocumentedThe fun had a long tail. Lodges opened at Susanville in 1860, Napa in 1862, Bear Valley and Coulterville in 1867, Colusa in 1878 and Cedarville in 1879, and in 1884 the Feather River Bulletin reported that at Sierraville “the Royal Platrix has sounded the hewgag.” But the lodges were thinning. The Calaveras lodge “only slumbers,” a Stockton paper wrote in 1871, its properties lost to fire; at Oroville by 1892 the order was “a thing of the past”; and at Marysville in 1899 “the paraphernalia has been stored away.”

DocumentedSteamboat Jake. The order’s best-loved story comes from Yreka in 1856. Jacob Ehrenbacher paid fifty dollars to join the Odd Fellows, the Masons and the “Eclampus Vitus” at a single sitting; his chanted response “Timbo” became “Steambo,” and the rest is in Harry Wells’s History of Siskiyou County (1881), the earliest source.
{{wide:ecv-initiation-1890}}

## The revival, 1931

DocumentedIn the spring of 1930, by the order’s own history, the idea came to Carl I. Wheat and Leon O. Whitsell; with George Ezra Dane they revived E Clampus Vitus at a luncheon at the Clift Hotel in San Francisco in 1931, with some ten men present. The first chapter was Yerba Buena No. 1. The link to the old order was Adam Lee Moore, an old member of Balaam Lodge at Sierra City, who “assisted and furnished much information on the ritual and general procedure in vogue during the mining days” (Credo quia absurdum, 1949) and was installed as Clampatriarch.

DocumentedThe revived order printed its own books, The Enigmatical Book of Vitus (1934), The Curious Book of Clampus (1935) and others, and played its most famous joke in 1936: the brass plate “found” near San Francisco Bay and hailed as Sir Francis Drake’s was a Clamper in-joke, as Edward Von der Porten and colleagues showed in 2002. Marysville’s 1915 incorporation of the old order passed to the revivers.
## The Clampers today

DocumentedE Clampus Vitus recognises 51 chapters in 11 western states (October 2026), from Yerba Buena No. 1 to the Doc Maynard Chapter No. 54-40 in Washington, chartered in 2006 as the 42nd. Its Grand Council meets each spring at Sonora. It publishes no total of members. The Historical Marker Database lists 1,876 entries in its E Clampus Vitus series (22 October 2026), counting markers the order shares with others; a 2025 study found its hand in at least 149 California Historical Landmark plaques, more than any other group. The red shirts, the hewgag and the cry of “Satisfactory!” carry on.
{{row:bodie-1972,ecv-hotaling-plaque,ecv-clampout}}
## Myth or record? Play along

Every old order gathers stories about itself, and the Clampers have always enjoyed theirs. Here are the twelve most often repeated. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the records show.

“Founded in 1845 by Ephraim Bee.”

No record

No document of 1845 mentions the order. The earliest dated record anywhere is the Connersville letter of February 1846. Bee first appears in connection with the order in 1853, in a Weston paper known only from a 1931 quotation, and then in the Wheeling Intelligencer of 1867. Bee’s own biographer, Boyd Stutler, wrote in 1931 that the ritual was “perhaps” worked out “as early as 1850.” The year 1845 first appears in G. Ezra Dane’s essay of 1938, reasoned from the date of Caleb Cushing’s return from China. Nothing yet found contradicts a founder in the 1840s; nothing yet found names one.

“Bee got his commission from the Emperor of China, through Caleb Cushing.”

An old joke

It is a joke, and an old one. By February 1867 the Wheeling Intelligencer was already reporting that Cushing “is said to be the man who brought the secrets of the order to this country, and communicated them to Mr. Bee,” and that Bee performed the mysteries in Chinese. No commission has ever been produced.

“The order began in California in 1849 or 1850.”

No

The order came to California; it did not begin there. It was on record in Indiana in 1846, in Pennsylvania in 1847 (brought “from the west”), in Missouri and Illinois in 1849, and in Virginia by March 1852. The earliest California record yet found is the Stockton notice of April 1852. The Hangtown lodge of 1850 rests on a newspaper reminiscence of 1896.

“Joe Zumwalt brought it to California.”

Remembered, not recorded

The story was told in his lifetime: in 1898 a Gridley correspondent wrote that J. H. Zumwalt of Mokelumne Hill “enjoys the distinction of being the man who brought the ritual of the Clampers to this State.” The account of how he bought it at Bowling Green, Missouri, in 1849 was printed in 1896. No record of 1849 to 1851 has been found to confirm it.

“Mokelumne Hill Lodge No. 1001 was the first, in 1851.”

Partly

A lodge was at work at Mokelumne Hill by March 1853. The number 1001 is first in print in 1867 and the date 1851 in 1896. Meanwhile Stockton called its own lodge “David Lodge No. 1” and was named in 1853 as “the grand centre and focus of the societies.” Both are probably true in their way: the order’s numbers were part of the joke. Even the plaques disagree: Mokelumne Hill’s (2010) puts Zumwalt’s first chapter there in 1851; Downieville’s (1987) says he founded the first chapter at Downieville.

“The old order died out in the 1880s.”

No

It dwindled, but it never quite died. Sierraville’s Moses Lodge was initiating in 1884 and still in 1904; Marysville revived its lodge in 1888, initiated Lord Sholto Douglas in 1896, and incorporated the order in 1915. An old Sierra City Clamper, Adam Lee Moore, helped revive it in 1931.

“Steamboat Jake was initiated in 1852, for $98.50.”

Later retelling

The earliest source, Harry Wells’s History of Siskiyou County (1881), sets the story at Yreka in 1856. The victim was Jacob Ehrenbacher, who paid fifty dollars to join the Odd Fellows, the Masons and the “Eclampus Vitus” all at once. The date 1852 and the fee of $98.50 come from a 1936 retelling.

“Mark Twain was a Clamper.”

No record

No record of his membership has been found in the California newspapers searched for this page, or in the order’s own histories of 1949 and 1966. The Mark Twain Project dates his hearing of the jumping-frog story to Angel’s Camp in February 1865, from Ben Coon, with no mention of the order. Today’s Samuel L. Clemens Chapter No. 1856 at Winnemucca honours him; a name is not a membership.

“It was a parody of the Odd Fellows and the Masons.”

Of all of them

The earliest descriptions say so in general terms: “in broadest burlesque of legitimate secret organizations” (Cassopolis, written 1875) and “a burlesque on all secret societies” (Bedford, written 1890). Its titles borrowed from several: Bedford’s “worthy patriarch” and “scribe” were the officers of the Sons of Temperance, Indiana’s “Tents” were the Rechabites’, and the “Noble Grand” in Noble Grand Humbug is the Odd Fellows’.

“Drake’s Plate of Brass was a Clamper joke.”

True

The brass plate “found” in 1936 and hailed as Sir Francis Drake’s was made as an in-joke by members of the revived order, aimed at the historian Herbert Bolton. The case was laid out by Edward Von der Porten and colleagues in California History in 2002.

“The name means something.”

Nobody knows

No one has explained it. In March 1852 an Alexandria writer claimed to have discovered the secret: “E. Clampus Vitas, is dog Latin, and means ‘squeezing the life out of you.’” The candidate’s hand, he said, went into a vice. That was a joke too.

“The Staff of Relief and the Poor Blind Candidate are gold-rush terms.”

Not found before 1931

Neither has been found in any nineteenth-century source searched for this page. Both appear in the writings of the revived order. The older words are real: the Noble Grand Humbug from 1852, “Satisfactory” from 1853, the Hall of Comparative Ovations from 1857, the Hewgag from 1884.

“the first Secret Society, of which there is any record”Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875), pp. 253–254 · written by James M. Shepard · the whole passage

The first Secret Society, of which there is any record, was a Lodge of the "Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus," which was instituted in the spring of 1846, with Dr. E. J. Bonine, Laban Harter, J. P. Osborn and Dr. L. Osborn as charter members.

The Order was in broadest burlesque of legitimate secret organizations and was afterward merged in the "Sons of Malta," which died from exposure (by Frank Leslie) in the next decade.

The candidates for admission were bound fast, blindfolded and dragged into the hall by halters. They were placed in the most ludicrous positions and required to pledge themselves to performances and courses of conduct which, by a cunningly devised double entendre in the wording of the pledges, were either impossible or eminently ridiculous.

A peculiarity of human nature, which renders the victim of a "sell" restless and unhappy until he has inveigled others into the same meshes, insured the rapid growth and financial prosperity of this monstrous hoax. Numerous neophites were found to assuage the grief and soothe the wounded pride of the earlier victims.

A grand ball was given by the Lodge in the winter of 1846–7, at the Union Hotel, at which over two hundred badges of the "Ancient and Honorable Order" were displayed, and that, too, by men who stood among the highest in popular esteem and respectability.

The (dis) Order collapsed in 1847, partly from lack of raw material and partly from a growing satiety amounting to disgust on the part of the better portion of the members, but it was successfully resurrected in 1860, under the alias of "The Brothers of Charity."

The second edition, although enlarged and improved, was of "few days and full of trouble" to all except the charter (?) members.

The Ancient and Venerable Order of Ecclampsis VitisWilliam M. Hall, Reminiscences and Sketches, Historical and Biographical (Harrisburg, 1890), pp. 121–127 · Bedford, Pennsylvania, 1847 · the whole chapter

In 1847, while I was reading law, there came to Bedford, from the west, a traveling agent for a patented invention of a cutting-box. He instituted a new secret society called the Ecclampsis Vitis. It was in truth a burlesque on all secret societies—an exaggerated travesty, full of fun and very enjoyable for the younger members. The secret of the thing was wonderfully well kept for many weeks, and the society flourished and had grown to large proportions, with numerous candidates for initiation, at the time of the dénouement, which resulted in its downfall.

The society was constituted with a worthy patriarch and two past grand worthy patriarchs, with out-door sentinels and in-door sentinels, and divers other officers. The ceremony of initiation was formal, solemn and imposing. The place of meeting was the grand jury room of the court house, quite a large room, now divided by a partition into two rooms, one of which is used as the sheriff's office and the other by the recorder of deeds.

Behind a long table sat the grand worthy patriarch, Joe Mann, as homely a specimen of humanity as you could find in a week's travel, who was then a student-at-law. He was supported on either side by the past grand worthies, John Ottinger and Ben Cromwell. The only light in the room was a short piece of tallow candle, which stood in the center of the table in front of the worthy patriarch, without a candle-stick, supported in an upright position by a spot of its own grease, dropped on the table for that purpose. The dim light only served to make darkness visible and show the eyes of the circle of members who sat around on chairs and benches.

The candidate for initiation was conducted by the friend who had proposed him, to the sentinel, who stood, armed with a musket, in the entry on the outside of the door, to whom he made known that he had a candidate duly voted on and now present for induction into the ancient and venerable order of Ecclampsis Vitis; whereupon the outside sentinel rapped thrice upon the door, which was opened an inch or so, and a stern voice from within demanded, "Who is there and what is wanted? By virtue of what authority do you venture into the sacred precincts of the ancient and venerable order of the Ecclampsis Vitis?" When informed in extended language, formal and precise, of the name of the candidate and of the member who vouched for him, the door was opened and the candidate turned over, in the dim light, to the charge of two stalwart inside sentinels, armed with bayoneted muskets, each of whom took him by an arm and marched him up in front of the grand worthy patriarch, whom one of them informed, in stilted language, "Most worthy patriarch of the ancient and venerable order of Ecclampsis Vitis, we present here to you, for initiation into the mysteries and benefits of our most wonderful, and benevolent, and exalted order, Mr. Blank, who is vouched for as being an intelligent, upright and virtuous citizen, free from bodily infirmity, by our most worthy Brother Blank, whose name, having been duly proposed, was voted on, and no single black ball having been cast against him, was duly accepted, and is now present for initiation into the signs and mysteries of our beloved, benevolent, and truly charitable order."

Whereupon the worthy patriarch arose and put on a hat made of brown paper, imposing-looking in the gloom of the room and the fright of the candidate, and in a short address informed the candidate that the origin of the order was lost in the mist of antiquity. That it embraced people of all nations—go where he would, he would find members who would welcome him with charitable hearts and hands to all social privileges. That he would be taken care of in sickness, and if he died he would be buried at the expense of the order. That the society was far superior to other secret societies which made greater pretensions—that it was older, wider spread and particularly that it excelled them in the fact that its benefits were extended without requiring of the members any fees or charges—that it conferred its benefits without money and without price. How it did this was a mystery that he could not then learn, but that hereafter, as he advanced to the royal arch degree, he would know more. That secrecy was essential to the existence and welfare of the society, and the members were all bound by a solemn oath, which would now be administered to him by the grand worthy scribe.

He was then sworn by the uplifted hand, "In the presence of the Great Creator of the universe, from whose all-seeing eye nothing can be hid, you do solemnly pronounce and declare that you will faithfully keep the secrets of the ancient and venerable order of the Ecclampsis Vitis, and you do solemnly agree that if you violate this oath, your heart may be cut from your living body and be burned, palpitating, before your eyes, and your body be disembowled, and quartered, and burned, and the ashes thrown to the four winds of heaven," etc.

The oath being taken, the candidate was again brought before the grand worthy, who said to him, "I will now initiate you into the signs of the order. Wherever you go the broad world around, you will be recognized by these signs by the brethren of the order, and be welcomed with joy. Place your chin in your hand, in this way, inserting the end of your chin between your thumb and forefinger and extending the hand held level in front of the chin." When the candidate had done this, he proceeded, "Now wave your hand up gracefully in this way three times, thus" (showing him, and the candidate doing it). "That," proceeded the grand worthy, "is to keep the oats from falling out."

This was the first intimation of the burlesque except the paper cap, but, in the novelty of the situation and the grave and solemn-looking surroundings and in the dim light, the candidate would fail to notice the intimation of the oats, as he had previously failed to notice the tallow dip and the paper cap. The G. W. P. would then proceed: "I will now teach you the grand hailing sign. Put your hands in this way, as I do." He would then put an extended hand on each side of his head, with his thumbs against his temples and the fingers upward, like a mule's ears, and required the candidate to do the same. "Now move them backward and forward three times, thus." Further addressing the candidate, "You will now repeat after me these words: When—repeat, sir! When—shall—we—three—meet—again?" This being done, raising his hand solemnly, the grand worthy would cry with a loud voice, "Even now," and would unroll in front of the new brother a large picture of two mules, which he was left to look upon, and the initiation was over, amid the uproarious shouts of laughter of the assembled throng, who up to this time had been as mute as mice. Some would stand dazed, some got mad; but in a few minutes all would get over it and be ready to enjoy the fun of initiating somebody else.

Well, we had a torch-light procession all over town and a speech. Jacques W. Johnson, a young lawyer, delivered an oration on the order in the court house. Judge Black was there to hear it, and old Mr. Russell and all the beauty and the chivalry of the village. Johnson's oration was in manuscript, and Judge Black borrowed it and read it through with a great deal of pleasure, he said. He couldn't understand, however, how the society existed without levying contributions on its members; he couldn't possibly see or comprehend where the funds came from. But that was a mystery only to be learned by initiation into the royal arch degree, and the judge did not seem willing to go that far.

John Ottinger and Ben Cromwell were made past grand worthies because of their ability to sit and look wise with grave faces. Nothing would stir the facial expression of either into animation except the immediate prospect of a drop of old rye.

One of the laughable features of the meetings was to call upon P. G. W. Ottinger for a story. During the intervals of initiation, a brother would rise and gravely move that P. G. W. Ottinger now favor the lodge with the narration of some little incident or story from his extensive repertory. This being voted, in response, Ottinger told always the same story, utterly oblivious that he had ever told it before. It became a matter of absorbing interest to see how often he would, with no glimmer of recollection that he had previously told it, retell the story, and as long as the institution survived, some eight or ten weeks, Ottinger repeated, with a grave face, the same little story, and wound up with a peculiar laugh, which contorted his face but gave forth no sound, except a rumble, as if a laugh was rolling around somewhere in the cavities of his capacious abdominal development.

Cromwell rode at the head of the torch-light procession, as chief marshal, on a gray horse. The regalia was a strip of muslin about two yards long and four inches wide, which passed over the right shoulder and was fastened in a knot at the waist on the left side, ornamented with a star cut out of the heavy purple colored paper that loaf sugar used to come in. For the officers the muslin was blue. The torches were balls of candle wick soaked in turpentine and fastened with wire upon upright sticks. The Bedford band headed the procession.

Samuel Shuck was chairman of the committee on regalia, and John H. Filler of the committee on torch lights.

Dr. Keyser was the first man to betray the order. He had been peculiarly anxious for initiation. His name was pending a good while before he was voted in. Somehow we feared he might divulge it, and hesitated to trust him. His anxiety to join sprang from an idea that the order was going to be a great power socially and politically—just the thing for a rising young doctor to belong to.

But Keyser, when initiated, got furiously mad, and would not be placated, and denounced the order as a burlesque. We talked some of drowning him, but didn't do it. Our fun was done for, and the ancient and venerable order of Ecclampsis Vitis passed away forever, so far as the village of Bedford was concerned. But we had fun—lots of it—while it lasted.

[Communicated.] Much curiosity having been expressed in reference to the new order introduced recently into Virginia, called the “E. Clampus Vitas,” [I] am happy to inform the public that I have discovered the secret, and hasten to make it known, notwithstanding the danger I run from the fraternity’s resenting the development. E. Clampus Vitas, is dog Latin, and means “squeezing the life out of you.” The candidate is brought into a room, blindfolded, his hand placed in a vice, and a tremendous wrench given, when the bandage falls off and all the spectators burst into a loud laugh, at the fright [. . .] of the victim. This is the whole cer[emony]. It is expected that this exposure will [. . .] the fraternity of E. Clampus Vitas.

## Where the rest lies
Every substantial source on the order we have found, grouped by what kind of witness it is, with where to read it.

Written at the time, 1846–1904

  • Indiana American (Brookville), 27 Feb 1846; Indiana State Sentinel (Indianapolis), 16 Jul 1846 and 7–14 Jan 1847; Richmond Palladium, 5 Jan 1847. The order in Indiana: Connersville, Tent No. 43, the Centreville bill. Hoosier State Chronicles, free
  • Journal of the House of Representatives of the State of Indiana, 31st session, 1846–47, pp. 259, 272, 345. House bill No. 242, Jackson Lodge of Centreville, and the committee’s report. Internet Archive, free
  • Alexandria Gazette, 13 Mar 1852, p. 2. The order “introduced recently into Virginia”; the “dog Latin” joke. Library of Congress, free
  • California newspapers, 1852–1904: San Joaquin Republican, Daily Alta California, Sacramento Daily Union, Placer Herald, Trinity Journal, Nevada Journal, Shasta Courier, Marysville Daily Appeal, Feather River Bulletin and others. Every California entry in the register, each linked to its page. California Digital Newspaper Collection, free
  • Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, 1 Feb 1867; Cheyenne Leader, 23 Dec 1868; Pacific Commercial Advertiser (Honolulu), 27 May 1882; San Francisco Call, 23 Jan 1896. Bee and Cushing; Boise City; Honolulu; Lord Sholto Douglas at Marysville. Library of Congress, free
  • Frank Leslie’s Illustrated Newspaper, Feb–Mar 1860; Vanity Fair, 25 Feb 1860; Thomas Williams, The Sons of Malta Exposed (New York, 1860). The exposure of the Sons of Malta, into which the Cassopolis order was said to have merged. Internet Archive, free (Leslie’s)

Written down years later

  • Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875), pp. 253–254; Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago, 1882), p. 174. Cassopolis, 1846, written by James M. Shepard. Mathews reprints Rogers and names Shepard; it is not a second witness. Internet Archive, free
  • Harry L. Wells, History of Siskiyou County (Oakland, 1881), pp. 108–112. Yreka’s hall and the initiation of Steamboat Jake, 1856. Internet Archive, free
  • Fariss & Smith, Illustrated History of Plumas, Lassen & Sierra Counties (San Francisco, 1882), p. 471. Sierra City, 1857; the brazen serpent. Internet Archive, free
  • William M. Hall, Reminiscences and Sketches, Historical and Biographical (Harrisburg, 1890), pp. 121–127. Bedford, 1847, by a member. Transcribed in full on this page. Internet Archive, free
  • J. A. Smith, “Early Days in Calaveras County,” Calaveras Prospect, 30 May 1896. Zumwalt, the Bowling Green ritual, Hangtown 1850 and Mokelumne Hill 1851. Reprinted in Credo quia absurdum (1949)

The order’s own histories

  • Boyd B. Stutler, “Ephraim Bee, Grand Gyascutis,” West Virginia Review, Aug 1931. Bee’s life, and “perhaps … as early as 1850.” Reprinted in Credo
  • Carl I. Wheat, The Enigmatical Book of Vitus (Yerba Buena, 1934), and later books of the revived order. The revival’s own first book. HathiTrust
  • G. Ezra Dane, “The Origin of E Clampus Vitus,” Pony Express Courier, 1938; G. Ezra Dane with Beatrice J. Dane, Ghost Town (New York, 1941). The first to date the order to “about 1845”; the Metropolis record book. Internet Archive (borrow)
  • Credo quia absurdum (Placerville, 1949). Documents and trivia: Hall, Stutler, Dane, the 1896 Prospect, Adam Lee Moore. HathiTrust, free
  • Carl I. Wheat, “The Clampers,” Pacific Historical Review 18:1 (1949), 67–69. The revival, by its prime mover. JSTOR
  • Albert Shumate, ECV News from the Miners, 1856–1860 (1960); A Note on ECV in the Gold Fields (1961). Extracts from the 1850s papers; Placerville, 28 Nov 1855. HathiTrust, free
  • Dave Dunlap, R. Coke Wood and others, Then and Now (Stockton, 1966). The order’s history to 1966, and its call for a list of the early lodges. Free from Joaquin Murrieta Chapter No. 13
  • Lois Rather, Men Will Be Boys: The Story of E Clampus Vitus (Oakland, 1980). 150 copies. Not yet read for this page. Huntington Library; her papers at the Bancroft Library
  • Albert Shumate, “The Mysterious History of E Clampus Vitus” (1991); Alan L. Wilson, “A Short History of E Clampus Vitus” (1995). Talks by the order’s historians. Julia C. Bulette Chapter No. 1864

Scholarship

  • Edward Von der Porten and others, “Who Made Drake’s Plate of Brass? Hint: It Wasn’t Francis Drake,” California History 81:2 (2002), 116–133. The 1936 plate as a Clamper in-joke. JSTOR
  • Michelle D.-L. Laguna, Landmarks, Plaques, and Practical Jokes: E Clampus Vitus and Memory Making in California (M.A. thesis, CSU Sacramento, 2025). The plaques; at least 149 California Historical Landmark plaques. Open access

Archives

  • E Clampus Vitus Archives, Mss101, Holt-Atherton Special Collections, University of the Pacific (43.75 linear ft.). The revived order’s papers and photographs. Online Archive of California
  • E Clampus Vitus records, 1933–1984, mssEClamp, Huntington Library. Platrix Chapter and Sidney Platford files. Online Archive of California
  • E Clampus Vitus Records, 1935–1970, LSC.1796, UCLA Library Special Collections. Online Archive of California
  • Boyd B. Stutler Collection, Ms78-1, West Virginia State Archives. Bee’s biographer’s papers. West Virginia Archives
## The poster

The whole story on one page, for a lodge hall, a classroom or a refrigerator door: “E Clampus Vitus on Paper,” 1846 to today, every date from the record. Letter size, landscape; it prints well larger.

stories.headline: The day 3,000 people came to watch one log
stories.short: The day 3,000 came to watch one log
stories.dek: Twenty-four men carried the first log of the Pioneer Log Cabin while a band played. Four weeks later the cabin was finished.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. At half past eight on the morning of 23 May 1923, a black walnut log twenty-six feet long was carried to its place by twenty-four men. A band played and the crowd sang. About three thousand people stood and watched, and many had driven up to fifty miles to be there.
It was the first log of the Cass County Pioneer Log Cabin. A note written on the back of one card of the day says fifty-two volunteers did the first morning’s work.

The logs came from families across the county, given from their own land. Each log was numbered, and a list kept the family’s name, the town and the kind of tree. The card printed for the occasion gives the whole job in one line: May 23 to June 20, 1923. Four weeks, from the first log to Pioneer Day.
The cabin still stands in Cassopolis today, as the Pioneer Log Cabin Museum.

stories.headline: Where Kellogg made its telephone cabinets
stories.dek: For years the oak cases of Kellogg telephones and switchboards were made in Cassopolis. An old postcard shows the plant, the lumber stacked by the railroad, and the words “Cabinet Shops” painted on the wall.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. The card is a real photograph. Long stacks of sawn boards lie in the grass in front, a flatcar stands on the siding, and behind the tracks rise the long, many-windowed buildings of the Kellogg Switchboard & Supply Co. A chimney smokes. On the nearest wall, if you look closely, are the words “Cabinet Shops.”

DocumentedThe company was a Chicago maker of telephones and switchboards, founded in 1897. In August 1906 a Paw Paw newspaper reported that Kellogg would put its new woodworking department in Cassopolis. The citizens of the village were to turn over the land and buildings of the late Cassopolis Drill Co., and the title would pass to Kellogg once it had spent an agreed sum on labour and additions.

DocumentedThe plant grew. In 1909 the trade journal Telephony counted seven buildings with 46,000 square feet. In November 1910 the company filed papers at Lansing for its Cassopolis woodworking plant and said it had a $75,000 plant there, where “the cabinet work for Kellogg switchboards and telephones” was made. By 1915 there were eight buildings, two warehouses and a dry kiln.

DocumentedIn April 1917 the South Bend News-Times reported seventy men at work and six more wanted. There were orders from Italy, from the Dutch East Indies and from the Russian government, and some departments worked until nine at night. That August Telephony walked its readers through an eight-acre plant with a two-acre lumber yard, where tiers of oak waited for the kiln and a new building was going up.
ReadingThe work did not stop with the war. A Kellogg advertising budget printed in Printers’ Ink in 1929 still lists taxes for “Chicago & Cassopolis.”

OpenWhen did the Cassopolis plant close, and what stands on its ground today? Where exactly were the old drill works? If you know, or if you have a Kellogg telephone with a Cassopolis case, write to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: The courthouse that became the Colonial
stories.short: The courthouse that became the Colonial
stories.dek: The Colonial Opera House on a card of 1913 had served Cass County as its courthouse for more than half a century before it was moved across the village.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. A white frame building with tall columns, a pediment and a domed cupola. Across the front, in capitals: THE COLONIAL. The caption, written across the foot of the card, reads “Colonial Opera House, Cassopolis, Mich.” The card dates from 1913.

DocumentedThe building was older than it looks. It was the county’s second courthouse, a two-storey frame building finished in 1841, and for more than half a century it stood on the northeast quarter of the public square. When the stone courthouse replaced it, it was sold and moved to the south side of State Street, west of Broadway. In 1906 the county history found it there “used as a storage house.”

DocumentedBy the time of the card it was a place of entertainment. In April 1917 the high school chorus gave a comic operetta at “the Colonial theater.” The Film Daily Year Book of 1927 lists the Colonial at Cassopolis with 476 seats. It was remodelled in 1937 as the Gem Theatre, showed films until 1960, and was torn down in 1968.

OpenWhen did the old courthouse become an opera house? A theatre history says it opened as the Colonial Opera House in 1899, with 420 seats, and became the Colonial Theatre in 1909. But the county history of 1906 calls it a storage house. And where did the name come from? In 1906 the historian wrote that its lines combined “the Greek temple with Colonial residences.” If you have a programme, a ticket or a diary entry that settles it, write to research@projectscroll.com.
