stories.headline: Race day at the Cassopolis fair grounds
stories.short: Race day at the fair grounds
stories.dek: A horse and sulky on the track, a crowd at the rail and a covered grandstand behind. Whose track was it, and where did the county fair run its races?
body: Cassopolis, Mich. The card is a real photograph taken on the track itself. Men in hats and dark suits stand along the left. A horse in harness, hitched to a light sulky, is being led along the dirt. To the right is a raised judges’ stand, and beyond it a long line of people at the rail. Under the trees at the far end the dust hangs in the air.

DocumentedThe Cass County Agricultural Society was organised in the spring of 1851 and held its first fair that fall. According to the 1906 county history, its grounds had to move three times because of “the right of eminent domain.” Until 1857 the fairs were held on Samuel Graham’s land at Cassopolis. The railroads then took two sites in turn, and in 1871 the society bought twenty acres from Samuel Graham in the north part of the village for $3,000. After the 1884 fair a mortgage on the grounds was foreclosed, and the village of Cassopolis bought the land. In 1906 the village still owned it.

DocumentedThe society held no fairs after 1884. Then, in 1905, “a new organization was effected and held a successful fair.” The Billboard listed the Cassopolis fair for 22 to 25 September 1908. A harness-racing paper of 1916 records a horse that had started at Cassopolis in 1911.

DocumentedThe fair then stopped for three years. In October 1915 the South Bend News-Times reported that the Grangers had brought it back. Tents went up on the Cassopolis fair grounds again, the association got “the neglected race track” into shape, and the state master of the Grange spoke from the grandstand. Baseball and a motorcycle race came first, with horse races to follow on the Thursday and Friday.

OpenWas the track on this card the village’s twenty acres of 1871? Is any of it under today’s fairgrounds on North O’Keefe Street, where the Cass County Fair is still held? If you can place the grandstand, or you have a race programme from these years, write to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: Dr. Goodwin’s hotel on Broadway
stories.dek: A Civil War cavalry captain who became the village doctor built a hotel on Broadway and kept it himself. It took guests into the 1950s, and nothing of it is left.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Three storeys of brick under a mansard roof, with a pointed tower on the corner and HOTEL GOODWIN carved into the parapet. On the card of 1916 a covered wagon and two white horses wait at the kerb, there are striped awnings in the windows, and the last shop on the right has a sign that reads BAKERY.

DocumentedThe man behind the name was Dr. Fairfield Israel Goodwin. He served in the Civil War with Taylor’s Chicago Battery, was wounded at Iuka, and then raised Company C of the 8th Michigan Cavalry as its captain. He took his medical degree at the University of Michigan in 1874 and began to practise at Cassopolis the same year. The county history of 1906 says he was also active in real estate, and adds: “He built Hotel Goodwin and is its landlord.” He died in 1918.

ReadingA walking tour by the county and the Cass District Library’s Local History Branch says he built the hotel probably in 1896–97, in place of an earlier Goodwin hotel of 1887 at 130 South Broadway, a building that still stands. The tour says the Goodwin was a hotel until 1951 and was torn down in the late 1950s or early 1960s. A parking lot in front of Cassopolis Auto Supply is now on the site.

DocumentedIn the autumn of 1920 the hotel was badly damaged by fire, most of all inside. The South Bend News-Times called it “Cassopolis’ only hotel.” Two weeks later contractors had nearly finished the roof, and the proprietor, Carrie Ellis, planned to remodel and reopen within a month.

OpenIn 1906 the county history placed the Goodwin House at the north edge of the old public square, on the west side of Broadway. The walking tour places the hotel near the southwest corner of Broadway and State. Which is right? And in what year did the first guest sign the register? Write to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: Summer on Diamond Lake: Forest Hall and the island
stories.dek: A tennis net on the lawn, a windmill over the roof and the name along the ridge: Forest Hall, 1909. Across the water, a hotel on an island, with a cannon on its grass.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. A tennis net is stretched across the lawn. Players stand at the net with their rackets, others watch from the shade, and a windmill stands above the roof. Along the ridge, in big letters, is the name: FOREST HALL. The card was published in 1909 by O. L. Yerty of Cassopolis, and the caption on its face reads “Forest Hall – Diamond Lake.”
## What Forest Hall was

ReadingThe Diamond Lake Association keeps a timeline of the lake, compiled by Jean Schultz from local sources and crediting Lois Webster Welch’s book A Diamond Sparkles. It says the house began in 1872 as “The Chicago House,” a vacation home on the north shore built by three officials of the Michigan Central Railroad. In 1880 it was renamed Forest Hall and leased as a public resort, and in 1891 a Mr. Rudd and a Dr. Laughton bought it and made it a health resort. A nine-hole golf course was laid out on its grounds in 1921. Forest Hall closed as a resort hotel in 1926 but stayed on as the clubhouse of the Diamond Lake Golf Club, and in 1935 it was torn down and its wood used to build a new clubhouse.

DocumentedThe county history of 1906 bears out the date of 1891. In the life of the hotel’s proprietor, Glover writes: “In 1891 he purchased the Forest Hall Hotel, which he has since been conducting.” He adds that the hotel had become “a favorite summer resort.” Forest Hall was not alone. The association’s timeline counts five resort hotels on the lake by 1900, and Glover describes another of them, Shore Acres, as “an attractive summer hotel.”
## The island

DocumentedThe island was known long before the hotels. Mathews, in 1882, gives Diamond Lake an area of 1,083 acres, and he gives a section of his book to Job Wright, “the recluse of Diamond Lake Island,” and tells of Wright’s prediction of “Harrison’s early death.” The association’s timeline says Wright built a log cabin on the island in 1829 and lived there until he died in 1842.

ReadingThen the summer crowds came. By the association’s timeline, picnic parties were going over to the island in 1873. In 1878 Fred Moon and Colonel Allen built a croquet court, a roller skating rink, an outdoor dance platform and an amphitheater there, and the Cassopolis Vigilant reported in 1879 that there were now enough buildings on the island “to shelter 5000 people from storms.” In 1889 Captain John Bartlett bought the island and took over the Diamond Lake Island Hotel. The hotel closed in 1919, and in 1925 the island was platted for sale as residential lots.

OpenOne postcard in the strip at the top of this site is captioned “The Island House, Diamond Lake, Cassopolis”: a long frame building with a deep porch, young trees along the path, and a field gun on its wheels on the lawn. Was the Island House the same building as the Diamond Lake Island Hotel? Was that the gun fired on the Fourth of July in 1882, when the timeline says the island celebrated “by shooting off fireworks and artillery”? And who was the proprietor Glover wrote about? His life begins on page 755 of Glover. If you know, or have a card or a photograph, write to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: Band night at French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake
stories.dek: A brass band on folding chairs under the trees, a flag strung overhead, and buggies and motor cars drawn up behind. A summer evening at Eagle Lake, on a card of 1912.
body: Edwardsburg, Mich. The band sits in a ring of folding chairs on the bare ground under the trees. The players wear peaked caps, their music is clipped to stands, and the trombones and the big bass drum stand out among the brass. A flag is strung on a line overhead. Around them the crowd stands close: men in shirtsleeves and straw hats, women in white, and in front one man grinning at the camera with a cigar in his teeth. Behind them are horses and a buggy, and motor cars with their tops up.

DocumentedThe words are written across the top of the card: “Band Concert, French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake, Mich.” It is a real-photo postcard of 1912, now in the David V. Tinder Collection at the University of Michigan. No photographer’s name appears on its face.
## French’s

DocumentedEagle Lake is in Ontwa Township, Edwardsburg’s own. The village’s history, as the Edwardsburg Chamber tells it, says that in summer “city folks detrained in the village” and were “driven by horse and carriage to French’s Resort on Eagle Lake.”

The Edwardsburg Area History Museum has gathered the resort’s life in postcards, many of them provided by Floyd Jerdon of Dowagiac. Its gallery has French’s Landing about 1901 and in 1907, French’s Hotel in 1910 and 1911, another band concert at the resort in 1917, and “Hotel French’s, Eagle Lake Resort” still on a card of 1941. The Eagle Lake Sailing Club says it had its “early beginnings in 1936 at French’s Hotel.”
## Open questions

OpenWhich band is this: Edwardsburg’s own, a band from Elkhart or South Bend, or the resort’s? Who was the French of French’s, when did the hotel open, and when did it close? Can you name anyone in the crowd? If you know, or if the band played in your family, write to research@projectscroll.com. The museum on Main Street in Edwardsburg is the place to see the rest of the cards.

stories.headline: Edwardsburg in 1910, through J. Inbody’s camera
stories.dek: A meat market and a bakery, a druggist selling ice cream soda next to the post office, and a frame school with a bell tower. Three cards by an Indiana photographer who made picture postcards.
body: Edwardsburg, Mich. About 1910 a photographer came to Edwardsburg and made three views of the village. Each card has its caption printed in white along the bottom, and each ends with the same two words: “Copr., Inbody.” All three are now at the Library of Congress.

DocumentedElkhart St. A row of frame stores with tin awnings. On the left, the window of a shop selling tobacco and cigars; next along, a sign for a MEAT MARKET and another for a BAKERY. A bicycle leans at the edge of the walk, a man stands under an awning, and a horse and wagon wait further down the street.

DocumentedPost office. The village post office sits in a low frame building beside a brick corner store whose sign reads “B. C. Fisk, Druggist.” Its awnings advertise ICE CREAM SODA and CIGARS. Three people stand at the post office door, and on the fence to the left are show bills dated the 18th of June. The post office itself was old by then: the Chamber’s history says it was set up on 4 December 1828 as St. Joseph, renamed Edwardsburgh on 1 February 1830, closed for a time, restored on 23 August 1841, and lost its final “h” on a postmaster’s order in 1845.

ReadingPublic school. A two-storey frame school with a pedimented front and a bell tower on the roof, standing in an open yard among young trees. The Chamber’s history says a two-storey frame school was built on the north side of Church Street in 1861, and a new brick school on Section Street in 1923. The card is probably the school of 1861, but we have not proved it. Our gallery has a second view of the same building, an Inbody card of 1911.
## Who was J. Inbody?

DocumentedJohn Inbody, born 16 June 1866 and died 10 June 1915. On the back of his own portrait, taken about 1890 at A. J. Dawdy’s studio in Goshen, someone wrote: “He was a photographer, made picture postcards.” The Library of Congress catalogues one of his cards as published by “J. Inbody, Elkhart, Ind.” The site’s gallery holds his cards of Cassopolis, Edwardsburg, Elkhart, Goshen, Bristol and Pine Lake at La Porte, from 1909 to 1915. He worked the valley on both sides of the state line.
OpenWho kept the meat market and the bakery? What show was coming on 18 June? Zoom in on the cards: the smaller signs are there to be read. Send what you find to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: The Newton House, a farmhouse museum near Decatur
stories.dek: One family lived in this Volinia Township house from 1844 to 1930. Today it is a museum, open on the first Sunday of each month from June to September.
body: Volinia Township, Mich. On the 1860 wall map of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien counties, Volinia is the third township along the top row of Cass County. Directly above it, across the heavy county line, is Decatur Township in Van Buren County, and the plan of Decatur village is one of the small insets on the map’s left side. In Volinia, on the Marcellus Highway, stands the Newton House.
## The house

DocumentedBy the Cass County Historical Society’s account, the house was “built by Colonel James Newton in 1844.” In 1868 his son George Newton “commissioned the architect Christian Haefner to design and build an addition,” and the house is “a fine example of nineteenth century Italianate architecture.” The family lived in it until 1930. The state marker on the road, put up in 1977, puts it more briefly: “Designed by Christian Haefner in the 1860s, this house belonged to George Newton, a state legislator.”

DocumentedRogers’s county history of 1875 has the Newtons’ lives. Colonel James Newton was born in England in 1777, came to America as a boy and moved to Ohio in 1804. George was born in Preble County, Ohio, in 1810 and came to Michigan with his father in 1831. George taught the first school in the Higgins schoolhouse, the winter after it was built in 1836, and in 1858 he was elected to the state legislature.

DocumentedIn 1931 Fred Russ bought the house and the timberland around it, and in 1942 the land went to Michigan State University as a gift. It became the Fred Russ Experimental Forest, 580 acres, and the house was restored by the Cass County Historical Commission. A 40-acre stand of oak and hickory in the forest, named Newton Woods after George Newton, was made a National Natural Landmark in 1976. The house was entered on the state register of historic sites in 1974 and on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982.
## Visiting

The Newton House is at 20689 Marcellus Highway, Decatur, and opens its doors on the first Sunday of each month from June to September, 1:00 to 4:30 pm. The 2026 season is over; check the society’s website before you go next summer. Its rooms show daily life across the years the Newtons lived there, and several are set aside for reading and research on the family, the woods around the house and local history. The county has leased the house from the university since 1980; in June 2026 the university’s trustees agreed to sell it to the historical society, and we have not yet been able to confirm that the sale has closed. One more thing to try: open the 1860 map, find Volinia, and see whether the Newton name is on its farms.

stories.headline: The night 3,000 were invited to the Oliver Hotel
stories.dek: James Oliver, the plow maker, built South Bend a grand hotel at Main and Washington. It opened the week before Christmas 1899 and stood until 1967.
body: South Bend, Ind. On the evening of 20 December 1899 the new Oliver Hotel held its first reception. About three thousand invitations had gone out, to South Bend, Chicago and other cities. Palms and cut flowers filled the rooms, a buffet supper was served all evening, and every part of the house was open for guests to look over. The next day it opened to the public.

The host was James Oliver, the South Bend plow maker. With him stood his wife, his son Joseph D. Oliver and his wife, and his only daughter and her husband, George Ford. The Indianapolis Journal’s man in South Bend called it “probably the largest” reception ever given in the city.
## Built for the plow trade

Customers of the plow works came to South Bend from overseas, and until then, the History Museum says, there was nowhere fit to put them up. So the Olivers built a hotel themselves. The first stone of the foundation was laid in July 1898 at the northwest corner of Main and Washington Streets, and James Oliver, then in his seventies, watched over most of the work.

The hotel had 250 guest rooms, and its first manager was Charles Baur, who had come from Terre Haute. It made its own electricity, with three dynamos to light 1,700 lamps. The lobby and rotunda were done in the Italian Renaissance style and trimmed with gold, and sixteen painted women at the top of the rotunda stood for the seasons, the arts and the four elements. The South Bend Tribune called it “the most magnificent hotel in Indiana.”
## What became of it

In later years it was the Pick-Oliver. Its big sign was taken down in November 1957, and in the late summer of 1967 the wrecking ball brought the building down while people on the sidewalk watched. A bank tower went up on the corner, and it is now the Chase Tower. OpenDid you stay at the Oliver, or eat in its dining room? Do you have a menu, a key or a piece of its china? Write to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: City Hall, Mishawaka, and the mayor on the card
stories.short: Mishawaka City Hall and its mayor
stories.dek: A postcard of 1910 names the building and the man in charge of it. Who was Mayor Herzog, and where did his city hall go?
body: Mishawaka, Ind. The card was made in 1910, and its captions do two jobs at once: “City Hall, Mishawaka, Ind.” and, under a portrait set into the sky, “Mayor Herzog.” The building was only six years old. The city had put it up in 1904 at First and Church Streets.

Mishawaka was a young city, too. Its voters had turned the town into a city in 1899 and chosen Manuel Fisher as the first mayor. By the census of 1910 the city held 11,886 people, more than twice as many as in 1900. A new high school and St. Joseph Hospital both opened that year.
## The mayor

DocumentedHe was John A. Herzog, a Democrat, elected in November 1909; the papers printed his name in their lists of the new mayors across Indiana. Herzog was also State Chief Ranger of the Catholic Order of Foresters, and in July 1911 an Indiana paper introduced him as “State Chief Ranger John A. Herzog, mayor of Mishawaka.” The Foresters chose him again in June 1913.

That autumn an earlier mayor, Melville W. Mix, ran again, and the South Bend News-Times said Mix would take up the work “continued along the same lines by Mayor Herzog.” In the election of November 1913 Mix lost by 423 votes to Ralph W. Gaylor, who ran as an independent.
## Where did it go?

OpenThe South Bend Tribune wrote in 2022 that an older city hall on Church Street had stood where the police station is now, and that the city moved its offices to the old Bingham school in 1984. Today City Hall is at 100 Lincolnway West. Was the Church Street building the one on this card? When did it come down? If you know, write to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: Springbrook Park, halfway between two cities
stories.dek: For more than sixty years the park on the river between South Bend and Mishawaka gave the valley baseball, a summer theatre, band concerts and rides. Very little of it is left.
body: South Bend, Ind. In 1901 a Walkerton paper put it in one line: Springbrook Park lay “midway between South Bend and Mishawaka.” It stood on the St. Joseph River, on what is now Lincolnway East. On the card a crowd in summer white walks along a pond, with a pavilion and the frame of a ride behind them.
DocumentedBaseball came early. In June 1896 a team was to play all its games “on the new diamond at Springbrook Park,” and in 1897 the South Bend “Senators” played Whiting there.
## The railway’s park

In June 1899 the papers reported that a vaudeville theatre would be built at the park, and in March 1901 that the railway company would put up a new summer theatre. By 1904 there were matinees at the Springbrook Park Casino. In April 1907, under the headline “White City for South Bend,” the Walkerton Independent reported that the Chicago, South Bend & Northern Indiana Railway, “which owns Springbrook park,” had leased it for ten years to the Interurban Amusement Company, which promised a big theatre, a dancing pavilion and other attractions. In the summer of 1914 there were Sunday band concerts, and families came out for picnic suppers.
## Playland

ReadingIn the 1920s Earl J. “Pete” Redden took over the park and held a contest to rename it, and the winning name was Playland Park. The ballpark stayed. In the years after the Second World War the South Bend Blue Sox of the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League played their home games there.

OpenThe park closed about 1960, and the land later became a golf course and then student housing for Indiana University South Bend. Pieces of the concrete grandstand are said to remain. Did you ride at Playland, or see the Blue Sox play? Do you know the year the gates closed for good? Write to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: Five minutes with Roosevelt at Dowagiac
stories.dek: On Saturday, 30 March 1912, Theodore Roosevelt’s train stopped at Dowagiac on its way across Michigan. Oscar C. Haight’s camera caught the crowd.
body: Dowagiac, Mich. The news came the day before. As the Dowagiac museum’s Steve Arseneau retold it in 2016 from the Dowagiac Daily News, the paper called it an “exclusive announcement”: the former president would halt his special train in Dowagiac “and make a five minute speech from the rear platform.” Few people in the town had ever seen him.

It was Saturday, 30 March 1912, and Roosevelt was campaigning to take the Republican nomination from President Taft. The stores were to close for the visit. A whistle at the water works was to sound when the train left Niles, and the interurban from Benton Harbor and St. Joseph ran a special schedule to bring people in from Berrien County.
## Late, and brief

The train had left Chicago late and came in about an hour behind time, at half past three. Roosevelt began, as the paper reported it, “Ladies, gentlemen and babies,” and spoke for about five minutes, mostly about a bill to give Michigan a primary election. He wished he could stay longer, the paper said, but all he could say was “good luck and good bye.” The Daily News headline read “Monster Crowd Sees Roosevelt: Colonel Talks For 5 Minutes.”
## Twelve hours in Michigan

DocumentedDowagiac was one stop on a long day. A wire story printed in Michigan papers the next week said the colonel put in “12 strenuous hours” in the state, with speeches from the car platform at Kalamazoo, Battle Creek and Ann Arbor. That night he spoke for an hour at the Light Guard armory in Detroit. The hall was full an hour early, about a thousand people waited in the street, and it was announced from the stage that he would speak to them from a balcony of the Hotel Cadillac.

Haight’s card, signed “Haight Photo.”, shows the crowd packed across the tracks by the depot, with the train at the right. OpenIs your family in that crowd? Do you have another photograph of the day, or a copy of the Daily News? Write to research@projectscroll.com.

stories.headline: Who told Shepard?
stories.dek: The only account of the 1846 lodge was written by a man who was a small child when it happened. Somebody told him. Who?
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Everything we know about the lodge of 1846 comes from one account, written by James M. Shepard and printed in Rogers’s History of Cass County in 1875.

Shepard did not see the lodge. He was a small child in 1846 and came to Cassopolis only in September 1868, as the village dentist. When he wrote, about 1875, three of the four charter men could still be found in or near the county: Dr. Evan J. Bonine at Niles, Jordan P. Osborn at Cassopolis, and Dr. Leander Osborn at Vandalia.
And he was not sure of everything he had been told. In the 1875 text the founders are “the charter (?) members,” with his own question mark. Mathews, reprinting the passage in 1882, dropped it.

So Case 1 asks: who told him? A founder, a member, a guest at the ball, the hotel’s keeper? The answer, if it survives, is in the record: in the books, the papers of the 1870s, or the lives of the men themselves.

Case 1 was first opened on 15 October with a different question, whether the lodge ever had a real charter. That question answered itself in Shepard’s own question mark, so the case now asks the one beneath it.

stories.headline: A depot, a water tower and three clues
stories.short: A depot, a water tower, three clues
stories.dek: An old real-photo postcard of a station somewhere in the valley. Can you name the town?
body: A small wooden depot. A water tower on iron legs. A field of tall grass, and not one person in sight. The card’s caption has been cut off, and the station sign blurred.
Clue one. The railroad here was the Michigan Central’s Air Line, which ran from Jackson to Niles.
Clue two. The town is in Cass County, east of Cassopolis.
Clue three. The Air Line came through in 1871, and the station was set up the same year.
stories.reveal: Vandalia. The caption at the foot of the card reads “R.R. Station Vandalia Mich.” The town’s other cards show the same depot with a train at the platform, and with passengers and a baggage cart. The Air Line between Jackson and Niles was abandoned in 1937.

body: Cassopolis, Mich. The old hotel stood at the northwest corner of Broadway and State Street, at the heart of the village.

It was the Union Hotel, where the lodge of 1846 held its grand ball. In 1852 the Masons held their first meeting under the same roof, and on the 1860 wall map of the county the engraver cut one word on its block: HOTEL.
Then, in 1867, the building was hauled across the village and turned into a mill, and a new hotel rose on its ground.
Where did the old hotel end up, and is any of it still standing? That is Case 2 on the board. The first sources are the county histories of 1882 and 1906, free to read online.

stories.headline: Fly over Cassopolis, laser point by laser point
stories.dek: 355,650 real laser points from the 2015 survey, in 3D, with the 1860 town plan laid on the ground.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. In 2015 an aircraft flew over Cass County firing laser pulses at the ground, hundreds of thousands a second, and timing each echo. Every dot in the new model is one of those echoes, from the blocks around the courthouse: 355,650 of them.
The buildings and trees stand where the laser found them, 125,189 points of roofs and 230,461 of trees, over the bare ground of the town.
Press “1860 plan” and the old town plan from the county wall map is laid on the ground beneath them. Raise the heights, tilt it, fly around it, or go full screen.
Fly over it, and you earn the Laser surveyor badge.

stories.headline: Stoves, lures, wagons and guitars
stories.dek: Twenty-three makers from the valley: what they made, how they ended, and where you can still see their work.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. For a century the towns of the valley made things the whole country knew by name.

Round Oak stoves came out of Dowagiac from 1871. James Heddon’s Sons made fishing lures there from 1902. Studebaker built wagons in South Bend, then cars. Gibson made mandolins and guitars in Kalamazoo, and C. G. Conn made band instruments in Elkhart.
The new Made in the Valley page follows twenty-three of them: who founded each one, what it made, when it peaked, how it ended, and the museums where its work is still on show.
Every maker is pinned on a map, and set on a timeline that runs from the 1850s to today.

stories.headline: Company D: the 85 men Dowagiac sent in 1861
stories.dek: Raised at Dowagiac in the summer of 1861: who they were, where they fought, and the nineteen who did not come home.
pic: /img/news/company-d-sixth-michigan
Monument Day, Dowagiac, Mich.: a great crowd around a monument, on a real-photo postcard
Monument Day, Dowagiac, on a real-photo postcard. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan.
body: Dowagiac, Mich. In the summer of 1861 a company was raised at Dowagiac, the second organized in Cass County, under Captain Charles E. Clarke. It became Company D of the Sixth Michigan Infantry.

The regiment gathered at Kalamazoo and left for the East on 30 August 1861, 944 strong. After garrison duty at Baltimore it went to New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, fought at Baton Rouge, and joined the assault on Port Hudson on 27 May 1863, where Lieutenant Frederick J. Clarke was killed. It ended the war as heavy artillery, and was discharged at Jackson, Michigan, on 5 September 1865.
Of its men, four were killed or died of wounds and fifteen died of disease. As in the whole war, sickness killed more of them than battle did.
The roll of all 85 men, as Mathews printed it in 1882, is now on the site, checked line by line against the page scans, with this week’s anniversaries from their service.
sources: Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), pp. 117–120, University of Michigan

stories.headline: Who was in town in 1860?
stories.dek: 331 names from the business directories printed beside the old town plans, with the men of Company D, in one roll you can search.
pic: /img/news/who-was-in-town-in-1860
The Cassopolis business directory beside the village plan on the 1860 wall map: hotels, merchants, physicians and surgeons
The Cassopolis directory beside the village plan, 1860 wall map. Library of Congress.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. Beside each town plan on the old county maps, the mapmakers printed a business directory: the lawyers, doctors, merchants, smiths, hotel keepers and county officers who paid to be listed.
Now 331 of those entries, from Cassopolis, Dowagiac, Niles and Paw Paw in 1860 and Goshen in 1861, are in one roll you can search by surname, trade or town, together with the 85 men of Company D.

A directory is not a census. It lists the people who paid to appear, so most farmers, labourers, women and children are not in it. But a directory line puts a person in a town, in a trade, in a year, and that is often the first step to finding a family.
Every entry links to its map, so you can find the name in the engraving yourself.

stories.headline: Eleven more old postcards
stories.dek: The Pioneer Log Cabin going up in 1923, the depots at Cassopolis and Vandalia, Chicago Street in Edwardsburg, Main Street in Niles and a steam shovel at White Pigeon.
pic: /img/news/eleven-more-old-postcards
Main Street, now Broadway, Cassopolis: a long arched brick block with awnings, on an early postcard
Main Street, now Broadway, Cassopolis, about 1905 to 1912. Private collection.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Eleven more cards have joined the old postcard gallery, all from before 1931 and so in the public domain.

Two show the Pioneer Log Cabin going up in May and June of 1923. There are the Michigan Central depots at Cassopolis and Vandalia, the corner of State and Main in Vandalia, the north side of Chicago Street in Edwardsburg, a crowd on Main Street in Niles, and the long arched block on what was then Main Street, now Broadway, in Cassopolis.
White Pigeon joins the gallery for the first time, with a steam shovel at work on the paper mill track.
Every card can be searched, found on the map, and sent as a postcard of your own.

stories.headline: The harvest trail: a mill, an orchard and the stove town
stories.dek: Stamp three places in your passport this fall, from September to November, and earn the harvest badge.
pic: /img/news/the-harvest-trail
An orchard at its best, near Benton Harbor and St. Joseph, Mich., on a linen postcard
An orchard at its best, near Benton Harbor and St. Joseph, about 1930 to 1945. Boston Public Library, Tichnor Brothers Collection.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. Fall is harvest time in the valley, and the passport has a trail just for it.
The mill. Bonneyville Mill near Bristol, Indiana, a county park around a historic grist mill that still grinds flour, open Tuesday to Sunday until mid-November.
The orchard. Jollay Orchards near Coloma, where the same family has farmed since 1857: u-pick fruit, fresh cider and apple-cinnamon doughnuts.
The stove town. The Dowagiac Area History Museum, free, where the story of the Round Oak Stove Company is told.
Press “I’m here” at all three between September and November of the same year, and the harvest badge is yours. Check each place’s hours before you go.

stories.headline: A paper passport to stamp, and a teachers’ pack
stories.dek: A passport booklet with a stamp box for every place, a one-day field trip for classes, and the valley kitchen as a little book.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. The passport on Project Scroll lives in your phone: press “I’m here” at a museum, a walk stop, a table or a festival, and the stamp lands in it.
Now there is a paper one too. Print the booklet, fold it, and carry it. Every place in the valley has its own stamp box.
For teachers there is a one-day field trip, with the Broadway walk, the Local History Branch and the photo spots, and two worksheets: rephotographing an old postcard, and reading an old record.
And the recipes of the valley kitchen are now a little book to print and keep in the drawer.
pic: /img/news/a-paper-passport
The printable Project Scroll passport: its cover and a page of stamp boxes
The paper passport: the cover, and a page of stamp boxes.
